Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We are inspired to make the analogy and we ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. For two prompts followed by the same continuation, the difference of their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-α}$, where $α=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget faster ($α\approx0.55$--$0.7$) than untrained ones of the same architecture ($α\approx0.2$--$0.5$). For finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits and non-degenerate pre-norm activations, we prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for prompt length $P$ and depth $L$: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} through continuation tokens adds only logarithmic factors. Conditional on the generated text, the prompt's influence on the next token thus vanishes. The bound fixes only the asymptotic shape and is uninformative at the lengths we measure in trained networks; an exactly solvable linear relay model shows that it cannot be improved and accounts for the untrained curves. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training, and training suppresses relay by about one billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A toolkit that measures $α$ for any Hugging Face causal language model is publicly available.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: JointGV: Structure-Aware Correction of Visual World Models with Parallel Graph Dynamics for Long-Horizon Modeling
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: JET: Just-Enough Exploration Tuning for Efficient Tool-Calling Agents in Repository-Level Question Answering
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In repository-level question answering (QA), an agent explores a code repository with tools and should answer a question once enough information is gathered. Nevertheless, we find that LLM agents often continue to invoke tools even after the gathered information is already sufficient to answer. We call this phenomenon over-exploration. Moreover, even though existing methods improve task performance through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on expert trajectories, SFT also propagates the over-exploration in the trajectories to the agent. To mitigate over-exploration, we propose Just-Enough Exploration Tuning (JET), a fine-tuning method that trains the agent to answer once the gathered information is sufficient. JET truncates each training trajectory at the step where the gathered information becomes sufficient, inserts a rationale that explains why the agent can answer at that step, and fine-tunes the agent with a higher loss weight on the rationale. Experiments on two repository-level QA benchmarks with two open-weight 8B models demonstrate that JET reduces tool calls by 11 to 33% on self-generated trajectories while largely preserving the score. On expert trajectories, JET makes 18 to 28% fewer tool calls than SFT while retaining most of the score gain of SFT. In both cases, JET also lowers the inference cost.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2611.20811

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Evaluating and Mitigating Skin Color Bias in Skin Lesion Classificatio
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Skin lesion classifiers may overlook performance disparity because of subtle skin tone variations by treating skin tone as a categorical attribute. This study proposes a method that represents skin tone as a continuous attribute and assigns individual weights to each sample based on its nonlinear relationship with classification performance. Evaluations on two dermatological datasets showed that fairness metrics were sensitive to skin-color categorization. The proposed method also demonstrated more stable fairness improvements than conventional categorical reweighting while generally preserving classification performance.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: DGF-Asym: Adaptive Peer Weighting for Collective Estimation under Noisy and Faulty Sensing
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Collective estimation under unreliable sensing requires robots to adaptively balance personal observations and social information from peers. We propose DGF-Asym, a decentralized collective estimation method extending the DeGroot-Friedkin model with asymmetric peer weighting based on retrospective predictive performance. The method supports consensus formation without prior sensor-noise statistics or explicit fault models while keeping inter-robot communication asynchronous. We evaluate DGF-Asym in simulated collective navigation under noisy observations and time-varying sensor faults. Compared with three baselines, it produces more stable estimates and more reliably sustains the decision criterion, at the cost of longer decision times. However, overall performance depends on fault ratio, group size, and influence-threshold selection. Our results demonstrate the potential of adaptive peer weighting for stable model-free collective estimation under unreliable sensing.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Right Labels, Wrong Reasons: Signed Feature Attribution for Multi-Label Explainability
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: When a multi-label classifier assigns the right labels, it may do so for the wrong reasons. Diffuse feature combinations may vary across classifier families and lack a dominant feature. This paper proposes FLEX (Fisher LDA Explainer), a global surrogate that fits a single direct multi-label Fisher LDA over the full binary label matrix, producing signed feature attribution lists for each label in a single coherent coordinate system. Across the evaluated benchmarks and classifier families, FLEX reproduces the black box's predictions with consistently high fidelity. Pooling covariance across labels outperforms a per-label alternative on most datasets, with the advantage growing largest where labels are numerous and positive examples are scarce. FLEX's fidelity-complexity Pareto curve is monotonically increasing, giving practitioners a predictable path to higher-fidelity explanations as more features are used, and its in-sample fidelity matches or leads Binary Relevance alternatives once a modest feature budget is allowed. The magnitude of each discriminant weight vector bounds its label's separability, flagging labels that may be predicted correctly for the wrong reasons. The evaluated classifiers largely agree on which predictions to make, but reach those decisions through different feature subsets when no single feature dominates.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted at the 2027 IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence (IEEE SSCI 2027), Gold Coast, Australia, February 2027

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: RustMC: Automated Verification of Real-World Concurrent Rust
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: RustMC is a stateless model checker that targets push-button verification of unmodified concurrent Rust programs. As both Rust and C/C++ compile to LLVM IR, RustMC builds on GenMC which provides a verification framework for LLVM IR. This allows verification of Rust code and any foreign function dependencies. In this tool paper we present key implementation challenges, use-cases, and an empirical evaluation of RustMC. The challenges include intercepting threading operations, promoting memory intrinsics, and handling uninitialised accesses, all stemming from Rust's unique compilation strategy. Case studies adapted from real-world programs show RustMC finds concurrency bugs in unsafe Rust code, FFI calls to C/C++, and atomic operations. We evaluate our tool's functionality on the Loom model checker test suite and a set of production-level Rust concurrent data structures.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 1 table

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: How well does graph superoptimization transfer? Adapting tensor-graph superoptimizer to a Triton-based NPU
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: For automatic optimization systems, performance portability across increasingly diverse AI accelerators remains a challenge. We investigate how well graph-level superoptimization transfers across architectures by adapting Mirage from its CUDA-oriented design to the Huawei Ascend 910B3 through a Triton-based compilation stack. We evaluate the adapted system on transformer-relevant workloads, including matrix multiplication, softmax, RMSNorm+MatMul, gated MLP, FNN, and attention. The results show that graph-level optimization can successfully transfer and outperform available reference implementations by up to 87.0% on fused workloads. However, performance is highly dependent on tensor shape and workload structure, with substantial regressions for other configurations. We identify target-specific tensor partitioning, execution-resource modeling, backend lowering and fusion, and search and verification costs as key limitations. Our findings demonstrate that a portable graph representation and programming model do not imply a portable optimization space, motivating modular target-specific mechanisms within otherwise reusable compiler infrastructure.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Accepted for FlagOS Forum at MICRO 2026 - OASIS-AI workshop: Open Compute Architecture and Software Infrastructure for Heterogeneous AI Systems

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Statically Typed Purely Functional Definitional Interpreters for {\it Essentials of Programming Languages}
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Definitional interpreters provide an executable and pedagogically effective way to explain programming language semantics. However, when implemented in a dynamically typed and effectful metalanguage, semantic components such as stores, continuations, handlers, substitutions, and scheduling states may remain implicit in the host-language implementation, making it harder to see how language extensions affect interpreter structure. This paper reconstructs the family of interpreters from \textit{Essentials of Programming Languages} (EOPL) in Haskell, a statically typed and purely functional metalanguage, for pedagogical use. We preserve the object languages, examples, and tests of EOPL while making their semantic components explicit through algebraic data types, evaluator signatures, and explicit semantic domains. Across 15 interpreters and 6 type checkers, language extensions are exposed as systematic type-directed changes.
  The reconstruction is currently used in undergraduate and graduate programming language courses, where students learn interpreter construction through incremental and test-driven development. We further illustrate its pedagogical use through three case studies that progressively extend students' experience: composing mutable state and exception handling, deriving an actor-based interpreter from the typed structure of the EOPL thread interpreter, and translating the CHECKED interpreter and type checker into Rocq to mechanize type safety. Together, the classroom experience and case studies suggest that the reconstruction provides a concrete bridge from learning programming language concepts through executable interpreters to language design and mechanized reasoning.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: The 24th Asian Symposium on Programming Languages and Systems (APLAS 2026)

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Unifying Metatheorem on Weak-Memory Robustness
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Memory models specify the behaviors that concurrent programs may exhibit under compiler and hardware optimizations, which often deviate from Sequential Consistency (SC). Robustness is the property of a program P not exhibiting any weak behaviors when executing under a weak memory model MM, compared to SC. As such, the algorithmic problem of deciding whether $P$ is robust against MM has been studied extensively, and has been repeatedly shown to be in PSPACE for many memory models, such as TSO, PSO, and Release/Acquire. However, each model has required its own, dedicated proof, raising the natural question of whether robustness admits a unifying treatment across memory models.
  In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for a broad class of memory models definable in Kleene Algebra with Tests (KAT). We prove that robustness against any prefix-closed, KAT-definable memory model is in PSPACE. This metatheorem recovers nearly all prior PSPACE robustness results, and establishes PSPACE membership for several new models, including the full RC11 and the OCaml memory model. We have further formalized the correctness of our approach in Lean. On the other hand, we prove that robustness against the KAT-definable Relaxed model is undecidable, and thus prefix-closedness cannot be dropped, in general. Finally, we implement our algorithm in a prototype tool RoboKAT, and demonstrate its flexibility by checking robustness against nine memory models, several of which are not handled by prior work.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 20 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Software artefact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24106993

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Datatypes In, Zippers Out!
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
A zipper represents a focused position in an algebraic data structure together with the context needed to reconstruct the whole. Datatype derivatives determine one-hole context types, but do not by themselves choose a zipper's concrete representation or specify navigation costs and demands. We present Kamot, a tool that converts regular algebraic datatype declarations in a restricted Haskell fragment into zipper implementations with operational contracts. Navigation, replacement, and reconstruction are proved correct against a reference traversal. Kamot supports mutual recursion and regular containers inside containers.
  A compositional analysis derives sound bounds on transitions and constructor demands for certified traversal directions. These bounds are affine in trail depth (the number of saved frames) and guarantee termination of each move on productive, potentially infinite inputs. For inhabited families the analysis is complete: when no move certificate is emitted, no bound depending only on trail depth exists, and some productive input makes a move diverge. We prove that the generated code preserves results and the reference order of constructor matches, including finite prefixes of divergent searches. Lean 4 verifies simulation, bounds, and completeness for finite values of single self-recursive datatypes, in both directions.
  On 19 datatype models and 81 generated families, every generated module passes Haskell type checking, and independent checkers validate certificates, traces, and bounds. In a prefetching workload, starting only searches whose bounds fit a budget answers every local query and avoids discarded source evaluations on long returns, but conservative bounds can lose answers that fuelled search delivers.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues.
  In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: In Proceedings FMAS 2026, arXiv:2611.21375

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Compilation Model for Divergent Parallel Workloads
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Efficient execution on modern parallel machines requires more than abundant parallelism; it demands instruction coherence, memory coherence, and load balance to maximize SIMD utilization and memory bandwidth. Efficiently mapping \textit{divergent} parallel workloads to modern machines, where control flow, memory accesses, and unbounded iteration depend on per-thread runtime values, often requires global program restructuring that trades off increased coherence with reduced locality, parallelism, or extra work. We observe that the key optimizations used to accelerate divergent parallel programs can be expressed as compositions of well-known program transformations from the functional programming and loop optimization communities. We operationalize this insight through \textit{parallel dispatch graphs}: a compilation model that represents divergent programs by representing control flow, data flow between logical stages, and parallel loops within a single abstraction. To facilitate rapid exploration of points in the optimization space, we provide a scheduling language that includes composable transformations of data-dependent control flow and data flow, together with standard loop transformations and hardware bindings. This separation of concerns allows the core algorithm to remain portable, while the execution schedule can be specialized to the specifics of target hardware and input data values. We evaluate our system using popular applications from the domain of spatial computing, and show that the optimization strategies of hand-optimized parallel tree traversals, path tracers, and Monte Carlo PDE solvers can be reproduced as schedules in our system. Our generated code matches or outperforms the hand-optimized implementations (geomeans $1.02$--$2.95\times$ faster). Additionally, we demonstrate empirically that the best schedule varies across programs, machines, and inputs.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Warpline: Binary-Level Tracing and Unified Evidence for Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: LLM agents are becoming GPU kernel engineers, but they still tune kernels without seeing where the time goes. Hardware profilers report how busy each unit was, not where each warp's time went; intra-kernel tracers can show it, but only with hand-placed probes and a recompilation that alters the very kernel being measured. We present Warpline, which gives agents this view automatically while leaving the kernel essentially unchanged. Warpline analyzes the binary to decide which events to record and inserts probes into the binary itself without recompilation or any manual step. It then aligns the trace with hardware profiling data on one unified timeline. Because it needs only the binary, it can regenerate this evidence for every new version of the kernel at whatever level the agent edits it (source, IR, or PTX), closing the optimization loop without human intervention. On NVIDIA B200, across 35 kernels in Triton, CuTe DSL, and CUDA C++, Warpline adds a median overhead of 1.2% and leaves a median 99.9% of executed instructions unchanged, whereas existing tracers have median overheads of 1.6% to 13.2% and leave only 4.6% to 32.7% unchanged. Warpline also traces closed-source kernels, which these tracers cannot. On 10 SOL-ExecBench problems, agents using Warpline spend less time and fewer model requests than a bare coding agent and NVIDIA's Kernel Design Agents (KDA), yet lead both after every round in geometric mean and reach a 7.69$\times$ geometric-mean speedup, against 6.94$\times$ and 6.13$\times$. Two case studies further demonstrate that Warpline reveals hidden bottlenecks and provides actionable optimization insights.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 25 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logic for Computer Science
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logic for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 17 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.3% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Camera-ready version, NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Detecting Empty Abstractions and Pruning Dead Paths in the Linux eBPF Verifier with Abstract Step Functions
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set ($\bot$) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion.
  This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches. We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 23 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity.
  We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: The Best of Times, the Worst of Times: Moment-Based Analysis of Probabilistic Cost Structures
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Many practical costs---such as the completion time of a quantum repeater, the rounds of an RFID collision-resolution protocol, or the response time of a fork--join computation---are described by hierarchical cost expressions: a tree of independent subcomputations with nonnegative integer costs, combined by addition, max, and min. We compute their moments with sound error bounds. Moment-based analyses for additive costs do not apply, because the moments of $\max(X,Y)$ are not determined by those of $X$ and $Y$; propagating full distributions becomes expensive as trees grow; and scalable approximations are hand-derived for specific structures and lack error bounds.
  Our analysis proceeds bottom-up, summarizing each subtree by a surrogate distribution: an exact short-horizon prefix plus a compact parametric tail fitted to preserve the queried moment. Each prefix is computed exactly from the children's prefixes---for a retry, whose cost sums an unbounded number of attempts, by solving a local recurrence equation---so all approximation is confined to the tails. Abstraction introduces shape error but no moment error; nonlinear operators, such as max and min, convert shape error into moment error. The analysis tracks two bounds, one on shape error and one on moment error. Tracking both lets it report a sound interval for the mean, the second moment, and the variance. Lengthening the prefix, or solving subtrees exactly, narrows the interval at the cost of additional computation.
  For quantum-repeater chains of up to 4096 links with high swap-success probability, our Dickens tool bounds the mean completion time within 1%, whereas the exact Markov-chain solution exhausts memory with 16 links, and the best hand-derived approximation we evaluated has 47% error with 64 links. Dickens also bounds second moments, variances, and deadline-miss probabilities, and handles RFID and fork--join costs.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 52 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely ($R^2 > 0.99$) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027)

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 26 pages, 1 figure, 24 tables, including appendices. Code and reproduction artifacts at https://github.com/dqswordman/program-structure-certificates

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: New coding models advertise themselves on score improvements of coding benchmarks. Yet no study has tested if a model that scores higher on these benchmarks gets more real work done. On June 12, 2026, a U.S. export control directive banned access to Claude Fable 5 for 19 days, which forced users to switch to other models. During this time, most former Fable 5 users switched to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro compared to Fable 5). We treat this suspension as a natural experiment, where the people and projects stayed the same and only the model changed, so we could isolate the effect of Fable 5 on user productivity. We tracked GitHub pull requests of 297 Fable 5 users before, during, and after the suspension. We used 8,908 developers who stayed on Opus 4.8 all the time as the control group. We also repeated the comparison across five model upgrades before and after the suspension in 2026 (1,208 developers, 15,442 pull requests). Fitting a difference-in-differences model with developer and date fixed effects, we found that having access to Fable 5 increased the 7-day merge rate of pull requests by only 1.4 percentage points [-1.4; +4.3], which was not statistically significant. Similarly, no significant increases of merge rates were found with the upgrades (weighted mean: -0.9 percentage points [-1.9; +0.2]); all five estimates were negative (95% intervals included 0, did not differ from each other). We also did not observe a significant increase in the number of pull requests merged per week (+2.4% [-4.9%; +10.2%]).
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 20 pages, 4 figures

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Small language models that run on a laptop are attractive for writing signal-processing code offline, but they make systematic errors on digital signal processing (DSP) conventions. We apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to the Gemma 4 edge models E2B and E4B with 66 checked examples covering 11 signal-processing MATLAB subtasks, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized LoRA (QLoRA) on the integrated GPU (iGPU) of a laptop, and deploy the 8-bit integer (int8) models with the adapters through OpenVINO. On held-out variants scored by deterministic checkers, the pass rate rises from 18/66 to 37/66 (LoRA) and 37/66 (QLoRA) for E2B and from 32/66 to 47/66 for E4B (QLoRA). Reading all 159 failing programs shows that the adapters remove most errors of convention, such as the sign of a lag, units and array shapes, but few errors in building signals and noise. Applied at run time, the adapter costs 17-19% of the generation speed.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Identifying and Repairing Energy Smells with Agent Skills
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Energy smells are inefficient implementations that waste energy. Once code reaches production, these smells become costlier and riskier to fix, so energy efficiency checks should shift left, i.e., move earlier in the development lifecycle, to where code is written. Existing energy smell tools rely on fixed static rules and do not measure energy savings, whereas LLM-based optimizers mostly target execution time and rarely ground their changes in concrete smell definitions. To address both limitations, we present DR. GREENS, an agent skill that detects and repairs energy smells in Python code within the developer's coding environment. The skill grounds the coding agent in our taxonomy of 12 energy smells and 65 root causes, augmented with repair guidance drawn from 230 measured cases. The skill also encapsulates a static analyzer and an independent verifier to confirm behavior preservation and energy saving for each attempted repair. We evaluated DR. GREENS in 18 sessions on three open-source repositories, with two models and three skill configurations. Of the 258 measured repairs, 68.6% saved energy, with a median saving of 24.9%. Compared with a baseline skill that lacks the taxonomy, the full skill found more energy smells with verified savings in all three repositories with both models. DR. GREENS helps developers detect energy hotspots and fix them reliably without altering program behavior, which makes energy-efficient development more feasible.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: EmbeWebAgent: Embedding Web Agents into Custom Enterprise UIs
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Most web agents operate at the human interface level, observing screenshots or raw DOM trees without application-level access, which limits robustness and action expressiveness. In enterprise settings, however, explicit control of both the frontend and backend is available. We present EmbeWebAgent, a framework for embedding agents directly into existing UIs using lightweight frontend hooks (curated ARIA and URL-based observations, and a per-page function registry exposed via a WebSocket) and a reusable backend workflow that performs reasoning and takes actions. EmbeWebAgent is stack-agnostic (e.g., React or Angular), supports mixed-granularity actions ranging from GUI primitives to higher-level composites, and orchestrates navigation, manipulation, and domain-specific analytics via MCP tools. Our demo shows minimal retrofitting effort and multi-step behaviors grounded in a live UI setting. Demo Video: https://youtu.be/Cy06Ljee1JQ
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Technical Report; Demo Video: https://youtu.be/Cy06Ljee1JQ

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: stable-envs-v1: Fast and Reproducible Environments with Controllable Variations
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Training World Models (WMs) relies on processing large amounts of high-dimensional data, which typically needs to be stored, read into memory, and moved from memory to compute units. In principle, GPU-native rendering avoids this movement of large image tensors from memory to compute cores, allowing for better GPU utilization, and training speed-ups. Rendering on-demand also allows to control perceptual appearance through the application of visual variations on-the-fly, allowing for higher diversity in training. To this end, we introduce stable-envs, an open-source library for fast, GPU-native rendering allowing to apply controllable variations on multiple simulation environments. By rendering image observations directly on GPU, stable-envs allows end-to-end training speed-ups of up to 1.33x, with no loss of performance. Besides faster training runs, stable-envs also enables reproducible, large-scale evaluations through batched physics while maintaining full determinism. stable-envs currently supports 80 simulation environments across multiple CPU- and GPU-backends, and is openly available at: https://github.com/galilai-group/stable-envs

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that Code-driven PBT misses, while writing 2.4x fewer property tests. Though the two approaches surface a roughly equivalent number of bugs, there is little overlap: nearly 60% of the 169 total bugs are found by only one. Qualitatively, we find that the bugs unique to Spec-Driven PBT tend to violate documented product workflows whereas those to Code-driven PBT instead concentrate on implementation robustness, offering complementary value for bug discovery in agent-written code.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Accepted at the VeriCodeGen Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding at NeurIPS 2026

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Accepted at IAAI-27 (Innovative Applications of AI, co-located with AAAI 2027), Emerging Applications track. 12 pages (6 pages + references and appendix), 2 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RagHarnessDebugger: Jev-Guided Agentic RAG in Contract Inference Repair Auditing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Agentic systems using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must repair their own answers by gathering more evidence, testing alternative policies and deciding if, when, and what repairs are needed. Yet how do we know if a system's repairs are working when metrics like accuracy can be misleading? We present RagHarnessDebugger, a framework that records every repair decision in a Jev-guided harness for contract inference and audits the record to facilitate complete debugging of all decisions taken during a RAG repair journey. RagHarnessDebugger checks that each trace is intact, that each validation applies to the candidate it is counted for, and which answers the acceptance rule can reach. We tested our approach on ContractNLI non-disclosure agreements with two reader models and a replication set of separate contracts. Our debugger's audit layer exposed failure patterns that were hidden under aggregate metrics, policies acceptance cost of repairs vs regressions and policy acceptance gap of 77% and 76% of available but unrealised repairs on development and replication sets. Our audit, together with a labeled error analysis and replay mechanism, allowed following the execution path all the way to the terminal decision - uncovering where missing repairs became lost. Our revised harness improved accuracy over the initial BM25-only baseline by 3.6 points on development contracts and 3.7 points on the replication set, and even improved our full contract access reference score by 1.1 on development and 2.4 on replication set. While our work here demonstrates how the debugger can conduct decision root-cause analysis for missed repairs, the true value lies with providing this debugger for judgment visibility serving continuous improvement of RAG decisions and their explainability.
  Keywords: agentic RAG, AI evidence repair, harness explainability, counterfactual replay, Jev, ContractNLI

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Preprint

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: When Passing Checks Do Not Establish Completion: Evidence Interpretation in Coding Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Verification procedures in coding agents must preserve execution facts, interpret their scope and discharge checking obligations. We study these responsibilities through qualified repository checks, controlled evidence consumers and executable workflows. A prospective thirteen-task factorial study finds that correct reported facts need not yield the requested finite verdict. Conversely, all 122 delivered labels in a held-out receipt-supply study are correct, while sixteen responses misreport facts and eleven others exceed authorized scope. Production repair supplies successful controls and finite-supported preservation failures. Across 118 repair episodes on 31 tasks, source interventions separate startup reachability from repair and witness production from the claimed operation. Lifetime and resource controls delimit what passing validation establishes. Generated-note comparisons yield local repair differences but can state false explanations; strong ordinary baselines, new tasks and Skill-transfer studies supply no consistent overall advantage. These results characterize evidence interpretation, applicability and fulfilled actions while limiting claims of general diagnostic superiority, Skill deterioration or deployed folding effects.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: A Grey Literature Review of Graduate Students' Research Practices and Skills in the LLM Era
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Context: Graduate students in computing now use Large Language Models (LLMs) throughout their research, from literature reviews and coding to data analysis and writing. Yet there is little shared understanding of which skills competent use of these tools requires, so graduate programs struggle to teach, mentor, or assess it, and unverified outputs can propagate into the scientific record.
  Objective: We investigate which LLM-based practices graduate students employ in their research and which skills they need to benefit from these practices.
  Method: We conducted a grey literature review of Reddit discussions. We retrieved 1,383 posts from five research-oriented subreddits, screened them against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed the 54 included posts with thematic analysis, in which two authors independently coded each excerpt.
  Results: We identified seven categories of practices and nine categories of skills. Commenters locate the problem in accepting generated output without inspection rather than in using LLMs, and warn that delegating the effortful parts of a task, such as debugging, reading, or validating sources, delivers the output without building the skill the task was meant to develop. Traditional skills, such as programming and critical thinking, are what allow students to verify what an LLM produces.
  Conclusions: Our categories give graduate programs a concrete basis to teach students to work with LLMs without eroding the skills that research training should build, and they add research-specific skills, such as data sharing and scientific reproducibility, to existing AI competency frameworks.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 12 pages

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Python Code Generation for Isabelle/HOL
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The Isabelle theorem prover provides an environment for formalising mathematics and reasoning about programs. To make verified implementations practically usable, its code generator translates functions expressed in the executable fragment of its logic into conventional programming languages. Its targets have traditionally been functional languages (Standard ML, OCaml, Haskell, and Scala), recently joined by Go. Python, which is becoming the dominant language of scientific computing, data science, and education, has remained out of reach. In this work, we close this gap with a Python backend for Isabelle's code generator. This generator enables verified algorithms to be used in Python applications, or to serve as verified references against which established Python libraries can be differentially tested, without leaving the Python ecosystem. We validate the backend on regression suites covering large parts of the HOL library and by testing six verified data structures and algorithms against established Python libraries. The generated code is slower than hand-written libraries, but well suited as a verified reference.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 20 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables. Software artefact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24106993

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ReBoT-MiCS: Reliability-Aware Bounding Time for Enhancing Timing Behavior of Embedded Mixed-Criticality Systems
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: In Mixed-Criticality (MC) systems, considering multiple Worst-Case Execution Times (WCETs) for the same task, corresponding to different system operation modes, presents a fundamental challenge in MC system design. Identifying suitable WCETs for lower (LO) criticality system operational modes is inherently difficult. Tight low WCET values may trigger frequent mode switches that degrade Quality-of-Service (QoS) by dropping/degrading the lower-criticality tasks and reducing their functionality. However, more conservative values reduce resource efficiency. Moreover, low WCET selection affects exposure assumptions under the adopted transient-fault model, which is used in reliability-aware scheduling analysis. Although some studies have considered low WCET determination to make a reasonable trade-off between processor utilization, mode switching probability and QoS, reliability constraints are typically addressed separately through fault-tolerance mechanisms. This separation overlooks the opportunity to use execution-time bounds as part of design-time reasoning about exposure-related reliability constraints. In this regard, we propose a reliability-aware analytical scheme, named ReBoT-MiCS, to determine low WCETs at design time, jointly balancing utilization, QoS, mode switches, and probabilistic reliability constraints of each task criticality level under a transient-fault exposure model. Experiments conducted with various synthetic and embedded benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme, in which utilization can be improved by up to 27.6% and 11.67% on average, while bounding the mode switching probability by up to 5.48%, and satisfying the specified reliability constraints

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Coordinating integration of multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation codes with design structure matrices
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.
