Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/UEC-InabaLab/CounselTraj.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Gaussian Primitive Fusion for Any-Resolution Multimodal Images
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Multimodal image fusion integrates complementary observations from different modalities into a unified representation. Existing methods typically estimate modality contributions on a common discrete grid. When source modalities have different native resolutions, constructing such a grid generally involves resampling, which may introduce artifacts and affect subsequent fusion decisions. To address this problem, we propose Gaussian Primitive Fusion (GPF), which reformulates heterogeneous-resolution fusion in a shared continuous Gaussian space. Instead of first converting source images to a common resolution, GPF directly fits their native-resolution observations with shared Gaussian geometry and modality-specific content representations, and learns modality contributions within the resulting continuous representation. Once optimized, the fused representation is rendered at the finest native resolution without resampling the sources. With heterogeneous-resolution inputs, GPF produces clearer target contours and finer textures, with less blurring and blocking artifacts than resample-then-fuse pipelines. Quantitatively, it achieves the best results on multiple infrared-visible benchmarks against state-of-the-art fusion methods equipped with interpolation or super-resolution frontends.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Published in Proceedings of the 6th Wikidata Workshop @ ISWC 2026

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 AI Measurement Science Workshop

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent.
  We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 31 pages including appendix

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Composable Rewrites for Layouts of Algebraic Data Types
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Algebraic data types (ADTs) decouple the logical structure of data from physical layout choices that affect performance. For example, packing small fields into a word improves spatial locality, while storing co-accessed fields contiguously can enable vectorization. Such choices reinforce or undermine one another, with ramifications for compiler optimizations and memory management. Their interplay creates a combinatorial space of layouts with different runtime costs and memory footprints. The most favorable layout depends on the program's construction and destruction patterns, the characteristics of input data, and the target machine.
  Exploring this space requires control over layout decisions and a way to compose them while preserving program semantics. We provide both through rewrite rules over layouts, independent of any particular source language or bit-level encoding. Starting from a canonical layout derived from the ADT, these rules transform its representation while leaving the source program intact. We identify a local refinement criterion for proving each rewrite rule correct, so that layouts continue to represent every value and keep distinct values apart. Adding a new rule therefore only requires a proof satisfying this local criterion.
  We realize these rules in Isomer, a new pure functional programming language whose compiler specializes construction, pattern matching, and memory management to the chosen layouts. Using a default layout for all ADTs, Isomer achieves competitive performance against established functional compilers that automatically select layouts. Our rewrites further improve performance by tailoring layouts to each workload, permitting representations that prior work cannot attain or can only achieve through explicit changes to the source code.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Matching-Logic-Based Understanding of Polynomial Functors and their Initial/Final Models Revisited
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Many data types used in programming are initial algebras or final coalgebras of polynomial functors. We show how to specify them uniformly in matching logic, using the representation of polynomial functors as unary container functors $X\mapsto\sum_{a:A}X^{B[a]}$. For each container functor, we give a matching logic theory of its initial algebra and one of its final coalgebra. Besides the no-junk and no-confusion axioms and their duals, these theories include axioms about the elements that represent functions, for the initial algebra, and a bisimilarity axiom and a realisation axiom, for the final coalgebra; the existence axioms use free set variables to range over all subsets of a model. We prove that, in every model, the algebra extracted from the model is an initial algebra (a W-type) and the extracted coalgebra is a final coalgebra (an M-type) of the container extracted from the model, i.e., the one given by the model's interpretation of the shapes and positions, and that such models exist. So the data types are captured relative to the interpretation of the sorts of shapes and positions, and absolutely whenever these sorts are fixed by auxiliary specifications, which we show for finite sets, products, dependent sums, and (co)inductive sorts built from them. We derive the induction, coinduction, and bisimulation principles as theorems, and illustrate the approach on lists and on Moore machines. This paper revises and substantially extends a paper published in EPTCS 389 (FROM 2023): several axioms are corrected, and the adequacy and satisfiability proofs are new.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 44 pages. Revised and substantially extended version of arXiv:2309.13798 (EPTCS 389, FROM 2023); Appendix C lists the changes

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level.
  In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it.
  Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 19 pages, 13 figures, 1 table

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: DatalogBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Text-to-Datalog Synthesis
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Datalog underpins reasoning tasks such as program analysis, but its programs are hard to write. Existing synthesizers automate this task but require users to state their intent as input-output examples. Large language models (LLMs) suggest a more natural route, text-to-Datalog synthesis from a natural-language question, yet how well they do so has not been systematically evaluated. We present DatalogBench, a benchmark of 136 text-to-Datalog synthesis tasks curated from existing Datalog-based artifacts. Synthesized programs are graded by execution on held-out inputs against an oracle validated by mutation analysis. Across six LLMs and four prompting configurations, exact match peaks at 75.7%; an input-output example raises it by about six points, while relation descriptions add little. Under direct prompting, most failures occur at compile time, typically because a model invents auxiliary predicates that it never declares or types consistently. Two coding agents reach up to 86.8% and eliminate nearly all such failures, leaving mostly semantic errors concentrated in recursive tasks. DatalogBench thus identifies recursive reasoning and decomposition as open challenges for current LLMs and agents, and offers a reliable, execution-grounded measure of both.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 36 pages, 3 figures

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Mode Inference for Substructural Adjoint Types
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Adjoint types [Jang et al. 2024] provide a method of mixing substructural modes (for example, linear, affine, strict, or unrestricted) in a type system while preserving the proof-theoretic and computational properties of each mode. Uses of such a system include performing compiler optimizations or providing safety guarantees on parts of a program whose modes support them, while not restricting the programmer's ability to write other code as they usually do. However, Jang et al.'s algorithmic type system is monomorphic in the modes, requiring the programmer to anticipate a potentially large number of combinations of modes, and possibly copy code to conform to each of them.
  In this paper we define a mode inference algorithm for programs with adjoint types that produces principal modes, summarizing all possible substructural modes of a function in a simple constraint language. This removes the burden from the programmer to a priori analyze the substructural properties of their code, and, furthermore, allows a single function definition to subsume all its instances at different modes. We show that our system is sound and complete with respect to a mild restriction of Jang et al.'s monomorphic version.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 7 pages, 7 figures

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: MLIR-MRacle: Memory-Model-Aware Metamorphic Fuzzing of Concurrent MLIR
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Multi-level compilers built on MLIR lower concurrent programs through many stages towards targets with potentially drastically different memory models, where an optimisation which appears reasonable, can silently change program behaviour. Testing these lowerings is hard: a concurrent program often has no single expected outcome, and existing MLIR fuzzers often assume determinism. We present MLIR-MRacle, a memory-model-aware metamorphic fuzzer for concurrent MLIR programs. MLIR-MRacle applies metamorphic relations gated by the target memory model, so that both the original and transformed programs remain well defined - executing both repeatedly, and comparing their outcome sets or distributions withone of two statistical oracles. A coverage guided campaign driver built on libafl is used to perform continuous fuzzing. MRs, memory models, oracles, and execution backends all provide extension points for future researchers and compiler engineers to build off this package. In a case study on Armv8 hardware, MLIR-MRacle ran over 145k trials across four configurations, reaching up to 93.6k compiler coverage edges, and found a bug in the OpenMP dialect verifier that has since been fixed upstream. Video: https://youtu.be/lKtGk0H97Ts?si=dWLUHl2CJ24ep6JY
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 4 pages, 1 figure

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it.
  On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns.
  Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Everything Beneath the Policy. Code, specification, and every experiment's protocol, logs and findings: https://github.com/PlugRL

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: The Limit Is in the Input, Not the Model: State-Dependent Command Safety in Natural-Language Interfaces to Industrial Controllers
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Language models judging commands to industrial controllers may not receive machine state, the equipment's current condition. The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed commands and another always denied them. Their overall (raw) accuracies differed by 32 percentage points; both scored 50% balanced accuracy, which weights safe and unsafe cases equally, and no correct pairs. A rule evaluator matched all 15 pairs by applying the same rules that supplied the expected answers; this is not an independent safety test. The audit complements systems that check actions against safety rules: it checks whether the model receives the information needed for those decisions. This helps evaluators separate missing-input problems from model errors. These small-sample scores do not establish general model reliability.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 8 pages. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (ICDMW), 6th Machine Learning for Cybersecurity (MLC) Workshop

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the $(k+q)$-th power of its size, where $k$ is the dimension of the integration domain and $q$ is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Analysis of Commit Signing on GitHub
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Since 1999, the security community has known that managing cryptographic keys is hard for users of cryptographic systems. Git lets software developers use private keys they control to digitally sign the commits that record their code changes to a repository. This practice offers a rare opportunity to study how a large community manages cryptographic keys in everyday work. In this paper, we study end-to-end commit signing, using GitHub accounts as our sampling unit. Our 2% stratified sample of the GitHub population comprises 2,737,649 accounts, 71,694 of which have made at least one commit. For these accounts, we analyze 16,112,439 commits across 874,198 repositories and collect 208,546 public keys uploaded to the sampled accounts. We examine developers' signing key usage patterns and compare our findings with those of prior commit signing studies, most of which used repository-based samples and paid less attention to key management. We then outline a path toward more usable key management for developers.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 29 pages, 4 tables, 5 figures

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Prior Knowledge or Search? A Study of LLM Agents in Hardware-Aware Code Optimization
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM discovery and optimization systems are increasingly applied across domains, implementing a common propose-evaluate-revise loop. Such optimization or discovery progresses via context conditioning on received feedback from an environment. However, as modern LLM agents are increasingly complex in their structure, it is difficult to evaluate which components contribute the most, and when and how this exploration may fail. We answer these questions through three controlled experiments. Our findings: (1) In pure black-box optimization, LLMs act as greedy optimizers. (2) In zero-shot kernel generation, providing explicit input-size information has no measurable effect, models converge to the same kernel parameters regardless of size or temperature, as though the size instruction were invisible. Moreover, when tasked to perform kernel optimization for uncommon kernel sizes, performance sharply degrades regardless of the language used. (3) In feedback-loop kernel optimization, CUDA improves monotonically under iterative feedback, while TVM IR actively degrades, which demonstrates that kernel optimization degrades when models operate with low-density language. Our results conclude that LLMs in code optimization tasks highly depend on pretrained priors rather than provided feedback or agentic structure.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Presented at NeurIPS Workshops: (1) Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond, and (2) The 1st Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) at NeurIPS 2026

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 21 pages, 9 figures

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Accepted as main track paper at International Conference on Process Mining (ICPM) 2027

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Who Is Behind the Harness? Verifying Model Identity in Coding Agents through Behavioral Fingerprinting
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
LLMs increasingly operate through coding-agent harnesses that inspect repositories, invoke tools, and modify files. Substituting the model behind such an agent can therefore change security-relevant decisions, including whether it verifies changes or recovers safely from failures. Existing LLM fingerprints largely infer identity from direct text or token distributions. In coding agents, these signals are mediated by system instructions, controller logic, tools, and execution feedback, limiting their transfer.
  We present LIDAR (LLM Identification from Decisions and Actions at Runtime), an active black-box fingerprinting method for coding-agent execution. Three coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification--test conflict resolution under controlled changes. LIDAR represents the resulting trajectories with complementary instance-level and distribution-level features and compares them with clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier. It requires no access to model weights, logits, or provider internals.
  We evaluate 24 models from eight families on OpenCode, OpenHands, and mini-swe-agent, fitting separate references for each harness. Closed-set Top-1 accuracy ranges from 91.39\% to 98.89\% across the three harnesses, exceeding all three baselines in each setting. When the audit also includes unregistered models from the same families, balanced accuracy ranges from 79.58\% to 80.42\%. These results show that agent execution behavior provides model-identity evidence beyond final outputs.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A coding agent is a language model inside a harness: the system prompt, the tools, and the context management that let a chat model work in a repository. Most of the engineering on these agents goes into the harness, and vendors and leaderboards credit it with score gains. Earlier studies have fixed the model and swapped the harness, but have not measured whether the swap changes the pass rate more than running the same harness again. We run seven models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified and two benchmarks of other kinds, and rerun them unchanged. No harness leads consistently across models. Where the data can bound the difference between two harnesses, the bound is 2 to 5 points, and a harness swap changes about as many task outcomes as a rerun. The exceptions are harness effects in particular pairings of model and harness, whose direction changes with the model: OpenCode trails by 8 to 9 points on one model and leads by 14 on another. Cost differences between harnesses also depend on the model, from under 10% to 3 to 4 times. Which harness is better therefore has no answer apart from the model, and a harness difference should be reported next to a rerun.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Hearsay: Who Can Audit the Record a Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The record of an agent's run is written by the harness that drives the agent. When the run is later disputed, the auditor was not there and has only this record. We ask whether someone who was not there can check the record, and what decides the answer. It depends on who wrote what a check can rely on: if the harness wrote all of it, the record is only the harness's own word, and we call it hearsay. We build Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, model examiners from three vendors and a human panel read the records and answer questions about the runs, and every passage they cite is labelled mechanically by who wrote it. We also audit what is deployed: in all sixteen frameworks, the harness is the only writer. With one writer, readers can name the fault from the record, in up to nine runs in ten, but they cannot check the record. The model examiners claim corroboration for 18 to 55 points more of their evidence than the labels support, a gap we then predicted for runs driven by another vendor's model and found again. And the best of them notices only half of the alterations we make to a record, while the two that name the fault most often cannot tell what a harness left out. With a second writer, the record can be checked. Our sandbox keeps a ledger of what passes between harness and model, and reading the ledger against the record in both directions shows what the record leaves out and what it adds. We test this as an auditor would use it, on one unseen record at a time. On runs driven by a third vendor's model, with every rule committed before the records existed, it reports 64 of 66 alterations and flags none of 84 clean records. On held-out records in five formats it reports 109 of 115. What makes a record evidence is a second writer, not a better reader.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Exploring multimodal AI--XR interactions for software development: From expert perspectives to semantic code outlines
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI tools can generate code quickly, but developers still need to understand and check the results. We explore how the enriched multimodal context derived from the extended reality (XR) workspace might help developers manage this information. We first interviewed 13 experts in AI, XR, and related fields to identify opportunities and design challenges (Study 1). These interviews informed two prototypes explored with 12 professional developers (Study 2): four tried a version where the code faded to become invisible after it was looked at, and eight tried a version that replaced viewed code sections with short descriptions of their purpose. In the second prototype, head direction helped determine when to offer a change, while manual input let developers apply it and reopen the original code. A separate open-ended demonstration with seven software-engineering researchers provided complementary feedback. Participants' accounts suggested that descriptions could provide an overview of unfamiliar code and serve as reminders when revisiting it. However, difficulty comparing descriptions with source code, headset limitations, and controls that deviates from regular IDE routines could introduce additional effort. These exploratory findings identify requirements for attention support: make summaries easy to recognize and access, preserve straightforward inspection of the original code, and retain familiar navigation and editing practices. The study contributes to human-centered multimodal systems by showing how the coordination of input channels and AI-generated representations must account for users' attention, verification needs, and established ways of working.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy.
  We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Keeping Up with the Kernel: Can LLMs Adapt Linux Drivers to Interface Changes?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: We analyze collateral evolution in Linux, the coordinated updates that drivers require when the kernel interfaces they depend on change, over the 20 years since it was first studied, covering releases from v3.0 to v7.2. Since v2.6.13, the number of driver files and support libraries has grown about eightfold, a single change to the most widely used library can now reach about 5.3k driver files, and such changes arrive either in bursts or spread over many releases. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that asks models to adapt an old driver module to a target kernel and evaluates the result against the developer's reference patch. The benchmark contains 316 manually confirmed tasks from 202 mainline commits and 268 modules, spanning kernel releases v6.19 to v7.2. It distinguishes 134 build-breaking tasks, where the old driver fails to compile, from 182 build-compatible tasks, where the old usage still builds. Using CoEvoAgent, we evaluate Direct, SmPL, and mini-SWE-agent with DeepSeek Flash, and compare Direct with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol. With DeepSeek, default Direct generation achieves strict reference agreement on 41.0% of build-breaking tasks but only 3.3% of build-compatible tasks.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: The Comprehension Gap in LLM-Assisted Software Development: An Experiment
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. Participants needed significantly less time to solve programming tasks when working with the LLM. However, participants with high reliance on the LLM chat and low task engagement showed significantly decreased comprehension. Our qualitative results show great variability in individual perspectives on comprehension differences and strategies to mitigate issues. Strategies for dealing with comprehension differences range from accepting comprehension differences to adapting their LLM interactions or avoiding the tools altogether. Our results warrant further investigation into cognitive debt in larger systems and developer practices to mitigate issues.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: OmegaHyper: Explicit-State HyperLTL Model Checking on an omega-Automaton Diet
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: HyperLTL extends LTL with quantification over traces. AUtoHyper is the de facto explicit-state model checker for HyperLTL, complete for an arbitrary quantifier prefix: it eliminates quantifiers through products of the formula's omega-automaton with the systems, complementing on quantifier alternations. However, it suffers from state explosion, as it fully materializes input systems and intermediate automata. We present OmegaHyper, an overhaul of AutoHyper that keeps its algorithm but decomposes and reduces the size of the processed automata, and integrates the Kofola omega-automaton complementation tool. We compare OmegaHyper with existing explicit-state and symbolic HyperLTL model checkers, on 120 benchmarks from their published suites. OmegaHyper improves the performance of explicit-state HyperLTL model checking by up to orders of magnitude; bounded symbolic tools still reach further on violated instances with short counterexamples, as expected.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: MemoSync: Co-Managing Developer-Agent Metamemory Across Contexts
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI coding agents increasingly manage what context carries across sessions and projects, but developers have limited visibility into what these agents store, retrieve, and apply. This opacity creates a metamemory problem: the developer's meta-level judgments about what should be remembered are separated from the agent's object-level memory operations, disrupting the monitoring and control that keep the two levels aligned. We conducted a formative study with 12 developers and identified what they want to monitor and control across four dimensions of agent memory use. Based on these findings, we designed MemoSync, a co-management system that treats agent memory as a shared, operable representation: the agent proposes memory candidates and reports which items it uses, and the developer reviews, edits, and scopes them. In a between-subjects study (N=132) against two baselines, MemoSync participants achieved significantly higher task performance and the highest mean developer-agent memory alignment. In an exploratory mediation analysis, the alignment advantage was primarily driven by improved monitoring accuracy. Despite performing substantially more monitoring and control actions, participants reported no increase in perceived workload. A week-long deployment with nine developers showed that memory monitoring and control fit into everyday development work. MemoSync is open-sourced at https://github.com/SLEEPYBQ/MemoSync.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Assessing Vision-Language Models for Early Prediction of Unsafe Situations in Robotics
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process visual information and textual instructions and, by using their ability to understand and reason about context, are well-suited for predicting robot failures before they occur. However, evidence supporting this remains limited. To address this, we present an empirical evaluation of VLMs for predicting robot failures. In particular, we experiment with Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies (HuRoN, Pal Robotics, and CrowdBot), analyzing both video and odometry data for early failure warning (i.e., before an unsafe situation occurs). Specifically, we evaluate their performance in classifying situations as safe, potentially unsafe, and unsafe, together with uncertainty quantified using various metrics, and study the relationship between uncertainty and performance. Our results showed that Qwen provides the strongest overall classification and prediction-reliability performance, while InternVL shows stronger early-warning capability in several configurations. The results further show that the effect of robot-state information and temporal history depends on the model and evaluation objective. Overall, our findings indicate that general-purpose VLMs can support early robot-safety monitoring, but the most suitable configuration depends on whether the priority is accurate assessment of safety-state, reliable confidence and uncertainty, or timely warning before unsafe events.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Characterizing GitHub Security Actions Alerts For Web Application Tutorials
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The high frequency of cybersecurity incidents involving web applications highlights the importance of secure software development practices. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools help identify potential vulnerabilities in source code without executing the code. Integrating SAST tools into GitHub Security Actions enables security alerts to be reported during development. However, the characteristics of these alerts can make them difficult for developers with limited security expertise to understand, prioritize, and address. Many tutorials for learning web application development also involve source code with security implications. We investigated the properties of SAST alerts relevant to this learning context. We analyzed 6,609 alerts from four default GitHub Security Actions configurations across 60 Django and Spring tutorial repositories. We evaluated the alerts along four dimensions: alert volume, alert relevance, conceptual breadth, and remediation usability. Of the 6,609 alerts, 3,750 (56.7\%) targeted tutorial-related files, while 2,859 (43.3\%) targeted other repository files. The configurations triggered between 34 and 646 distinct rules, and the five most frequently triggered rules accounted for 25.2\%--68.2\% of alerts, depending on the configuration. Across configurations, 0.4\%--32.1\% of alert messages named concrete framework or code constructs, and 0\%--8.1\% met our operational criteria for remediation specificity. Overall, default GitHub Security Actions report a diverse set of security alerts, but these alerts do not consistently focus on tutorial code or provide concrete guidance for addressing the reported issues.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Live Noise Fingerprints for Quantum Program Analysis
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Quantum programs are probabilistic in nature, and noisy execution due to current imperfect hardware further complicates their analysis. In this paper, we study abstract semantics for analysing quantum programs under these conditions. We introduce noise fingerprints, compact descriptions of the observable effects of noise relative to a finite interface of input states and output measurements. We use them to define our abstract domain with respect to the concrete noise-related behaviour. We relate the concrete and abstract domains through a probabilistic Galois connection, extending the Galois-connection framework to distribution-valued interpretations. We study the resulting abstraction in terms of observational soundness, conciseness, efficiency, and ability to adapt to changing noise. We show that polynomial-size interfaces yield exponentially smaller fingerprints than full noise models while preserving the chosen observations, and that fingerprint distance characterises the largest observational discrepancy over the chosen interface. Further, we develop ChanShadow, which reuses noise fingerprints of commonly used short program fragments to analyse noisy execution of whole programs and provides a uniform finite-sample error bound. We construct working examples showing how fingerprints support program analysis. We evaluate fingerprint precision, representation cost, measurement requirements, and behaviour under noise drift. On a synthetic benchmark, fingerprints retain $(99 \pm 1)\%$ of the noise strength information of a full noise model. On simulated noise drift, reusing earlier measurements reduces the number of fresh measurement rounds needed to reach an error tolerance of $0.10$ by a factor of $2.3$ at $95\%$ confidence and by a factor of $27$ under the median-error criterion.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Quantifying the Intrusiveness of Retrofitting Retrieval-Augmented Generation onto Legacy Software Systems
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Enterprises increasingly add retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to existing REST and monolithic systems, usually by writing an ad hoc HTTP call into a handler, and have no way to quantify how intrusive that choice is. We present (1) a taxonomy of three retrofit patterns, sidecar, SDK-embed and naive-invasive; (2) the Legacy Intrusion Score (LIS), three code sub-metrics (churn, breadth, coupling), and an extension, LIS-X, with three operational sub-metrics measured on a live system (run-time overhead, fault propagation and silent feature degradation); (3) a static evaluation on five legacy systems, two of them real open-source codebases fetched from their repositories at pinned commits; and (4) a live case study that deploys all three patterns as separate OS processes. The code-level ranking sidecar < SDK-embed < naive-invasive holds in all five systems and under 2,000 random weightings, but it follows from component-wise dominance of the sub-metrics, so it validates the metric rather than testing a hypothesis. In the live study, outcomes are not fixed by definition. The sidecar adds no detectable latency to the legacy endpoint (0.07 ms, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.24]), whereas SDK-embed and naive-invasive add 569 and 475 ms and are not distinguishable from each other (p=0.62). Both pass a 2 s dependency delay on to legacy requests, and when the RAG layer fails fast they keep returning successful responses that no longer contain the AI field. Load on the RAG layer slows the legacy service by 1.51-1.57x on a shared host, and sidecar staleness averages 911 ms with a 2 s polling interval. Retrieval hit@1 is 0.95; three hosted LLMs answer all 12 test questions correctly and a local model 9/12, and the four backends are swapped by changing one request field. All dynamic results come from one host and one system.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Inference-Time Scaling in Agentic Hardware Verification Workflows: A Multi-Strategy Characterization Across Protocol Complexity
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Inference-time scaling, allocating more compute during generation rather than pre-training, has demonstrated dramatic quality improvements for LLM reasoning tasks. Its behaviour in structured hardware verification code generation, where outputs must satisfy compiler correctness, protocol semantics, and functional coverage constraints simultaneously, is less understood. We present a systematic, simulator-grounded study of inference-time compute scaling for agentic UVM testbench synthesis targeting AMBA protocol bridges. Four inference strategies---zero-shot (\$0.04), raw-feedback iterative (\$0.81), structured inner-loop (\$0.95), and full dual-loop agentic synthesis (\$1.06)---are evaluated across four AMBA targets (Protocol Complexity Index 11.8--22.6) using the Protocol Verification Completeness (PVC) metric, functional coverage, and a six-class UVM error taxonomy (E1--E6). Our central finding is that structured diagnostic feedback acts as an inference-time compute multiplier: the structured inner loop yields roughly $15\times$ more PVC per inference dollar than raw EDA-tool feedback (marginal efficiency, S1$\to$S2 vs. S0$\to$S1). The mechanism is fault targeting, not token reduction: raw compiler feedback drives the testbench to compile but cannot surface functional protocol faults that leave the code syntactically valid, whereas structured E1--E6 bundles diagnose and resolve them. All outputs are judged by a cycle-accurate Mentor Questa toolchain rather than by model self-assessment; the dual-loop strategy reaches PVC $\geq$ 0.95 with zero scoreboard errors on every target, and the generated environments surfaced a latent RTL bug in two of the four reference designs. These results establish a principled compute-quality trade-off curve for LLM-aided verification environment generation and motivate inference-budget-aware deployment strategies for industrial EDA workflows.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SWE-growth: Teacher-Guided Adaptive Self-Play for Software Engineering Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Self-play offers a scalable way to train software engineering agents by generating repository-level repair tasks. However, with binary repair rewards and finite rollout budgets, all-fail groups provide no reward-based group-relative advantage. Such tasks may still offer learning opportunities when a Teacher can provide verified repairs absent from the Student's own attempts. We introduce SWE-Growth, a teacher-guided adaptive self-play framework that uses verified Teacher outcomes to identify learning opportunities for the current Student. Tasks with all students failure but reliable Teacher success provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and post-SFT Student rollouts identify mixed-outcome tasks with a positive Teacher--Student gap for reinforcement learning. Task eligibility also guides Injector updates, connecting Student training with subsequent task generation. Starting from 101 seed issues, \textsc{SWE-Growth} improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 27.7% to 31.7% on SWE-bench Pro and from 11.0% to 17.2% on held-out TerminalBench 2.1 by Round~2. It exceeds Student-only self-play by 2.6 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, and Teacher-augmented self-play by 1.8 and 2.5 points under approximately matched budgets. These results support adapting both supervision and task selection to the Student's evolving repair capability.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). To distinguish different causes of UDC, we introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG), a diagnostic protocol that separates the identification of unresolved decisions, their resolution using evidence, and their translation into executable code. By examining each stage separately, we can determine where the decisions responsible for incorrect results were first missed or mishandled. We evaluate this framework on BIRD-Pandas with twelve models. The results show that answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors remain. Our findings suggest that the main difficulty lies not in answering clarification questions, but in recognizing which questions need to be asked in the first place.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Re-Testing LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translations Against Their Original C
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Most C-to-Rust translators use large language models (LLMs), and each reports a success rate from its own correctness check. We survey 34 C-to-Rust translators that use LLMs. Only one reports testing its check, and eleven release the original C and their Rust in runnable form. We re-test all eleven. We run the C and the Rust on generated inputs, compare every output, and count a divergence only where the C has no undefined behavior. All eleven release defective translations: we find 160 defects, 93 of them outright errors on ordinary inputs. Their own checks accepted 86 defective translations. For 81 of them, the released check never compared the programs on an input that exposes the defect. For three of the other five, it ran one but compared only part of the output. A success rate is only as good as its check. Before counting a translation as a success, authors should compare every output with the C's on inputs the repair loop never saw, check that a verifier reaches its assertion, release exactly what the check accepted, and report how they tested the check.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A patch to a robot's navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path. Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches. It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong. We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits. Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task's documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them. The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks. They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis. Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level.
  In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it.
  Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.
