Code and data: https://github.com/ocatak/quantum-measurement-budget-allocation

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts are highly sensitive to the fiber-orientation field supplied to the material model. In conventional workflows, that field comes from resin-flow analysis, which requires molding-specialist support and takes about 25 hours of work per part. We previously proposed a surrogate model that addresses this bottleneck by predicting the orientation field in about 3 minutes. This paper reports the implementation, validation, and operational design that turned the model into an engineering tool for Honda design workflows. We present staged validation from 2D plates to production parts, evaluation against a predefined engineering angular-error criterion, and the expert review that approved design use in March 2025; the system has since been transferred to the crash-safety group and is in initial, limited use in directed fracture-prediction scenarios. The developed system combines injection-gate setting support for cases in which gates are unknown (90% gate-count accuracy, mean position error 11% of flow length), voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and report generation in a single GUI. The complete orientation-preparation workflow takes about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the conventional 25-hour flow-analysis route, and can be run directly by crash CAE engineers without molding-specialist support. As evidence of practical impact, component-level crash analysis using the predicted orientation field reduced the absolute peak-force error from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%, while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region. The deployment lesson is that a surrogate model alone is not enough for practical adoption: gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and shareable reporting are what make the model usable as a design tool.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027), with technical appendices. 10 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Safe Subgame Resolving in Multiplayer Games
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Poker and other games with hidden information are too large to solve in one pass. Strong systems compute a complete blueprint strategy offline and refine it in real time inside the reached subgame. In 2p0s games, a safety theorem guarantees that subgame resolving never increases how much an adversary can gain by exploiting the resolved strategy relative to the blueprint strategy. With three or more players acting independently, no such guarantee exists yet, and heuristic resolving can increase the profile's best-response gap. We prove the first conditional safety theorem for uncorrelated multiplayer subgame resolving, a post-hoc certificate for any delivered update. The best-response gap of the resolved profile exceeds that of the blueprint by at most four terms. Two concern the resolver: the subgame value the blueprint promised without realizing ($A_i^{S}$) and the resolver's subgame solve error ($\varepsilon_i$). The other two are the opponents' best-response gains inside the subgame over their promised values ($\sum_q M_{q}$) and a structural tax ($Θ$), which measures how much the players' total utility can change. The tax is zero in constant-sum games, including every rake-free poker variant. Constructions attain each term with equality. On three-player Leduc poker and on Kuhn poker with up to six players, resolving without a certificate raises the gap beyond a small tolerance in 12% to 100% of the updates. The certificate flags every such update and accepts 41% (Kuhn) and 86% (Leduc) of the standard resolving updates. A resolver that keeps the blueprint whenever the certificate exceeds the tolerance delivers no harmful update. The certificate needs only one best-response pass per opponent inside the subgame, so real-time multiplayer solvers that refine a blueprint can attach it as a safety check. Code is available at https://github.com/lbn187/MultiPlayerSolver

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Multi-View Transformer with Geometry-Guided Multi-Modal ControlNet for 3D Virtual Try-On
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Editing a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) capture of a person so that they wear a new garment requires every rendered view to agree on the same garment details. Existing 3D virtual try-on (VTON) pipelines, however, edit training views largely independently and fuse them with hand-designed heuristics such as manually chosen reference views and fixed attention-blending weights. The resulting inconsistencies are baked into the 3D representation and surface as texture drift, blurred prints, and implausible geometry in novel views. We present GS-VTON-MVT, a three-stage framework that combines implicit and explicit 3D reasoning for consistent 3DGS try-on. (i) A multi-view inpainting transformer jointly edits a set of training views with full cross-view self-attention, so that cross-view correspondence is learned rather than imposed. (ii) A geometry-guided multi-modal ControlNet conditions the diffusion editor on the garment image together with depth and surface normals rendered from the current 3DGS state, supplying explicit structure where visual evidence is weakest. (iii) A pose-adaptive persona-aware attention replaces the fixed blending weight between current-view and reference-view features with weights derived from camera-pose proximity. On the 3D-VTONBench benchmark, GS-VTON-MVT improves FID, KID, LPIPS-based cross-view consistency, and user preference over general-purpose 3D editors and prior 3D try-on methods.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We tested whether energy estimates of open-weight large language models (LLMs) scale proportionally with an exactly stated food weight, and whether computing energy density times weight removes the error. Under a prespecified protocol, seven open-weight LLMs estimated the energy of 168 randomly drawn foods from the USDA Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies at nine stated weights, from 0.25 to 4 times the default amount. The primary outcome was the elasticity of the estimate with respect to weight (1: proportional scaling). A two-step estimate multiplied each model's own stated energy density by the weight in code. All seven models compressed their estimates, with elasticities from 0.548 to 0.979 (every 95% CI below 1); four compressed severely (0.548 to 0.709). These four overestimated a quarter of the default amount by 47% to 130% and underestimated four times it by 20% to 34%. Supplying the density restored near-proportional scaling in three of the four, and the two-step estimate cut the typical error factor at these extremes from 1.47-2.43 to 1.20-1.38. Compression persisted at full precision and grew in five of seven models under a plain question. The models hold the energy densities needed for proportional scaling and answer near a typical serving, reproducing the flat-slope syndrome of dietary recall. Accuracy at usual portions does not reveal it. Food-logging tools should compute the energy of weighed entries as density times weight, and evaluations should test fixed foods across stated weights.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: KernelOPT: Dispatch-Aware Agentic Search for GPU Kernel Optimization
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Deep learning inference and training performance depends critically on GPU kernel efficiency. Modern compilers such as PyTorch Inductor automatically generate GPU kernels from high-level model code, but frequently underperform expert-written implementations by wide margins. Recent LLM-assisted optimizers explore these opportunities through kernel generation and refinement; yet translating isolated kernel improvements into model-level gains remains a challenge. We present KernelOPT, a profiling-guided multi-agent system for GPU kernel optimization. It inspects generated Triton kernels and external library calls in compiler artifacts to guide synthesis and refinement, then assembles and evaluates the resulting model. Four stages of validation combine execution checks, multi-seed numerical comparison, model-level checking with a float64 fallback and end-to-end performance gating ($γ{=}1.03$). The system supports PyTorch nn.Modules, standalone Triton kernels, and Helion kernels. It is evaluated on all 250 KernelBench problems on NVIDIA H200 which includes 100 single-operator problems (Level1), 100 composite operators (Level2), and 50 model architectures (Level3). KernelOPT achieves geometric mean speedups over torch.compile of 1.40$\times$, 1.15$\times$ and 1.07$\times$ respectively across L1, L2 and L3. Among problems exceeding 1.03$\times$ speedup, the geomeans are 2.54$\times$ (36 L1), 1.84$\times$ (23 L2), and 1.37$\times$ (11 L3). These gains include arithmetic-precision changes and task-specific algebraic simplifications under the evaluated numerical tolerances. The evaluation also reveals discrepancies between isolated kernel improvements and end-to-end performance, motivating model-level measurement alongside kernel-level optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/TorchedHat/KernelOPT.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Periodic and Harmonic Periodic RoPE for Length Extrapolation in LLMs
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The ability to process long contexts is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to perform long-horizon tasks. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) gives every token a new rotation angle, so a model eventually meets angles it never saw in training, i.e., position exhaustion. We propose Periodic RoPE (P-RoPE), a positional encoding mechanism that operates in conjunction with sliding window attention. It repeats the first sliding-window-size \(W\) angles of the RoPE table, so the model needs only \(W\) distinct angles. P-RoPE works but introduces a wrap error at the window boundary. We further propose Harmonic Periodic RoPE (HP-RoPE), which removes the error by choosing frequencies that complete whole turns in \(W\) tokens. We compare models that share the same architecture, data, and schedule and differ only in the window-layer position encoding: standard RoPE, P-RoPE, and HP-RoPE. The results show that P-RoPE and HP-RoPE keep perplexity nearly flat from the training length \(768\) to \(16\)k, while RoPE, NTK, and YaRN rise. In a format-free Passkey test at \(16\)k, they remain at \(99\)--\(100\%\), against \(11\)--\(37\%\) for those RoPE interpolations. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Web search in Latin America: language models use less local and diverse news than search engines
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: AI platforms are becoming a major gateway to news and current events. This shift risks amplifying existing geographical biases that favour narratives from wealthier countries over those from the Global South. This is particularly relevant in Latin America, which accounts for the largest share of AI usage in the Global South. We examine how information about Latin America changes when users shift from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. We construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, craft realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models. We vary query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign user scenarios. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines. Across user types, the share of domestic news returned by language models is inconsistent. For local users, while search engines already return only 41.3\% local news, language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less. Taken together, our findings suggest that LLM-based search can reproduce and, in some settings, amplify geographical hierarchies in the reach and visibility of news sources. We release an open dataset to support multilingual and geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search, and highlight implications for more equitable information systems design.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: GaussTrans: A Gaussian Interface Framework for Multi-Layer Refractive Transport
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We investigate surface modeling of multi-transparent interfaces to achieve accurate light transmission. The interplay of errors in geometric structure, light paths, and observation results during the reconstruction of transparent media with a high number of layers makes this a challenging problem. Some existing techniques address the reconstruction of transparent scenes by reducing the number of layers or simplifying light paths; however, this limits their direct applicability to high-order transparent scenes. We propose GaussTrans, a compact framework for light transport in high-order transparent scenes, consisting of three components: Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection. Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces use a hybrid approach combining Gauss surfaces and fields to reconstruct different interfaces. Transport-Coupled Refinement reduces coupling errors by evaluating the entire light path. Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection combines primitive support regions to reduce errors in the intersection of interfaces and rays. In experiments on datasets such as RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher accuracy with relatively low spatial storage requirements.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Multi-Objective Structured Pruning of LLMs for Latency and Model Size Optimization
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption because of their strong reasoning and query-response capabilities. However, deploying them in embedded and edge computing environments remains challenging because of strict latency, memory, and energy constraints. Their large parameter counts and computational demands hinder efficient execution on resource-constrained platforms. Although model pruning has emerged as a viable solution for reducing scale while preserving performance, jointly optimizing layers, attention heads, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) dimensions remains highly complex. Exhaustively exploring this combined design space is computationally expensive and often leads to local optima or unstable configurations. To address these limitations, we propose a hardware-aware, multi-objective structured pruning framework. The proposed two-stage method explicitly targets latency and model size for efficient deployment on edge devices. In the coarse-grained stage, multi-objective depth pruning removes entire attention and MLP blocks to reduce computational load and memory usage. In the subsequent fine-grained stage, Parallel Bayesian Optimization (PBO) searches for the optimal layer-wise pruning ratios for pruning under latency constraints, while importance-based strategies rank the specific components to be pruned within each layer's allocated budget. Experimental results show that our approach reduces model complexity with minimal impact on commonsense reasoning tasks and zero-shot performance. Our method achieves a favorable trade-off among accuracy, latency, and model size, making it suitable for edge deployment. Across multiple LLMs at 37.5% and 50% pruning ratios, the proposed approach achieves better performance on commonsense reasoning tasks than existing methods while significantly reducing inference cost.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? Preliminary experiments show that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To trace this effect, we hold each problem fixed and vary its preceding history. The resulting changes in the model's internal states contain a recurring, problem-dependent component. To improve reasoning with retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). It captures attention keys and values from earlier response generation in a read-only bank. STAIR learns to reflect current query vectors to redirect attention over this bank during prompt processing. The backbone and stored entries remain fixed; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four reasoning benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history. The math-trained Qwen3.5-9B controller also improves code generation on HumanEval+ without further training.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 42 pages, 8 figures. v2: Expanded experiments and analyses; revised presentation

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: TELEVAL: A Benchmark Designed for Spoken Language Models in Chinese Interactive Scenarios
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Spoken Language Models (SLMs) are expected to support natural spoken interaction beyond task completion. Existing benchmarks assess a range of semantic tasks and conversational capabilities. However, high task scores do not necessarily imply reliable and appropriate spoken interaction. To address this gap, we introduce TELEVAL, a large-scale benchmark focused on Chinese spoken interaction. It evaluates responses to spoken inputs without additional task-specific prompts or predefined answer options. TELEVAL covers two complementary aspects: (1) Reliable Content Fulfillment, which measures semantic accuracy under diverse acoustic and linguistic conditions, and (2) Interactional Appropriateness, which assesses conversational naturalness and appropriate adaptation to auditory cues. Experiments reveal limitations in both aspects. Strong results on factual question-answering datasets do not consistently extend to locally relevant knowledge or challenging speech conditions, such as Chinese cultural questions and dialectal speech. Models also struggle to adapt their responses to auditory cues, even in cases where they explicitly recognize them. We further document a recurring failure pattern, termed the "Caption Trap", in which some responses describe a perceived auditory cue instead of addressing the user's conversational needs. Overall, the evaluated SLMs struggle to deliver consistently accurate and conversationally appropriate responses. TELEVAL provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating both content reliability and conversational adaptation.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: ROAM-GRPO: Enforcing Reasoning Diversity in GRPO via Routed Off-mode Approach Mining
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paired with Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become the dominant recipe for post-training LLMs on complex reasoning tasks, but has been shown to collapse the policy into a low-diversity mode. Repeated LLM outputs are nearly identical, and pass@k accuracy converges or degrades as a result. We propose ROAM-GRPO (Routed Off-mode Approach Mining for GRPO), an augmentation to the GRPO algorithm which incentivizes exploration of distinct reasoning strategies and aims to increase output creativity during evaluation. ROAM-GRPO detects well-solved problems during training and transfers them to an "off-mode" track. The model is prompted to produce distinct solution strategies to such problems, which are verified for logical validity and distinctness by an LLM judge and subsequently self-distilled into the policy. Training Qwen3.5-2b on a 1,000-problem subset of the MATH lvl5 dataset, ROAM-GRPO implementation increases peak pass@16 by 4.7% and correct embedding cosine distance by approximately 1.5-2x on a difficult evaluation set.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training Workshop

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Best-of-Depth: Learning Exploratory Dynamics in Looped Transformers
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Looped Transformers extend inference-time computation through repeated latent-state updates, but final-depth training does not directly encourage useful intermediate alternatives. We introduce Best-of-Depth (BoD), which trains a recurrent trajectory as a candidate set by minimizing prediction loss across depths. Different valid targets can be matched at different depths without architectural changes or depth-specific labels. An exact-match analysis connects this objective to solution coverage. On N-Queens completion and graph coloring, BoD improves coverage over final-depth and intermediate-supervision objectives. N-Queens coverage reaches 91.03%, versus 45.75% for final-depth training. Further experiments show discovery beyond the training depth and recovery of solutions withheld from teacher pools on familiar inputs. Fine-tuning a pretrained looped language model with BoD yields higher pooled code-generation success than final-depth training when programs are generated separately at evaluated fixed depths. These results support training recurrent computation for solution discovery along its trajectory.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: You Have Mail: Set-Theoretic Types for Actors
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
We present a type system for the processes of Elixir, a dynamic language based on the actor model whose static type system covers only its functional core. Each process is typed by $\mathtt{pid}(t)$, where the ``interface'' $t$ is the type of the messages the process expects in its mailbox: sends are checked against the recipient's interface, and receives rely on the interface of the process that performs them.
  One of the difficulties of typing Elixir is that mailboxes are implicit: a function shipped in a message may evaluate $\mathtt{self()}$ and execute receive instructions, and both refer to whichever process eventually runs the function---$\mathtt{self()}$ returns that process's pid, receive reads that process's mailbox---so the mailbox they act on is not known where the function is written. We solve this problem by inferring, for every function, bounds on the type of the mailboxes it can be used with; as a result, the system types higher-order functions that travel in messages even when they contain reference to $\mathtt{self()}$ and receive instructions.
  The only new annotation the programmer writes is the interface of each spawned process; everything else is inferred by reusing the existing subtyping and constraint-resolution machinery of Elixir, and the system is proved sound.
  For legacy code, the interface can be reconstructed from the receive clauses: what the branches do with their messages bounds it from above, and the most permissive solution is sharp enough to recover received pids and closures.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed lambda-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside beta-normal eta-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: On the semantics of conditional branching
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Motivated by the non-standard interpretations of if-then-else in probabilistic and quantum programs we review the different semantics of conditional branching and propose a unifying categorical structure for the interpretation of if-then-else. We show that many semantically important categories possess this structure, covering inter alia classical, probabilistic, quantum or non-deterministic computations. We examine algebraic structures related to and generated by this categorical structure, in particular on collections of predicates. In this setting we show that the skew-associativity rules of GKATs and barycentric algebras are two instances of a common skew-associativity rule.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 31 pages, proofs in the Appendix

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Inductive Grounded Arithmetic: Goodstein, the Hydra, and $Γ_0$
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: What does a recursive definition mean in a grounded logic, where a sentence is true only if a terminating process makes it so? This paper takes Kripke's answer for truth, the least fixed point, as a rule. Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) writes any recursive definition as one self-referential term; Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA) adds the elimination rule for every positive one, making each an inductive definition. IGA is omega-sound and proof-grounded: sound and complete for a semantics whose certificates are its own proofs. IGA proves Goodstein's theorem, the Kirby-Paris hydra game for primitive recursive strategies, and, along Gentzen's route, the consistency of Peano Arithmetic. IGA certifies the Veblen notation below every $\varphi(n,0)$: its accessibility ordinal there is $\varphi(ω,0)$, that of the paracomplete truth theory PKF. Every theorem is machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL; order types and PKF's ordinal are cited. IGA proves the Veblen notation well-founded exactly when it admits bivalence of accessibility for it, which it does not, and that bivalence is sound exactly when the order is well-founded. So $Γ_0$ lies exactly one instance of excluded middle away, and that instance, the well-foundedness sentence and one membership claim in an internal form of Kleene's $\mathcal{O}$ are interderivable over IGA. Bivalence at the Bachmann-Howard order keeps proof-groundedness. One such claim buys well-foundedness of the countable part of Buchholz's notation at every finite level, of type $ψ_0(Ω_ω)$, and $k$ stratified bivalence rules give a proof-grounded system proving the countable part up to level $k$ well-founded; $k$ iterated closings-off of truth do too, sound only for a closed-off model. Unrestricted conditional proof is inconsistent (Curry's paradox); the purchase is implication at a hypothesis not provably decided.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: major revision, now 79 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Triosecuris: Formally Verified Protection Against Speculative Control-Flow Hijacking
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: This paper introduces Triosecuris, a formally verified defense against Spectre BTB, RSB, and PHT that combines CET-style hardware-assisted control-flow integrity with compiler-inserted speculative load hardening (SLH). Triosecuris is based on the novel observation that in the presence of CET-style protection, we can precisely detect BTB misspeculation for indirect calls and RSB misspeculation for returns and set the SLH misspeculation flag. We formalize Triosecuris as a transformation in Rocq and provide a machine-checked proof that it achieves relative security: any transformed program running with speculation leaks no more than what the source program leaks without speculation. This strong security guarantee applies to arbitrary programs, even those not following the cryptographic constant-time programming discipline.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Appeared at CSF'26; extended version with appendices and a bit more related work. W.r.t. first arXiv version: extended with concrete protection against Spectre RSB and renamed to Triosecuris

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Function Contracts and Beyond: Machine-Checked Assurance Cases for Conformance of C Libraries to Their Requirements
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating interactive theorem proving, yet verification of real-world C codebases requires more than discharging individual proof goals. The task involves jointly constructing expressive function specifications and their proofs, and ensuring that library interfaces compose along intended call sequences even without a designated client. We present Accord, an LLM-assisted framework for building machine-checked assurance cases: structured, auditable artifacts supporting the claim that a C codebase meets its intended requirements. To model intended cross-interface use in open libraries, Accord constructs an interface protocol that exposes permitted call sequences and resource assumptions for review, with a conditional safety guarantee under verified contracts and caller obligations. Accord coordinates two complementary phases: (i) requirement-guided analysis and bottom-up construction of candidate specifications and protocols; and (ii) modular proof construction with feedback that revises the specifications and proofs. Implemented using VST in Rocq, Accord establishes memory safety for 259 function definitions across seven implementation cases from six benchmark families, including industrial cryptographic modules, and additional functional correctness for red--black trees and ML-DSA. Human review took an estimated 0.17--8.00 hours per case. The guarantees depend on disclosed contracts and assumptions; human review supplies the conformance judgments connecting the formal artifacts to the intended requirements.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Substantially revised and expanded; updated title, formal development, and experimental evaluation

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Tenon: A Unified Programming Framework for Retargetable PIM Compilation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) is emerging as a building block of heterogeneous systems for memory-bound workloads, and commercial prototypes now span near-bank SIMD engines, bank-level GDDR accelerators, programmable DRAM cores, and bit-level in-SRAM processors. Their programming stacks are fragmented: no abstraction or compiler is shared across vendors, and per-device models range from instruction sequences to C-like languages. Data layout further complicates the problem: tight compute-memory integration makes data layout a first-order optimization, yet existing PIM compilers lack a unified way to represent and optimize it. A key observation is that PIM compilation targets can be modeled as nested grids of compute and storage units connected by legal data-transfer paths. We present Tenon, a unified programming framework for retargetable PIM compilation. It decouples workload, compilation target, and cost specifications, so a workload is expressed once and compiled through a unified programming framework. Tenon generalizes the $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear layout algebra from GPU compilers to map logical work and data onto these compute and storage grids. It automatically constructs a minimum-movement data layout given a workload and a target specification. We evaluate Tenon on six PIM backends: five commercial backends and AttAcc, a state-of-the-art academic HBM-based PIM architecture. Across the commercial backends, it matches or outperforms vendor, expert, and compiler baselines, with geometric-mean speedups of up to $1.20\times$ and individual speedups up to $3.65\times$. For end-to-end GPT-13B decoding on AttAcc, Tenon-compiled workloads run $1.2$--$1.3\%$ faster than those compiled by DCC, a state-of-the-art PIM compiler, across all three batch-4 configurations. Together, these results demonstrate Tenon's performance portability across diverse PIM target families.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: HPCA 2027

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity.
  We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: The Bell Experiment, Monadically
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Bell's theorem says that no classical model satisfying certain independence assumptions can reproduce the correlations that quantum mechanics predicts and experiments observe. In this paper we write the two-party Bell experiment as a small Haskell program, and find those assumptions in its structure: in what each part of the program can see, and in how the parts are composed. The boxes of the two parties compute in one monad, and the experiment that schedules and repeats their trials computes in another; a \emph{membrane} runs the first inside the second. A run keeps the record of its trials, and both of its verdicts, the CHSH value and whether the boxes signal, are read off one table: the empirical model of that run.
  In this setting, a model is classical when it has three properties. It is \emph{blind}: the hidden strategy of the boxes is drawn without seeing the measurement settings. It is \emph{local}: given that strategy, neither box's outcome depends on the other party's setting. It is \emph{factored}: given the strategy and the settings, the two outcomes are independent. Together, they give the classical bound of $2$. We give them up one at a time and run what results. Without blindness, we get experimental loopholes and superdeterminism. Without factoring, we get quantum boxes, which reach $2\sqrt2$, and the hypothetical PR boxes, which reach $4$, both without signaling. Without locality, we get boxes that rewrite a shared hidden state; whether they signal depends on how that state is sampled.
  We also compare two ways to check no-signaling: reading it off the run's own table, and estimating it in separate experiments at fixed settings.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Static analysis tools such as Android Lint, PMD, and CodeQL let developers add custom checks for project-specific rules. However, authoring a check is a demanding programming task: a rule can be stated in a few sentences, yet turning it into a working, tested check requires detailed knowledge of the analysis framework and its issue-detection logic. Recent work generates such checks with large language models (LLMs), but each system needs more than the natural language description a developer always has: a bug-fix patch, a CVE record, or a developer-written test suite to repair against. No prior work measures whether an LLM can turn a description into a working check, or what external knowledge it needs to do so. We introduce LintBench, a human-validated benchmark of 113 real-world Android Lint checks, each paired with a natural language description and its original test suite as a held-out oracle. We evaluate four LLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models. We compare prompting strategies, then evaluate execution-guided repair with and without retrieved API knowledge. Prompting alone reaches 30%-65% (pass@5) across models. Execution-guided repair and retrieval reach 57%-85% test-passing rates within five calls. Our results show that execution feedback raises the pass rate, while retrieved framework knowledge raises the compile rate, which reaches up to 99%. The framework knowledge helps the low-performing models the most, providing the knowledge they need to fix compilation errors. Of the generated checks that compile but fail their tests, 87% have false negatives, missing an issue the generated check should report. Based on our findings, getting the issue-detection logic right remains an open challenge. We release LintBench and the evaluation harness to support future work on generating Android Lint checks.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027, Dublin, Ireland. 13 pages (11 pages plus 2 pages of references)

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 33 pages (12 pages of main text, 3 pages of references, 18 pages of appendices), 9 figures, 12 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Held While Waiting: What LLM Agent Sessions Reserve on Serverless and Agent Runtimes
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
LLM agents spend nearly all their time waiting for the model. On Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, our agents waited a median of 2.7 seconds for each model reply, then computed for an estimated 5 to 40 milliseconds. AgentCore does not charge for CPU during the wait. But it reserves a separate environment, a virtual machine with its own memory, for every conversation, and keeps it reserved until the conversation is closed. So 1,000 conversations reserve 1,000 environments to do the work of 2 to 15 processor cores. A service runs out of environments long before it runs out of processing power.
  The shortage has two causes, and each has a fix. An environment stays reserved after its conversation ends: in the customer-service benchmark we ran, a conversation lasts 33 seconds on average, but its environment is held for 15 minutes more unless the client closes it. And an environment serves only one conversation, which is mostly waiting: in our simulation, 64 conversations sharing one environment need 59 times fewer environments, and 99 of every 100 replies are delayed by at most 40 milliseconds.
  The milliseconds are an estimate because they are hard to measure: a stubbed model, a timer around the model call, and steps run back to back each gave a plausible number that was too low. We show how to avoid all three. Of the two fixes, closing needs only the client. Sharing needs the platform, and of the agent runtimes we surveyed only one allows it, in part. They keep conversations apart because an agent runs tools, and sometimes code, chosen by a model. The open problem is to keep them apart without reserving an environment for each while it waits.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes.
  In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code.
  We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance.
  In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Scaling GR(1) Synthesis via a Compositional Framework for LTL Discrete Event Control
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: We present a compositional approach to controller synthesis of discrete event system controllers with linear temporal logic (LTL) goals. We exploit the modular structure of the plant to be controlled, given as a set of labelled transition systems (LTS), to mitigate state explosion that monolithic approaches to synthesis are prone to. Maximally permissive safe controllers are iteratively built for subsets of the plant LTSs by solving weaker control problems. Observational synthesis equivalence is used to reduce the size of the controlled subset of the plant by abstracting away local events. The result of synthesis is also compositional, a set of controllers that when run in parallel ensure the LTL goal. We implement synthesis in the MTSA tool for an expressive subset of LTL, GR(1), and show it computes solutions to that can be up to 1000 times larger than those that the monolithic approach can solve.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Barriers to GenAI Integration During Large-Scale Agile Transformation: An Exploratory Case Study
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Organizations undergoing large-scale agile transformations are increasingly introducing generative AI (GenAI) tools into everyday work. While GenAI promises to accelerate software development, less is known about how organizations integrate GenAI into existing large-scale agile ways of working and how it interacts with tensions related to autonomy, alignment, learning, and coordination. We examine barriers to GenAI integration through an exploratory case study of a large Nordic media organization undergoing a large-scale agile transformation. The findings reveal team-level barriers, including diverging AI beliefs, lack of shared practices, and limited experimentation capacity, and organizational-level barriers, including uneven AI maturity, weak organizational learning mechanisms, and cross-unit coordination and alignment challenges. Our findings suggest that GenAI does not create new organizational challenges but becomes intertwined with existing tensions in large-scale agile transformation and may intensify challenges related to learning, coordination, governance, and trust. We contribute to large-scale agile transformation research by showing how GenAI interacts with ongoing organizational change and by identifying conditions for sustainable GenAI integration at scale.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Adopting Embedded AI Through an Innovation Team
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software organizations are increasingly embedding AI capabilities into products that existing teams already own and maintain, but how this development work should be organized is not well understood. We conducted a qualitative case study of a temporary cross-functional innovation team in a large Norwegian financial organization, drawing on 18 interviews with 15 participants, 10 days of office observation, observations of ten meetings, and internal documents. We found that structural separation, AI competence inside the team, high autonomy within a clear mandate, senior expertise, and flexible ways of working enabled the team to explore and build embedded AI solutions. While structural separation enabled this work, it also made adoption dependent on coordination with the permanent product team that would own the solution. Misaligned roadmaps, prioritization gaps, and a lack of co-location constrained that coordination. We identify seven success factors for adopting embedded AI through an innovation team and propose expertise awareness as an alternative to redundancy in the Agile Team Effectiveness Model.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: From Code Review Comments to Reuse in Production: An Industrial Study of Extracted Rules
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Much organization-specific code review knowledge remains embedded in comments on individual changes, and recent systems reuse it by turning those comments into rules a language model applies to later changes. Teams must then decide which rules to keep, and the evidence at hand is how often the system's later comments name each rule. Tracing the rules of one such system, Kleene, through 65 days of production use, we found that such a count does not show what a rule contributed. A rule attribution indicates neither whether the source content was preserved nor whether the comment requested a change. Of 56 clauses in 12 rules that later comments named as their reason, 2 were explicit in a source review thread, 38 added conditions to a corresponding passage, and 16 had no passage we could locate; 45 of 79 further comments naming those rules requested no change, 27 of them while stating that the rule applied. On 20 constructed code changes, a reviewer model given only the unedited source thread met the detection criteria on 8 of the 10 that require a report, against 10 of 10 with the extracted rule, a difference whose confidence interval includes zero. Stage counts locate where rules drop out but not why: of 464 rules deployed while the rule-based reviewer subagent ran in their repository, 259 (55.8%) were named, 195 (42.0%) produced a comment that was not withheld, and 94 (20.3%) one with a recorded code change; the largest reduction occurred before any rule was named. Nor did the deployment-time properties we tested settle the choice in advance: retaining the top-ranked half preserved 53.8% of the rules that later produced a non-withheld comment, against 49.2% at random, a difference whose confidence interval includes zero. Judging extracted rules therefore calls for recording each stage separately and comparing each rule against the threads it was extracted from.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Fast Computation of Lowest Common Ancestor in Version Control Commit Graph
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
The problem of finding the lowest common ancestor in the commit graph arises when a user wants to merge two (or more) development branches: for example, to add their own development into a common branch. At that moment, the version control system must determine the merge base - the common ancestor of the latest commits of the branches, in order to show the mutual difference between the branches. The problem is complicated by the fact that the commit graph is not a tree but an arbitrary acyclic graph. Moreover, if there is no common ancestor, searching for one may require traversing the entire graph. Traversing a graph with several million vertices takes tens of seconds, which becomes noticeable to users.
  We show that the commit graph has additional structure - supporting branches - and that this can be used to speed up the algorithm. By extracting supporting branches, the graph can be preprocessed and the search for the lowest common ancestor can be significantly accelerated. Moreover, if removing the supporting branches decomposes the graph into connected components of bounded size, the lowest common ancestor query can be answered in time comparable to searching for a common ancestor within a single component only.
  We present an algorithm running in time $O(δ_Gm_c + n_s\log^2 n_s + m_s\log n_s)$ and requiring $O(d)$ preprocessed data per vertex, where $δ_G$ is the maximum out-degree of a vertex in $G$, $n_c$ and $m_c$ are the maximum numbers of vertices and edges in a connected component formed after removing the supporting branches, $n_s$ is the number of supporting branches, $m_s$ is the number of edges in the reachability graph between the supporting branches, and $d$ is the maximum number of supporting branches adjacent to any single component.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Function Contracts and Beyond: Machine-Checked Assurance Cases for Conformance of C Libraries to Their Requirements
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating interactive theorem proving, yet verification of real-world C codebases requires more than discharging individual proof goals. The task involves jointly constructing expressive function specifications and their proofs, and ensuring that library interfaces compose along intended call sequences even without a designated client. We present Accord, an LLM-assisted framework for building machine-checked assurance cases: structured, auditable artifacts supporting the claim that a C codebase meets its intended requirements. To model intended cross-interface use in open libraries, Accord constructs an interface protocol that exposes permitted call sequences and resource assumptions for review, with a conditional safety guarantee under verified contracts and caller obligations. Accord coordinates two complementary phases: (i) requirement-guided analysis and bottom-up construction of candidate specifications and protocols; and (ii) modular proof construction with feedback that revises the specifications and proofs. Implemented using VST in Rocq, Accord establishes memory safety for 259 function definitions across seven implementation cases from six benchmark families, including industrial cryptographic modules, and additional functional correctness for red--black trees and ML-DSA. Human review took an estimated 0.17--8.00 hours per case. The guarantees depend on disclosed contracts and assumptions; human review supplies the conformance judgments connecting the formal artifacts to the intended requirements.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: On the Reliability of CyberGym Evaluation: Task Material Consistency and Reference-Target Identity
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: CyberGym evaluates vulnerability reproduction by checking whether a proof-of-concept input (PoC) crashes a vulnerable program version but not a fixed version. Interpreting this differential pass as successful reproduction requires consistent task materials and evidence that the PoC triggers the intended defect. We examine these requirements through a material audit of all 1,507 CyberGym tasks and an identity assessment of the final PoCs from one complete Level-1 GLM-5.3 run. Taking the defect associated with each reference crash report as the target, the audit assigns inconsistency labels to 338 tasks (22.4%) after correcting two labels identified by stratified blind review. The largest categories are coverage inconsistency (205 tasks) and descriptions and patches that jointly point to another defect (110 tasks). We assess PoC identity using an execution check, crash-signature matching, and LLM-assisted root-cause review. Of the 1,286 differential passes, the procedure assigns 89 non-target and 10 insufficient-evidence verdicts; requiring a target hit lowers the pass rate from 85.3% to 78.8%. Non-target verdicts also occur in tasks with no material inconsistency found: 39 of 1,052 differential passes (3.7%). Although the identity verdicts require independent validation, these findings motivate separate checks of task-material consistency and submission identity when interpreting vulnerability-reproduction scores.
