Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Auto-Alpha: A Framework for Autonomous Factor Research
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Autonomous factor research requires generating economic hypotheses as well as implementing and testing them. We present Auto-Alpha, a framework that connects report-guided initialization to self-directed research through a test-driven implementation loop. An idea agent proposes economic mechanisms and signal constructions; a research agent develops them with backtest feedback. Semantic audit, quantitative review, and human admission select factors for a persistent library, while an Experience Library retains research insights. Starting from 120 research reports, Auto-Alpha builds an initial library of 32 factors. It then generates new ideas and refines existing candidates, producing 420 implementations and retaining 62 additional factors. We evaluate factor quality and portfolio performance using a fixed library snapshot of 105 factors. The median 1-day Rank IC is 0.0301, and a weekly Top-300 portfolio returns 16.81% annualized after stated costs over 2020-2026, versus 1.71% for the CSI 1000 price index. These retrospective results document an operating research process and its artifacts; controlled evaluation is needed to isolate the contribution of its components.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Technology-Enabled Fuel Supply Chain Resilience: An Integrated Information System for Real-Time Monitoring and Decision Support
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: This study evaluates and extends the transactional information system described in an earlier fuel logistics study, focusing on data reliability, monitoring, and decision support. An author-led re-evaluation examined available Delphi and SQL code and compared a reconstructed source-derived baseline (R0) with a revised SQL Server system (R1) across twelve evaluation scenarios. Synthetic transactions and public US energy data were used for technical assessment, while organizational processes and supply delays were simulated. R1 improved data integration and reporting accuracy in controlled SQL Server tests and introduced stock-movement records, automated alerts, and recovery controls. On comparable data feeds, integration defect rates decreased from 2.90 to 3.46 percent in R0 to 0.14 to 0.49 percent in R1. For national weekly demand forecasting, selected methods did not significantly outperform the previous-year mean. Process and disruption simulations suggested improvements in manual workload and replenishment delays, although these outcomes depended on modelling assumptions and were not observed in operational settings. The study presents a revised transactional architecture for fuel logistics and distinguishes experimentally measured information-system performance from simulated organizational outcomes. Its findings highlight the potential of traceable inventory records, early exception detection, and recoverable information systems to support supply chain resilience.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity.
  We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Model Compression vs. Adversarial Robustness: An Empirical Study on Language Models for Code
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Transformer-based language models for code have shown remarkable performance in various software analytics tasks, but their adoption is hindered by high computational costs, slow inference speeds, and substantial environmental impact. Model compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation have gained traction in addressing these challenges. However, the impact of these strategies on the robustness of compressed language models for code in adversarial scenarios remains poorly understood. Understanding how these compressed models behave under adversarial attacks is essential for their safe and effective deployment in real-world applications. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of how common compression strategies affect the adversarial robustness of compressed models. We assess the robustness of compressed versions of three widely used language models for code across three software analytics tasks, using six evaluation metrics and four commonly used classical adversarial attacks. Our findings indicate that compressed models generally maintain comparable performance to their uncompressed counterparts. However, when subjected to adversarial attacks, compressed models exhibit significantly reduced robustness. These results reveal a trade-off between model size reduction and adversarial robustness, underscoring the need for careful consideration when deploying compressed models in security-critical software applications. Our study highlights the need for further research into compression strategies that strike a balance between computational efficiency and adversarial robustness, which is essential for deploying reliable language models for code in real-world software applications.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: A four-level executable validation protocol for evaluating LLM-generated topology specifications of physics-based HVAC digital twins
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Physics-based digital twins of air conditioning, a principal energy consumer in manufacturing and buildings, can be generated automatically from a declarative specification of its equipment, connections, and sizing. Large language models (LLMs) now write such specifications from plain-language descriptions. Evaluations of these specifications stop at parse success, completed runs, or textual similarity, and cannot reject a model that converges in simulation but is physically wrong. In this study, a four-level protocol is proposed that tests whether an LLM-written specification not only executes but also yields a physically valid digital twin. Each specification is executed through static validity, model build, simulation convergence, and behavioral equivalence with a hidden reference model within bands calibrated by $\pm$20% sizing perturbations. The protocol was applied to eight LLMs and fourteen HVAC topologies, five describing an existing low-humidity test chamber. To test for authorship bias, engineers and a second model family also described six topologies. Within three repairs, seven of eight models built in 98.6 to 100% of trials, with simulations converging in at least 80.0%, but reached behavioral equivalence in only 50.0 to 98.6%. About half of the failed trials converged, but not to the reference steady state, mostly in desiccant rotor systems. Pooled pass rates varied by under five percentage points across description authors. These results imply that the physics hardest to model in each field, here the desiccant rotor, must enter the generation framework as validation levels. The protocol can be adapted to other fields that generate executable digital twins from declarative specifications.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Behavioral Containment: Source-to-Binary Function Matching for 1-Day Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Vulnerabilities in reused open-source code often propagate into deployed binaries. Detecting them requires source-to-binary function matching, which locates the affected source function in a binary. Applying prior binary-to-binary approaches to this task would require compiling the source code with the same build configuration as the target binary, which is usually unavailable. Decompiling the binary does not make prior source-to-source approaches work either, because decompiled code differs substantially from the original source code.
  We observe that compilation transforms the code of a function but largely preserves its behavior. A binary function that implements a source function therefore contains its behavior, a property we call behavioral containment. Building on this, we present SBIND, which decompiles the binary and checks behavioral containment instead of comparing code. SBIND represents each function by behavioral paths, sequences of normalized operations from its entry to its exits, and aligns source paths with binary paths in order. To detect 1-day vulnerabilities, SBIND compares the binary with the vulnerable and the patched source only on the paths through the changed lines. On stripped binaries built with two compilers, two optimization levels, and four architectures, SBIND ranks the correct function first in 77.87% of 32,008 searches, against 45.69% for the state-of-the-art approach SBridge. On 26 1-day CVEs, SBIND reaches an F1 score of 0.70 on stripped binaries, against 0.51 for SBridge. Our replication of SBridge also revealed several issues in its implementation and evaluation, and its authors have acknowledged them.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Distilling Reasoning Traces into Advisory Prompts for Software Engineering Tasks
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Language models are widely used for generating and otherwise processing code (e.g., predicting behavior, outputs, or likely inputs), and this paper asks whether better performance can be achieved without always incurring the cost of reasoning. Human students of programming learn to avoid mistakes by (a) first identifying them, (b) reflecting upon cognitive lapses that led to these mistakes (essentially, "thinking through" the errors), (c) inferring general rules or lessons from these reflections, and (d) internalizing these lessons into rules. In tutorial sessions with an instructor, this is a very common Socratic interaction with students. Examples of such internalizable rules might include the nugget "Before coding, restate the requirements to clarify them". Inspired by this process, this paper describes an approach where we first identify examples in which "thinking mode" in a (low-resource) LLM avoids errors; then, these errors, and their avoidance via "thinking" in the same LLM, are examined by a bigger LLM to generate summary explanations; these are then summarized by a large LLM into brief advisory prompts. This approach works on many modestly sized models; in some cases, the "advisory prompts" thus learned can also be gainfully transferred to other models. We also present some investigations into the nature of coding errors that language models make, and a characterization of when this approach can be helpful.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Comment and Control: Hijacking Agentic Workflows via Context-Grounded Evolution
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Automation platforms such as GitHub Actions and n8n are increasingly adopting so-called agentic workflows, which integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents for tasks such as code review and data synchronization. While bringing convenience for developers, this integration exposes a new risk: An adversary may control and craft certain inputs, such as GitHub issue comments, to manipulate the LLM agent for unwanted actions, such as credential exfiltration and arbitrary command execution. To our knowledge, no prior academic work has studied such a risk in agentic workflows. In this paper, we design the first detection and exploitation framework, called JAW, to hijack agentic workflows hosted on automation platforms via a novel approach called Context-Grounded Evolution. Our key idea is to evolve agentic workflow inputs under the contexts derived from hybrid program analysis for hijacking purposes. Specifically, JAW generates agentic workflow contexts through three analyses: (i) static path-feasibility analysis to identify feasible agent-invocation paths and the input constraints required to trigger them, (ii) dynamic prompt-provenance analysis to determine how that input is transformed and embedded into the LLM context, and (iii) capability analysis to identify the actions and restrictions available to the agent at runtime. Our evaluation of JAW on GitHub workflows and n8n templates showed that 4714 GitHub workflows and eight n8n templates can be successfully hijacked, for example, to leak user credentials. Our findings span 15 widely-used GitHub Actions, including official GitHub Actions for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen CLI, and Cursor CLI, and two official n8n nodes. We responsibly disclosed all findings to the affected vendors and received many acknowledgements, fixes, and bug bounties, notably from GitHub, Google, and Anthropic.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Bridging the Mobile Trust Gap: A Zero Trust Framework for Consumer-Facing Applications
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) has become a widely adopted model for securing enterprise environments, promoting continuous verification and minimal trust across systems. However, its application in mobile contexts remains limited, despite mobile applications now accounting for most global digital interactions and being increasingly targeted by sophisticated threats. Existing Zero Trust frameworks developed by organisations such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) primarily focus on enterprise-managed infrastructure, assuming organisational control over devices, networks, and identities. This paper addresses a critical gap by proposing an extended Zero Trust model designed for mobile applications operating in untrusted, user-controlled environments. Using a design science methodology, the study introduced a six-pillar framework that supports runtime enforcement of trust through controls including device integrity, user identity validation, data protection, secure application programming interface (API) usage, behavioural monitoring, and live application protection. Each pillar was mapped to relevant regulatory and security standards to support compliance. A phased implementation roadmap and maturity assessment model were also developed to guide adoption across varying organisational contexts. The proposed model offers a practical and standards-aligned approach to securing mobile applications beyond pre-deployment controls, aligning real-time enforcement with Zero Trust principles. This contribution expands the operational boundaries of ZTA and provides organisations with a deployable path to reduce fraud, enhance compliance, and address emerging mobile security challenges. Future research may include empirical validation of the framework and cross-sector application testing.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 43 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Working Paper - Version 1.0. Submitted under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license. Also available as an SSRN Working Paper. Feedback and collaboration are welcome

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Specification-Grounded Adaptive Triage and Formal Invariant Exclusion Synthesis for Autonomous Silicon Coverage Closure
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Closing the final 5%-15% of code and functional coverage remains a major schedule bottleneck in silicon tapeouts. Existing LLM-based coverage closure loops feed raw uncovered RTL lines or branches directly into iterative prompts, failing on industrial subsystems due to: (1) token and context explosion from querying thousands of correlated holes independently; (2) illegal stimulus that violates cross-signal invariants and yields dirty coverage; and (3) unsafe exclusion hallucination on structurally unreachable dead code.
  We present ARGUS (Autonomous Reachability & Guided Unified Stimulus), a specification-grounded, dual-regime coverage closure and formal exclusion synthesis engine. ARGUS mines microarchitectural specs and SystemVerilog Assertions into a formal Block Contract (C), then runs adaptive Macro-Clustering vs. Micro-Surgery triage gated by a per-module hole-density threshold (tau): dense modules collapse correlated holes into root-cause mode, FSM, and backpressure clusters, while sparse modules use AST and loop-domain reachability to separate reachable corners from provably unreachable invariants. Directed tests pair with bit-exact golden scoreboards, and unreachable invariants emit tool-native .el exclusions with formal proofs.
  Across five core benchmarks -- three open-source LowRISC OpenTitan IPs (uart_core, i2c_core, aes_cipher_core) and two commercial AI accelerator Tensor Layout Converter datapaths (53 SV modules, 376,127 coverage points) -- plus a 2,626-module industrial interconnect subsystem, ARGUS triages 2,626 modules in 0.265 s, cuts token usage by 27.2x to >180x, achieves zero dirty merges via 3-step sanity gating, and reaches 99.32%-100.0% effective coverage with 0 false exclusions across 21,071+ proven exclusions.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Automatic Detection of LLM-Generated Code: A Comparative Case Study of Contemporary Models Across Function and Class Granularities
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation risks incorporating vulnerable code into software systems. Existing detectors face two critical limitations: a lack of systematic cross-model validation and opaque "black box" operation. We address this through a comparative study of code generated by four distinct LLMs: GPT-3.5, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-OSS.
  Analyzing 14,485 Python functions and 11,913 classes from the CodeSearchNet dataset, we generated corresponding code with all four LLMs. Using interpretable software metrics, we trained CatBoost classifiers for each configuration. Our analysis reveals that granularity effects dominate model differences by a factor of 8.6, with negligible feature overlap, indicating that function-level and class-level detection rely on fundamentally disjoint structural signatures.
  We discover critical granularity-dependent inversions: while modern models (Claude, GPT-OSS) are more detectable at the class level, GPT-3.5 is an anomaly that uniquely excels at the function level. SHAP analysis identifies the Comment-to-Code Ratio as the sole universal discriminator. However, its predictive magnitude varies drastically across models, explaining why detectors trained on specific LLMs fail to generalize.
  Our findings demonstrate that GPT-3.5's exceptional detectability (AUC-ROC 0.96) is unrepresentative of contemporary models (AUC-ROC approximately between 0.68 and 0.80). Robust detection requires moving beyond single-model studies to account for substantial diversity in structural fingerprints across architectures and granularities.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Submitted to a journal for publication. This is the version after major revision round 2

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: How developers split roles among them and a coding agent and what "collaboration" means
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Background: Coding agents such as Claude Code become more and more competent, so that their role in the development process can grow.
  Objective: How do developers characterize the role-split between them and their agent? How would they ideally want to collaborate with their agent?
  Methods: We perform a 3-step, mixed-methods study. We apply qualitative open coding to 2025 early adopters' blog articles; perform a quantitative survey of 2026 practitioners; develop and apply a method for coding-agent-supported open coding of survey freetext responses.
  Results: The 2025 practitioners have the agent work in supporting roles only. Accountability was firmly human. In 2026, both are fundamentally still true. Gradually, however, the role-split is now different, with much more agent involvement. The developers' notion of collaboration has three facets: Predominantly a separation into human-only, agent-only, and collaborative work steps, with defined conditions and goals. Second, accommodating personal preferences without engineering justification. Third, a holistic view of collaboration covering the entire development process.
  Conclusions: Defining one's role relative to the agent will need to be a recurring activity. The different views on collaboration are likely a source of friction and conflict for teams; future work should find out how to cope with that.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 32 pages (plus 27 pages of appendices), 4 figures, 10 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Which Archived Results Survive a Rule Change? A Case Study in Revalidating Decisions
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A research workflow can retain a correct numerical result after the evidence or approval that supported its use has expired. Common incremental build methods identify reusable computations, while deciding what remains usable also requires knowing which policy justified each approval. We examined a recorded parser migration across 312 paired research records, replayed both parsers with the same inputs, applied a calculation-file omission to the complete cohort, and evaluated current proof in a GNU Make comparison. Treating the prior projections as current would change at least one field in 11 of 312 records, and controlled cases show that even matching values can lack a current proof. The study separates numerical recovery from applicable approval and sets out the conditions under which a maintained dependency graph can preserve both.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 1 table

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Testing Settlement Flags after Late Evidence and Process Restart
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: A settlement flag can survive an application restart while the economic effects remain ambiguous. We define a contract linking the fixed plan, source admission at two cutoffs, identity-keyed ledger effects and post-invocation state. We generated 504 synthetic histories, ran each through a file implementation and a separately coded SQLite implementation, and observed 672 controlled process exits. The file implementation missed 54 same-identity payment-date conflicts, including 27 that credited cash early, and a monitor using run flags, artifact presence and purchase counts accepted all 54. The same contract distinguishes a purchase awaiting closure from a correct quote wait for a single writer on a running kernel and filesystem.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: How Far Can LLMs Go in Generating Android Lint Checks from Natural Language?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Static analysis tools such as Android Lint, PMD, and CodeQL let developers add custom checks for project-specific rules. However, authoring a check is a demanding programming task: a rule can be stated in a few sentences, yet turning it into a working, tested check requires detailed knowledge of the analysis framework and its issue-detection logic. Recent work generates such checks with large language models (LLMs), but each system needs more than the natural language description a developer always has: a bug-fix patch, a CVE record, or a developer-written test suite to repair against. No prior work measures whether an LLM can turn a description into a working check, or what external knowledge it needs to do so. We introduce LintBench, a human-validated benchmark of 113 real-world Android Lint checks, each paired with a natural language description and its original test suite as a held-out oracle. We evaluate four LLMs, including proprietary and open-weight models. We compare prompting strategies, then evaluate execution-guided repair with and without retrieved API knowledge. Prompting alone reaches 30%-65% (pass@5) across models. Execution-guided repair and retrieval reach 57%-85% test-passing rates within five calls. Our results show that execution feedback raises the pass rate, while retrieved framework knowledge raises the compile rate, which reaches up to 99%. The framework knowledge helps the low-performing models the most, providing the knowledge they need to fix compilation errors. Of the generated checks that compile but fail their tests, 87% have false negatives, missing an issue the generated check should report. Based on our findings, getting the issue-detection logic right remains an open challenge. We release LintBench and the evaluation harness to support future work on generating Android Lint checks.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027, Dublin, Ireland. 13 pages (11 pages plus 2 pages of references)

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: From Observation to Explanation: Mechanistic Interpretability of LLM-Generated Code for Principled Repair
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed software development, yet our understanding of how they generate code remains critically underdeveloped. We address this gap by triangulating evidence across three layers. Longitudinally, autonomous agent-attributed code is statistically indistinguishable from human code under a semantic modification definition (HR = 1.019, p = 0.490), yet attracts disproportionately corrective modifications in production (49.1% vs 37.9% human baseline). This finding demands a causal explanation. Empirically, existing benchmarks overestimate LLM capabilities: models that achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks attain only 24 to 35% on real-world class-level code. Behaviourally, detection systems reveal puzzling asymmetries: GPT-3.5 is far more detectable than modern models (AUC-ROC = 0.96, a 27-point gap), even though modern models produce mutually similar code structures; yet no single feature reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human code at the class level, and the leading commercial detector achieves only 15 to 64% recall. Together, these findings raise a question that empirical studies cannot answer: why do LLMs generate code with these properties? This thesis proposes mechanistic interpretability, a causal token-level circuit tracing, as the bridge between empirical observation and principled correction. By identifying the transformer circuits responsible for detectable stylistic signatures, hallucination patterns, and systematic defects, we aim to drive an agentic repair framework that intervenes at the causal source of defects rather than patching surface symptoms.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: This camera-ready version was accepted at the EASE 2026 doctoral symposium

Security & Program Analysis.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
Security & Program Analysis.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026.
  Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$.
  Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{O} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{O}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof.
  Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{O}=\mathsf{BQP}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{O}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{O}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

Security & Program Analysis.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

Security & Program Analysis.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables. Project page: https://rogue-ai.surge.sh

Security & Program Analysis.title: No Country for Old Privacy: The Evolving Challenges of Anonymity in Bitcoin
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We present a longitudinal measurement study on the adoption of detectable, second-generation anonymisation protocols in the Bitcoin network, including CoinJoin, CoinSwap, CoinShuffle and Stealth Addresses. By implementing and refining a suite of heuristic filters, we identify over 5 million candidate CoinJoin and 23.3 million candidate CoinSwap transactions. Notably, the use of CoinShuffle was unexpectedly found to be closely aligned with the operation of coordinator-based CoinJoin services such as Wasabi and Whirlpool. Our analysis reveals consistently low adoption rates, with these protocols typically constituting less than 1% of network transactions, and a sharp decline in detectable usage following key regulatory events. Furthermore, we find no evidence of standardised Stealth Address adoption, indicating a failure to converge on a common privacy standard. This study provides a comprehensive picture of a niche ecosystem whose on-chain visibility has been largely suppressed, strongly suggesting the migration of privacy-seeking users to less transparent and less detectable methods.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, Accepted to the 2nd IEEE International Conference on Distributed Ledger Technologies (ICDLT 2026)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 33 pages (12 pages of main text, 3 pages of references, 18 pages of appendices), 9 figures, 12 tables

Security & Program Analysis.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ROPE: Routed Origin Policy Enforcement against Indirect Prompt Injection
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Tool-using LLM agents execute consequential operations on behalf of users. Because the LLM driving an agent processes trusted user instructions and untrusted content in the same context, agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks that induce unintended actions by mixing malicious instructions into benign data. Defenses based on prompting or content detection are easily evaded by paraphrasing attacks, while system-level defenses that constrain tool calls using inferred user intent, or restrict which sources can supply values to sensitive tools, greatly compromise utility. We present ROPE (Routed Origin Policy Enforcement), a defense that greatly improves the utility-security tradeoff by leveraging system roots of trust to create and enforce per-task policies on sensitive tool parameters. Our key insight is that authentication and integrity protection provide a basis for identifying the source of content independently of instructions embedded in it. Before a task unfolds, an LLM router reads only trusted task input to set a provenance rule for each sensitive tool parameter, accounting for the nature of the task and the values and sources the user specified. As the agent works, an origin labeler records where each piece of content came from, using the user's request, platform metadata, and protected record fields as trust anchors. Before any sensitive tool executes, a deterministic verifier requires each of its origin-guarded values to match a value in a source its rule accepts. We show that ROPE provably guarantees parameter value provenance to sensitive tool calls and is immune to paraphrasing attacks. Against eleven defenses on AgentDojo and AgentDyn under static, adaptive, and long-horizon attacks, ROPE exhibits near-perfect security while compromising far less utility than the best baseline defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xhOwenMa/ROPE.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SST-Guard: Detecting and Characterizing Server-Side Google Analytics in the Wild
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As web browsers increasingly implement anti-tracking features, the web tracking ecosystem has been shifting from the client-side to the server-side. Instead of sending requests directly to the tracker's endpoint, server-side tracking (SST) sends tracking requests to publisher-controlled or intermediary endpoints that then forward the information to trackers from the server-side. As a result, client-side tracking protections are becoming fragile because direct client-to-tracker requests may no longer be observed. In this paper, we investigate the server-side Google Analytics (sGA), the most widely deployed third-party tracking service on the web today. We present SST-GUARD, a multi-modal browser-based approach for detecting sGA. The key insight behind SST-GUARD is that common sGA deployments change the standard Google Analytics endpoints, but still leave semantic artifacts of data collection by Google Analytics in the browser, including identifiers, event metadata, cookies, and JavaScript state. SST-GUARD detects these artifacts using value-templates, which use regular expressions to match semantic value patterns across multiple modalities: network requests, cookies, and the window object, providing robustness against obfuscation of one modality. We validate SST-GUARD on Tranco top-10k websites, detecting 4.0% (401) sGA domains with over 93.0% accuracy across three modalities, with network request classifier demonstrating the highest accuracy (99.8%). Additionally, SST-GUARD identifies atleast 43.2% more websites that integrate sGA as compared to prior approaches. Deploying SST-GUARD at scale, we detect sGA on 6,314 of Tranco top-150K websites. Our analysis shows that many sGA deployments use first-party subdomains, direct A/AAAA records, custom paths, or encoded payloads that circumvent existing defenses. We reported our findings to the authors of EasyPrivacy, who have integrated them.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
Security & Program Analysis.summary: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,δ)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $Θ((\varepsilon β)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $β$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: v2:accepted to Quantum Science and Technology, November 2026, 25pages; v1:23 pages, 2 figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: When Suspicion Adds Up: A Stochastic Framework for Optimizing Honeypot-Based Insider-Threat Detection
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Insider threats pose security risks when employees or other trusted users misuse their access to organizational systems. Detecting these threats is difficult because harmful activity can resemble routine behavior. Honeypots, or decoy resources monitored for suspicious interactions, can provide evidence of potentially malicious activity. We develop a decision framework that models evidence accumulation through honeypot interactions using a continuous-time Markov chain and jointly selects honeypot counts and monitoring horizons to minimize expected losses from malicious activity and false detections. For thresholds of two and three interactions, we derive closed-form true- and false-detection probabilities and expected detection times conditional on detection within the monitoring horizon. We characterize boundary cases and establish stochastic-ordering results. Our numerical results highlight the value of the proposed framework across different settings.

Security & Program Analysis.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Evaluating LIM Trading Agents: A Critical Review of Backtesting Validity and Reporting Practices
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Withdrawn by the submitter because not all co-authors agreed to the posting of this preprint

Security & Program Analysis.title: Why Trust Your Agent? Empirical Security Gains from TRiSM-Guided Agentic Workflows in Healthcare
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agent-based AI has enabled the automation of tasks by exposing application tools and resources to large language models (LLMs). However, to improve scope and accuracy, agents are often given access rights that exceed those of ordinary users, introducing significant security risks and potential regulatory breaches. This paper applies the AI Trust, Risk, and Security Management (TRiSM) framework to a medical report-generation application to demonstrate how an insecure baseline workflow can be transformed into a security-conscious agentic workflow. Both designs were evaluated with five LLMs (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash) across 800 report generations and 500 attack trials covering RAG poisoning, data-field injection and client-side network injection. The redesign reduced attack success from 31% to 10% for RAG poisoning and from 42% to 25% for data-field injection (McNemar p < 0.001 for both), removed network injection by construction, and raised report accuracy from 72.5% to 86.5%. In an exploratory post-hoc grouping by attack goal, success against attacks aimed outside the report task, such as data disclosure and tool abuse, fell from 21.7% to 2.5% and no patient record was disclosed under the redesign. Attacks altering the reported Covid-19 diagnosis remained effective, accounting for 32 of the 35 successful attacks against the redesign. Least-privilege architecture limits what an injection can reach, but not whether a model follows injected content within its task, so clinical outputs need verification independent of the LLM. No model resisted all three attack vectors, so model selection cannot substitute for secure workflow design.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. v2: Substantially revised. Adds threat model and attack-goal analysis; corrects Gemini 2.5 Flash cost figures (output-token price); revises statistical analysis and limitations

Security & Program Analysis.title: Products of Distinguisher Hulls
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The distinguisher hull of two distributions is the convex hull of the pairs of acceptance probabilities of tests in a specified class. We study its behavior under independent products for size-bounded Boolean circuits. We derive a geometric consequence of Dwork and Tankala's supersimulator theorem (FOCS 2026), giving a substantially different proof of approximate product containment for distinguisher hulls. In particular, our construction uses nonadaptive sampling in place of adaptive score corrections.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Multidimensional Reconciliation in Continuous-Variable QKD: Review, Coding Schemes, and Open-Source Simulation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) requires highly efficient reconciliation techniques to operate at low signal-to-noise ratios and long distances. Multidimensional reconciliation addresses this challenge by transforming the physical Gaussian quantum channel into a virtual binary-input additive white Gaussian noise (BIAWGN) channel, enabling the use of modern errorcorrecting codes. In this work, we review the principles of multidimensional reconciliation, with a particular focus on high-dimensional constructions beyond the algebraic dimensions 1, 2, 4, 8. We describe the construction of the virtual channel, discuss practical coding schemes for reverse reconciliation, and analyse their integration with linear error-correcting codes. We also present an opensource simulation framework, HDirac, implementing multidimensional reconciliation for arbitrary dimensions, and use it to evaluate state-of-the-art LDPC codes. The results highlight key trade-offs between dimension, reconciliation efficiency, and frame error rate, providing practical guidance for CV-QKD system design.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Link to the open-source project: https://github.com/aff3ct/HDirac

Security & Program Analysis.title: SCARVA: Interpretable Agentic Reasoning in Software Supply-Chain Analysis
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Complex applications may inherit security vulnerabilities from their dependencies, though a vulnerable dependency does not necessarily endanger the application. Existing tools flag dependencies associated with public vulnerabilities, and more advanced ones analyze the call graph to assess whether the vulnerable code is reachable. However, these approaches are limited to specific programming languages and ecosystems. LLM agents are promising candidates for this task, yet they hallucinate, take shortcuts, and reward hack. As these behaviors are opaque, the agents' conclusions may not be trusted.
  We present SCARVA a framework designed to produce interpretable reports. SCARVA combines advanced agent reasoning with an evidence-collection methodology that assesses the agent's analysis and improves its trustworthiness. Specifically, the ANALYST performs a software security assessment while SCARVA records every tool call, file access, and web request. Then, one or more independent JUDGE agents inspect the ANALYST's result and produce an evidence-backed report. We evaluate SCARVA on 54 manually curated cases, balanced across exploitable, non-exploitable, and vulnerability-free projects, using both open-weight and frontier models. The best ANALYST model, Qwen 3.8, reaches 82% balanced accuracy and surpasses the evaluated proprietary models. Human annotation validates the JUDGE findings: Claude Opus 5.5 performs best, agreeing with annotators in 94% of claim checks. Finally, we discuss the most common failure modes of agents on supply-chain vulnerability assessment.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ChronoPatch: Black-Box Energy-Latency Attacks on Vision-Language Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as generative inference services, where autoregressive decoding makes response length a key determinant of latency and computational cost. This creates an availability risk: adversarial visual inputs can prolong generation and increase serving overhead. Existing energy-latency attacks typically rely on gradients, logits, or token-level feedback, leaving open whether such risks persist when an attacker observes only the final response. We present ChronoPatch, a black-box attack that induces prolonged VLM generation requiring only the final response. It discovers visual delay anchors through response-length-guided evolutionary search, then minimizes perturbation magnitude through subspace-calibrated decision-based optimization. Across four open-source VLMs, ChronoPatch increases inference latency by 47.86%--293.34% and GPU energy consumption by 41.44%--249.70% under a 5% spatial budget. It also induces more repetitive outputs, as reflected by increased n-gram repetition ratios. On three commercial VLM APIs, ChronoPatch increases response length by 37.6%--81.5% and client-observed latency by 1.82x--2.29x under query budgets of 500 per API. These results reveal a generation-based availability risk that persists under final-response-only access and motivate generation-aware safeguards for deployed generative AI services.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Causal Overtaking in Fair Transaction Ordering
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Fair transaction ordering protocols aim to mitigate front-running using replica-local arrival orders, but prior work often assumes a single submission origin for each responsive transaction. We identify causal overtaking, in which corrupted replicas observe a target and submit identical signed copies of a responsive transaction through multiple client entries. The copies' first arrivals at different replicas can collectively provide ordering support that no individual path achieves, allowing the response to execute before its target. We formalize a class of receipt-order protocols, including Themis, characterize the timing and network conditions under which the attack is feasible, and show that delayed gossip does not rule it out. We further prove that, under our network model, histories requiring opposite transaction orders can produce identical receipt evidence. Thus, receipt-only mechanisms cannot always preserve earlier-submission priority while preventing responsive overtaking. We propose a mitigation and analyze its assumptions and limitations. Finally, we evaluate the attack and mitigation on Themis through simulations driven by AWS and WonderProxy latency measurements.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Triosecuris: Formally Verified Protection Against Speculative Control-Flow Hijacking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: This paper introduces Triosecuris, a formally verified defense against Spectre BTB, RSB, and PHT that combines CET-style hardware-assisted control-flow integrity with compiler-inserted speculative load hardening (SLH). Triosecuris is based on the novel observation that in the presence of CET-style protection, we can precisely detect BTB misspeculation for indirect calls and RSB misspeculation for returns and set the SLH misspeculation flag. We formalize Triosecuris as a transformation in Rocq and provide a machine-checked proof that it achieves relative security: any transformed program running with speculation leaks no more than what the source program leaks without speculation. This strong security guarantee applies to arbitrary programs, even those not following the cryptographic constant-time programming discipline.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Appeared at CSF'26; extended version with appendices and a bit more related work. W.r.t. first arXiv version: extended with concrete protection against Spectre RSB and renamed to Triosecuris

Security & Program Analysis.title: Detecting Formation-Preserving GNSS Spoofing of UAV Swarms through Transmitter Parallax in Pseudorange and Doppler
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) detect Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing by checking the drones' reported positions against their known formation. Formation-preserving spoofing evades this check: in GNSS-WASP, one transmitter per satellite, a few kilometres away, shifts the whole swarm while keeping its formation. We show that such an attack still leaves a trace below the position level. Because the transmitters are close, each drone sees them under a slightly different angle, and this parallax bends the signal arrival times across a 90 m swarm by 20-40 cm for a transmitter at 5 km, whatever delays the attacker applies. We propose a likelihood ratio test that reads this trace from the pseudoranges and Doppler every drone already measures, with all clocks and attacker delays unknown and no extra antennas. In simulations with real GPS and Galileo orbits and white receiver noise, 16 drones detect GNSS-WASP at 5 km in 13-60% of 10 s windows in straight flight and in every window during a formation turn with a precise Doppler receiver, where the countermeasure proposed with GNSS-WASP detects at most 5%. The same test also catches single-transmitter and ground-array spoofing.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 16 pages, 7 main figures, 7 main tables. Includes supplementary appendices

Security & Program Analysis.title: BlockJack: Cross-Tenant Redirection Fault Attacks on Paged KV Cache Address Translation in LLM Serving
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Large language model (LLM) serving frameworks accelerate inference by retaining previously computed states in a key-value (KV) cache. Paged serving frameworks such as vLLM organize this cache through block tables analogous to OS page tables, which map each request's logical KV blocks to physical KV blocks, forming a software-managed address translation layer. Although fault attacks such as Rowhammer have exploited OS page tables to redirect memory accesses, prior fault attacks on LLMs have largely targeted the data plane, i.e., model weights or KV-cache contents, leaving KV-cache mapping unexplored.
  We present BlockJack (i.e., Block Hijack), the first KV cache address-translation fault attack in LLM inference. By corrupting block-table entries, BlockJack redirects a request's KV cache reads to blocks assigned to another tenant's request without modifying model parameters, prompts, or cached KV states. It achieves both confidentiality violation (victim information appears in attacker responses) and integrity violation (attacker-supplied context steers victim answers). We study paged KV cache mappings in vLLM and formally characterize when redirect targets are predictable. Across seven models spanning the Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Phi families, a faulted mapping exposes victim context. For the integrity attack, we examine how topic proximity, intra-topic divergence, and model behavior shape redirected responses. On a 248-scene medical benchmark, the integrity attack causes up to 41.1% of responses to recommend less urgent care, while still appearing consistent with the victim's question. We demonstrate physical feasibility of BlockJack with Rowhammer and subsequently evaluate assignment validation as a defense. Following responsible disclosure, vLLM and Sonar confirmed the vulnerability and proposed patches that we reviewed and validated.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Question, Then Affirm: Restoring Commitment Does Not Restore Refusal
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We find that safeguards for image generation can be bypassed without changing what a message says. A sign stating a harmful proposition is blocked, but the same proposition phrased as a question and followed by a check mark is generated, even though the resulting image endorses the original claim. On a 300-case challenge set, gpt-image-2 returns images for 43.3% of question-affirmation requests versus 16.3% of direct statements, with 41.3% versus 15.3% of cases yielding images that endorse the original proposition. We define this as Deferred Semantic Commitment (DSC): commitment is withdrawn by the question and restored by a separate element, while safety behavior follows only the withdrawal. To investigate why, we study an open-weight language model and find that re-endorsement only partially reverses the refusal-related change introduced by questioning. These findings reveal a mismatch between recovered meaning and refusal behavior, motivating safeguards that assess the completed message rather than its individual elements.

Security & Program Analysis.title: RAVEN: A Self-RAG Based Agent for Threat Classification and Response
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Security event analysis in large enterprises can be overwhelming, as each alert typically requires manual in- spection by human operators. This process is time-consuming and prone to inconsistencies, especially in high-volume Secu- rity Operations Center (SOC) environments. In this work- in-progress paper, we present RAVEN: Retrieval-Augmented Vulnerability & Event aNalysis, an agentic framework designed to support SOC analysts by automating the initial stages of alert investigation. The proposed system leverages a Self- Reflective Retrieval-Augmented Generation-based approach to provide an initial classification of security events and enables interactive refinement through analyst-in-the-loop queries. Un- like traditional approaches that rely on generic mitigation strategies, RAVEN generates context-aware remediation sug- gestions by incorporating knowledge of the target enterprise infrastructure. We implement an early-stage prototype and report preliminary results on three balanced test sets of 400 curated web payloads each (SQLi, XSS, SSTI) and a qualitative case study of mitigation generation; an evaluation on IDS- generated alerts and a user study are ongoing and outlined as remaining work.

Security & Program Analysis.title: GPUThor: Amplifying Rowhammer Attacks via Non-Uniform Patterns to Exploit ECC-Protected GPUs
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
GDDR memory in GPUs is vulnerable to Rowhammer attacks, where rapid memory accesses induce bit flips in adjacent cells, enabling data tampering and privilege escalation. However, prior GPU Rowhammer attacks trigger only tens to hundreds of bit flips, orders of magnitude fewer than CPU attacks, severely limiting their practical impact. This gap stems from the reliance of existing GPU Rowhammer attacks on uniform hammering patterns that activate aggressor and decoy rows equally, which results in low hammering intensity for aggressor rows.
  We present GPUThor, a high-intensity Rowhammer attack on NVIDIA GPUs leveraging non-uniform hammering.
