We trace this to imperfect recall: appending an instruction is always cheap, but once an instruction's latent reasoning is gone, deleting it without risking a regression costs O(2^|D|) in a prompt of |D| instructions. Successive edits destroy that latent reasoning, additions outrun deletions and prompts grow until agents become non-functional -- catastrophic remembering. First, we characterize this phenomenon across 247,694 instruction lifetimes in 1,867 repositories: agentic prompts grow nearly monotonically, more than tripling over their lifetime (+226%) at +4.7 net instructions per commit. Deletion hazard decays geometrically with instruction age, consistent with imperfect recall and with no other rival we test. Then, we show that prompt comments can halt the growth: in verifiable worlds built by inverting IFEval, comments encoding latent reasoning remove 99.3% of excess size (+211.3% to +1.4%). Finally, we show comments yield smaller real-world and coding-convention prompts than existing context maintainers, grow more effective with model capability and, at small scale, improve instruction-following in real repositories by 17.7%. If English is the new code, why don't we have comments yet?

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic.
  The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Git History Is a Pangenome: Repetition in Code Training Corpora and What Deduplication Removes, Keeps and Misses
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Code models are increasingly trained on the full history of software repositories, every version of every file, rather than on a single snapshot. The tools that deduplicate training data were built for snapshots, and what they do to a history has not been measured. We measured it on a pre-registered random sample of 306 public repositories, 25 mature projects, and the 12 repositories behind the SWE-bench benchmark. A history is mostly repetition: in the vocabulary of text indexing, a pangenome, one text in many near-identical variants. The history of a typical repository holds the equivalent of 19 copies of its current code, and a mature repository holds 89. The reason is that each edit changes a few lines and leaves the rest of the file in place: nine tokens in ten of a changed file already existed before the change. Exact-match deduplication removes none of these copies, since no two versions are identical. Large training pipelines already deduplicate their snapshots by grouping near-identical files and keeping one. Applied across versions, the same step brings the repetition down to about two copies. But two problems remain. The deduplicator keeps one version of each file, and in widely used implementations, including the one we measured, the rule for choosing that version ignores dates, so for half of all files the version kept for training is an old one. Sorting versions newest first before deduplicating fixes the problem at almost no cost. The second problem is benchmark answers. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench test a model on real bug fixes, and a merged fix survives in a median of 18 later versions of the files it changed. Therefore, removing benchmark fixes needs a separate step that checks every version. We turn the measurements into a short set of rules for teams that train on code history, and release the instruments and frozen outputs.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Your Camera Can Hear You: Side-Channel Acoustic Eavesdropping via Android Camera2 Metadata
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
To prevent motion sensors from acting as covert microphones, Android 12+ caps SensorManager gyroscope and accelerometer rates at 200 Hz by default, requires HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS for higher rates, and throttles sensors back to 200 Hz when the microphone toggle is off. We show that Android's Camera2 subsystem bypasses these defenses. During an active Camera2 session, Camera HAL stabilization pipelines record high-rate gyroscope measurements and export them via vendor CaptureResult metadata. Loudspeaker speech excites chassis vibrations that couple into this path. Across 50 smartphones (2020-2026) from 10 vendors, 37 expose gyroscope metadata via Camera2, and 26 exceed 200 Hz--including six flagship models at 800-1000 Hz, double SensorManager's 400-500 Hz ceiling. This channel requires neither RECORD_AUDIO nor HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS and defeats privacy switches: turning off the microphone toggle does not throttle metadata, and turning off the camera toggle blanks only video frames while 800-1000 Hz metadata keeps streaming.
  To build a zero-profiling attack that generalizes to unseen phones, we introduce Source-to-Leakage Learning (S2L). Prior attacks train on real sensor traces, entangling speech with a specific phone's mechanical resonances and sampling rate. S2L decouples speech content from hardware acoustics using a physics-constrained forward simulator. Trained exclusively on simulated leakage without target-phone traces, our universal recognizer CamEar achieves 52.1% mean word accuracy (up to 61.8%) and 74.3% character accuracy (up to 80.7%) across the six 800-1000 Hz phones. In contrast, ISpyU models fine-tuned on real target-phone data drop to 25.9% word accuracy on unseen phones; CamEar improves cross-device accuracy by 101.4% and outperforms ISpyU's same-device models on every tested phone.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
Security & Program Analysis.summary: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together. The benchmark and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MemJoin-01BF/.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Metadata-Private Voice Communication over Tor using Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Encrypted voice communication systems commonly protect call content but expose significant metadata, including the network identities of both parties, call timing, and traffic patterns. Simultaneously, advances in quantum computing threaten the asymmetric primitives underlying conventional key exchange, creating a harvest-now, decrypt-later risk for long-lived sensitive communications. Existing systems address at most one of these concerns: secure VoIP applications such as Signal and Wire rely on centralized infrastructure and classical cryptography, while anonymous communication tools built on the Tor network support only text messaging and lack post-quantum key encapsulation. This paper presents SAPEC (Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator), a peer-to-peer voice communication system that simultaneously addresses anonymity, decentralization, and quantum resistance. SAPEC routes all traffic exclusively through Tor hidden services, concealing the IP addresses of both parties, and augments the standard TLS handshake with a custom protocol layer that performs ML-KEM-1024 key establishment, a settle on AES-256 symmetrical keys and mutual Dilithium identity verification before any audio is transmitted. All audio is subsequently encrypted under AES-256. A removable Crypto Ignition Key prevents identity key material from being stored on the device. Empirical evaluation across 45 independently circuit-rebuilt test runs yielded a median one-way audio delay of 355 milliseconds and a median connection setup time of 7.61 seconds on same-region Tor circuits, demonstrating that interactive voice communication over onion routing is practically achievable.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 8 Pages, 5 Figures, Project was also presented in the german youth science competition Jugend Forscht under the name SAPEC - Secure Anonymous Peer Exchange Communicator

Security & Program Analysis.title: AnimalFarm: Auditing the Generation and Detection of Hateful Images Featuring Anthropomorphic Characters
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Anthropomorphic non-human characters have long been used to convey hateful messages targeting human groups, from Nazi-era propaganda to recent AI-generated imagery on social media. However, the safety risks posed by such imagery remain largely unexplored. We thus conduct the first systematic study of hateful image generation and detection involving anthropomorphic non-human characters. We construct a benchmark from conservatively screened source scenes, covering five character types and three image generation tasks: text-to-image generation, image editing, and conversational image generation. Across 14,250 scheduled queries, image generation systems produce images for 92.1\% of queries, of which 95.9\% contain hateful content. We further collect 4,370 hateful images and evaluate five popular hateful-content detectors. Even the strongest detector, GPT-5.5, identifies only 73.9\% of hateful images, while most detect fewer than 58\%. Our analysis reveals that existing detectors often misclassify hateful images as benign when their main subjects are non-human characters. We explore two effective mitigation approaches: a training-free pipeline that maps non-human characters back to human representations before classification and a detector fine-tuned for this type of hateful content. These approaches achieve F1 scores of 0.962 and 0.979, respectively. Our findings expose significant safety gaps in both image generation and hateful-content detection.
  Disclaimer: This paper contains hateful text and imagery.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Asymmetric Phase Coding Audio Watermarking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The proliferation of deepfake audio challenges voice-based authentication, and passive forensic detectors are sensitive to evolving generative models and to real-world channel distortions. We propose Asymmetric Phase Coding (APC), a training-free cryptographic signing layer for audio that anyone holding the public key can verify offline, designed as a compact and auditable provenance primitive that can stand alone or be stacked with learned watermarks. APC combines Ed25519 digital signatures (EdDSA, FIPS 186-5; 64-byte signatures) with Reed-Solomon error correction, pseudo-random STFT phase-bin selection, and a redundant quantization-index-modulation (QIM) code on log-magnitude differences of adjacent bin pairs, yielding a compact, non-repudiable, blind-extractable watermark. A successful verification proves who signed the embedded message and that the message is intact. On 1,905 LibriSpeech test-clean clips (10 s, 44.1 kHz) under eight attack configurations (identity, 10% and 20% end-cropping, 8 kHz low-pass, 16 kHz round-trip resampling, FLAC, MP3 at 128 kbps and OGG-Vorbis at 128 kbps), APC verifies 98.3% to 99.8% of clips on every condition at an identity PESQ of 3.82 and accepts no wrong-key or unsigned clip. On 2,048 clips from 18 sets of 15 public corpora spanning music, meeting, telephone, multilingual and mostly vocoded speech, it verifies between 97.1% and 99.4%. It also survives platform processing chains, repeated MP3 and OGG coding at 128 kbps, cropping up to bounds predicted in closed form, integer time shifts through an optional decoder-side search, and the DNS64 and DeepFilterNet3 speech enhancers on most clips, and it verifies a signed 10 s clip in 3.17 ms on one CPU core. We compare APC with neural baselines (reproduced AudioSeal and WavMark, and published SilentCipher results), including a capacity-matched operating point, and show that it stacks with AudioSeal.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). Preprint version. 40 pages, 17 figures, 17 tables. Project page: https://gy19a.github.io/asymmetric-phase-coding-audio-watermarking-js/

Security & Program Analysis.title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed.
  Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

Security & Program Analysis.title: BinXSight: Fast Binary Program Summarization via Hierarchical Modular Decomposition
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Binary code summarization (BCS) is crucial in fields such as cybersecurity. Particularly, program-level BCS can quickly provide a comprehensive overview of an entire stripped binary without in-depth manual reverse engineering. However, a binary often contains numerous functions with complex interactions, making it challenging to extract its functionality efficiently. Moreover, existing methods focus solely on function-level without considering contextual information, limiting their applicability to program-level analysis. Towards comprehensive and fast program-level BCS, we propose BinXSight, an LLM-powered framework based on hierarchical modular decomposition. Specifically, we first propose binary graph, a new data structure composed of four graphs, to comprehensively represent a binary. Then, based on the binary graph, we hierarchically decompose functions into modules and select the most significant ones. Finally, BinXSight generates a program-level summary from these module summaries. We evaluate BinXSight on stripped binaries across various sizes, fields, platforms, and architectures. Results show that BinXSight outperforms baselines by 23.18% to 46.99%, and summarizes a binary with about 3K functions in 24.3 seconds on average. In addition, a user study with 27 experts shows that BinXSight's high-quality summaries help users quickly understand the whole binary. Our case analysis on recent real-world malware further demonstrates its practical utility.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SYSEVOLVE: Safe, Autonomous Attack-Defense Co-evolution for Evolving Cyber Defense
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The offensive capability of large language models (LLMs) has crossed from research demonstration into documented reality. Frontier models have autonomously breached real production systems, and open-weight models now deliver frontier-level exploitation at negligible cost. Existing defenses cannot keep pace with such attacks: human-intensive defense updates over days to weeks, while AI-based defense, on the other side, trained on fixed historical data, does not adapt to an evolving attacker. We trace these persistent failures to one root cause: defense evolves in isolation, cut off from the adversary that should be driving its evolution. That isolation manifests at three layers: the deployment layer, the capability layer, and the adversarial layer. To build a defense that evolves at the speed of attack, we propose co-evolution as the integrating insight, replacing isolated evolution with mutual driving between attack and defense. Based on this insight, we present SysEvolve, a safe and autonomous co-evolutionary system built from three co-designed components, SysField, SysSpear, and SysArmor. SysField constructs realistic multi-host ranges via declarative topology-driven construction. SysSpear generates efficient, safe attack schemes via task-sliced local search, a bidirectional expert-knowledge base, and static-analysis verification. SysArmor performs real-time, interpretable defense via state tracking, CTI-context fusion, and stage-matched response. In evaluation, SysField achieves zero-loss collection at 2.1\% overhead and orchestrates 257 CVEs into 1,148 ranges. SysSpear improves red-team success by over 25\%, attains the best completion on complex multi-vulnerability ranges. SysArmor achieves 10--1000$\times$ greater precision than prior systems and detects real APT attacks in production at Huawei and Sangfor. Our evaluation also reveals four findings about LLM agent capabilities.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Technical Report For SysEvolve System, version 261120

Security & Program Analysis.title: Post-Quantum Migration in Brownfield 5G Core Networks: Verified Hybrid Key Establishment, Performance, and Rollback
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Migrating brownfield 5G Core networks to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is difficult because deployed network functions, base images, and TLS libraries evolve under different upgrade constraints. This paper evaluates a deployment-controlled migration strategy that enables hybrid post-quantum/traditional key establishment through externally deployed Boundary Cryptographic Execution Entities (BCEEs), without modifying participating network function source code. The approach is evaluated using the Open5GS AMF-NRF Service-Based Interface as a representative 5G Core scenario. Classical and hybrid configurations are compared under an unchanged mediation topology. Packet-level analysis confirms successful negotiation of X25519MLKEM768, and functional validation demonstrates that representative SBI procedures remain operational through the mediated path. In 120 NF-registration transactions, the median AMF-facing registration latency increased from 22.968 ms under the classical state to 26.351 ms under the hybrid state, reflecting a 3.383 ms (14.73 percent) increase, with a whole-block 95 percent confidence interval of [1.193, 7.872] ms. At the mediated TLS boundary, the hybrid configuration shows a 4.599 ms higher median segment-local TLS-establishment time than the classical configuration. These two reported differences reflect system-level runtime effects and do not isolate key-encapsulation cost. Packet evidence verifies rollback from hybrid-mediated operation to classical mediated operation and, separately, restoration of the native direct path. NF-facing compatibility legs remained plaintext and outside the hybrid post-quantum scope. The results demonstrate a packet-verifiable and manually reversible brownfield mechanism for introducing hybrid post-quantum key establishment on a controlled 5G SBI segment.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted at ICCSAI 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
Security & Program Analysis.summary: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Too Fast to Doubt? Skipping Reasoning Leaves Jev-like Models Vulnerable
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Fast decision models offer low-latency actions and explicit confidence estimates. We audit four state-of-the-art decision models on 1,440 paired synthetic browser tasks, injecting false conclusions or evidence interpretations through external comments. Across models, clean accuracy averages 91.0%, yet two-shot attack success reaches 81.2%. Mean expected calibration error rises from 2.6% on clean inputs to 36.7% under conclusion poisoning and 36.1% under evidence poisoning. Clean accuracy and calibration therefore do not ensure reliable decisions under injection. We further compare GPT-6 Luna and Luna Decisions, which share the same base model, on 48 matched tasks. With a chain of thought averaging fewer than 30 reasoning tokens per response, low-effort GPT-6 Luna answers 95.83% of poisoned inputs correctly, versus 38.54% for native Luna Decisions, while mean selected-generation latency increases from 0.29 to 1.94 seconds. These results expose a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: skipping reasoning for sub-second speed leaves fast decision models substantially more vulnerable to deceptive web content.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Differentially Private Manifold Denoising
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Modern data analysis increasingly relies on manifold-based methods that use local geometry to extract low-dimensional structure from noisy observations. Yet in domains such as biomedicine and public health, privacy regulations restrict access to individual-level data, while perturbations introduced to protect privacy can distort the geometric information needed for analysis. We introduce a manifold denoising framework that uses private reference data to correct noisy public queries, bringing differential privacy to local geometric estimation. Starting from a hard correction based on the estimated tangent space, we develop a noise-adaptive soft correction that avoids specifying the intrinsic dimension. Furthermore, we construct a shared Gaussian field that couples evaluations across locations and bandwidths with moderate marginal noise inflation. Under standard assumptions on manifold regularity and sampling density, we establish non-asymptotic utility guarantees that characterize how denoising accuracy depends on sample size, noise level, bandwidth, and the privacy budget. Simulations and UK Biobank applications demonstrate accurate signal recovery under moderate privacy budgets. These results illustrate clear utility--privacy trade-offs and provide a practical DP component for manifold-based workflows in regulated environments.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Forensic Analysis of Metadata and Information Leakage in Swedish Public Documents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybersäkerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Manipulation-resistant reputation for peer-to-peer scientific publishing: a combination-therapy approach
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In open peer-to-peer networks, where publishing is nearly free and identities are cheap, reputation systems decide what deserves attention, and their metrics become targets for manipulation. We study how to choose and combine reputation signals so that manipulation does not pay while genuine contribution does. Inspired by combination therapies in medicine, we describe each gaming action by its effects on all signals. For aggregation by the minimum of the signals, we prove that, in a global linear model, either some mix of gaming actions raises every signal by more than it costs, or the net gain of gaming is bounded by the imbalance of the attacker's honest profile; locally, gaming brings no first-order gain exactly when an admissible weighting is supported on the attacker's weakest signals. We then specify, without implementing it, MagMell, a two-tier system for peer-to-peer scientific publication: a protocol that orders signed events by Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus, enforces budgets and settles staked assessments, and open reputation algorithms that any node can run. Simulations on synthetic data show that minimum aggregation makes networks of fake identities, collusion rings and floods of generated papers lose rank beyond small intensities, at the price of a lower correlation between rank and quality for honest accounts. They also show that criticism is rarely settled, because the evidence needed is seldom available. The replicated log should grow by about 26 kilobytes per identity and year (analytic estimate), and a full recomputation of reputations takes 1.0 to 1.6 seconds for 100,000 identities (measured).

Security & Program Analysis.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Mjolnir: Finding and Reproducing Vulnerabilities in Root-of-Trust Firmware and RTL with Project-Grounded Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
A root of trust (RoT) anchors secure boot and attestation for the system above it, so a bug in RoT firmware or hardware undermines every layer that trusts it. LLM agents now find real vulnerabilities in general-purpose software, but RoT code presents two challenges. First, many security-relevant bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic vulnerability patterns, and may cause no crash. Second, without RoT hardware, agents must exercise RoT inputs through the project's own hardware model, mocks, or RTL testbenches.
  We present Mjolnir, an agentic pipeline that supplies each project's threat model and design conventions to discovery and skeptical review agents, and reproduces surviving findings as proof-of-concept tests in the project's own toolchain. We evaluate Mjolnir on six firmware and RTL targets in Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT. On Caliptra's runtime firmware, it reaches 83.3%-100% precision across three models under blind expert labeling, including 100% on Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for four single-agent baselines on the same model. On 34 known security-relevant bugs in Caliptra's core firmware fixed after the models' training cutoffs, it finds 10 with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 7 for the best baseline, and 17 with Gemini 4 Argon versus 12. Across our evaluation scans, maintainers have confirmed 64 of Mjolnir's findings as previously unknown security-relevant bugs: 37 across three models on Caliptra's runtime firmware and 27 across single scans of the other five targets.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Quadratic Gradient: Accelerating Privacy-Preserving Logistic Regression Training with Homomorphic Encryption
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Training logistic regression over encrypted data has emerged as a prominent approach to addressing security concerns in recent years. In this paper, we introduce an efficient gradient variant, termed the \textit{quadratic gradient}, which is specifically designed for privacy-preserving logistic regression while remaining equally effective in plaintext optimization. By incorporating this quadratic gradient, we enhance Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient (NAG), Adaptive Gradient (AdaGrad), and Adam algorithms. We evaluate these enhanced algorithms across various datasets, with experimental results demonstrating state-of-the-art convergence rates that significantly outperform traditional first-order gradient methods. Furthermore, we apply the enhanced NAG method to implement homomorphic logistic regression training, achieving comparable performance within only four iterations. The proposed quadratic-gradient approach offers a unified framework that synergizes the advantages of first-order gradient methods and second-order Newton-type methods, suggesting broad applicability to diverse numerical optimization tasks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely. We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
Security & Program Analysis.summary: There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Poisoning Attacks and Collaborative Defense Framework for LightRAG-Based Construction Regulation Knowledge
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used in construction, yet the security of building-regulation knowledge bases has received little study. This thesis reports a pre-registered experiment on one fully instrumented LightRAG system built on the UK Approved Documents. Using a 150-item benchmark labeled with safety consequences and tampering directions, it evaluates four attacks (text layer, graph layer, fabricated amendment narrative and a defense-aware adaptive attacker) together with a three-layer retrieval-graph-generation defense in a full factorial design. Text-level poisoning succeeded, with success rising with the budget; graph-level poisoning was less effective, contrary to the registered hypothesis. The full defense met the registered criterion and six of the seven configurations met its threshold, but those containing the generation layer did so by refusing 69-80 percent of poisoned queries, costing up to 74 points of clean accuracy, whereas provenance-based retrieval filtering cost no measurable clean accuracy in the configuration used. A second experimental batch showed that excluding a legitimate unregistered amendment caused no measurable loss of accuracy either, as its wording reached the generator through the graph's entity and relationship descriptions, the route the poison took, which no layer inspects. Interactions were strong, so no layer's contribution can be isolated. A reported zero attack success rate is not evidence of detection unless the refusal rate is reported with it: zero arises either because provenance filtering removes every document outside the manifest without judging its content, or because the system refuses. Layered defenses must therefore be evaluated factorially, and regulatory RAG assistants require corpus admission control and version-aware verification before they can support safety-critical decisions.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Master's thesis, SWISS UMEF, November 2026. 60 pages, 35 tables, 10 figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

Security & Program Analysis.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

Security & Program Analysis.title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
Security & Program Analysis.summary: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Suspected Until Inspected: Neuro-Symbolic Detection of Broken Access Control in Server-Side Web Applications
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Broken access control (BAC) has topped the OWASP Top 10 since 2021. Unfortunately, a decade of detectors still leaves a gap on every front. Static analyzers are tied to one language or framework, dynamic testers cover only the endpoints they manage to exercise, and LLM-based auditors leave the final verdict to an error-prone model. In this paper, we design and implement FLINT, a neuro-symbolic framework that detects BAC in server-side web applications without language- or framework-specific rules. Our key insight is to separate the proposal from the verdict -- an LLM may flag any data access as needing a guard, but only a symbolically verified check can clear it. The neural component enumerates every endpoint and distills each, via demand-driven code slicing, into an authorization certificate whose claims are all grounded in cited code. The symbolic component verifies each claimed check through origin tracing and a lattice-based interprocedural dataflow analysis, so that no access is cleared on the model's word. When applied to popular real-world open-source applications, including Gitea, Grafana, and Strapi, FLINT detected 112 zero-day, exploitable BAC vulnerabilities, 30 of them in projects with over 20,000 GitHub stars. We have responsibly disclosed all of them to the developers. Mattermost, for example, has already confirmed our report and is assigning a CVE identifier.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Differentially Private Contrastive Learning via Bounding Group-level Contribution
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Differentially private (DP) contrastive learning aims to learn general-purpose representations from sensitive data, alleviating privacy leakage concerns associated with embedding models trained on private user content. However, standard contrastive objectives compare each sample with all other samples in the batch, so a single record affects the gradient of every sample in the batch. These inter-sample dependencies make it difficult to bound each record's influence while retaining useful training signals under DP.
  We propose DP-GCL, a DP contrastive learning framework that jointly localizes contrastive dependencies and bounds the resulting gradients. Its core module, Bounding Group-level Contribution (BGC), partitions each batch into disjoint groups, restricts comparisons to within-group samples, and clips each group's gradient separately before aggregation. This design confines each record's influence to one group while allowing signals from multiple groups to accumulate under a sensitivity bound independent of the number of groups. Because grouping reduces the available negatives, we further introduce intra-group sample augmentation to enrich local negative views without additional privacy cost.
  Across eight datasets, DP-GCL improves image classification and image-text retrieval accuracy over the strongest baseline by an average of 5.6 and 20.0 percentage points, respectively. Further ablation studies indicate that these improvements arise primarily from the joint design of group-local contrastive objectives and group-level gradient clipping. Moreover, DP-GCL exhibits favorable batch-size scaling and remains compatible with diverse network architectures and parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies such as LoRA.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Proactive Defense Benchmark against Deepfake Generation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Despite the proliferation of proactive defenses against deepfakes, the lack of a unified evaluation protocol precludes fair comparison and masks critical vulnerabilities. To bridge this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark that systematically assesses disruption, robustness, and transferability encompassing pixel, perceptual, and identity metrics. Our extensive analysis reveals that fidelity and identity metrics capture orthogonal performance axes, often leading to conflicting interpretations when relied upon individually. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental trade-off where peak white-box performance signals overfitting, and we introduce a calibrated evaluation to correct generator-induced identity bias. By exposing these blind spots, we establish a rigorous standard to guide the development of genuinely generalizable protections. Project page is available at: https://proactivedefensebenchmark.github.io/

Security & Program Analysis.title: PCC: Proof-Carrying Credentials for Enhanced Anonymity and Post-Quantum Delegation
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Delegatable Anonymous Credentials (DACs) support anonymous exercise of authority delegated through intermediaries, as in DeFi credit delegation. Existing DACs require holders to possess and process chain-shaped lineage material for presentation. We call this limitation \emph{prover awareness}: presentation cost grows with delegation depth, while holder-visible topology can enable lineage-based vetoes, strategic disintermediation, and de facto censorship.
  We formalize the privacy dimension as \emph{Enhanced Delegation Anonymity} (EDA), a leakage-parametrized two-observer notion combining verifier-side anonymity with holder-side topology obliviousness. We give simulation and indistinguishability formulations over paths with identical allowed holder leakage. Our framework, \emph{Proof-Carrying Credentials} (PCC), addresses both limitations by replacing the explicit chain with a recursively updated proof-carrying state via Non-Uniform Incrementally Verifiable Computation (NIVC). PCC makes presentation independent of delegation depth and hides topology beyond permitted leakage, while preserving restricted delegation and expressive presentation.
  Unlike pairing-based constant-size DACs, PCC is hardness-agnostic and admits a post-quantum-compatible instantiation in the QROM using transparent FRI-based recursion and hash-based signatures. On consumer-grade hardware, the Halo2 instantiation keeps a constant 7.344\,KB verifier-facing proof with 35--36\,ms verification across all tested depths. The 128-bit Plonky2 instantiation keeps a constant 157.9\,KB proof with 3.8\,ms verification across depths $L\in\{1,2,4,8,16\}$, at 1.03\,s per delegation step. These results demonstrate practical depth-independent presentation and holder-side topology hiding.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty step can still end in a violation. We call this failure correct-precedent generalization and find it in 13 open-weight models from nine developers. A single correct precedent can cut the safe rate of the most affected agent roughly in half, and the risk compounds when a refused request is simply sent again in a new session. Interventions on the agent's history indicate that it carries its decision on the released item over to the restricted one instead of checking that item's status. Building on this finding, we propose Paired Decision Distillation (PDD), which distills the decisions of a weakly affected teacher into a LoRA adapter. PDD restores the safe rate to nearly 100% in every distilled model, without extra prompt text or model calls.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. To address these issues, we target the bottleneck at the ciphertext operation level. Concretely, we propose a novel packing strategy that supports batching over a flexible number of inputs, making it well-suited for fine-tuning workloads. In addition, we design operation-specific matrix evaluation algorithms that significantly reduce (i) the number of ciphertext rotations and relinearizations, and (ii) the number of bootstrapping invocations. Additionally, we exploit functional bootstrapping to fold the evaluation of element-wise activation functions directly into the bootstrapping step, thereby reducing overall computational complexity. As a result, our framework achieves a $30\times$ reduction in ciphertext rotations and relinearizations across all matrix operations, as well as a $2.5\times$ reduction in FHE bootstrapping invocations over the entire computation flow, compared to the latest state-of-the-art work. It is worth noting that our system completes fine-tuning of a 2-layer BERT-style model with a batch size of 16 in 650 seconds, achieving a $8\times$ speedup over the state-of-the-art work.

Security & Program Analysis.title: "More Than You Expect!": Leakage-Abuse Attacks on Encrypted Vector Search
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Vector databases support semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embeddings, queries, and record labels may contain sensitive information. Although encrypted vector search protects these contents, some schemes expose records retrieved together across queries. We identify semantic neighborhood leakage, whereby co-retrieval relationships derived from access patterns reveal semantic categories of encrypted records and queries. We present SAGE (Semantic Access-pattern Graph Exploitation), a passive, persistent leakage-abuse attack that infers record labels and query categories from access patterns. SAGE builds a weighted co-retrieval graph and offers two variants requiring different auxiliary knowledge. SAGE-Dist matches anonymous spectral groups to semantic categories using estimated class proportions and refines labels via optimal transport, without known record labels. SAGE-Known combines graph-based label propagation with spectral-group anchor voting using a small set of known labels. We evaluate SAGE on four text and image datasets. With 1% known record labels, SAGE-Known achieves up to 84.3% mean record-label accuracy and outperforms the strongest corresponding baselines on all four datasets. With only estimated class proportions, SAGE-Dist achieves 66.9% record-label accuracy and 68.1% query-category accuracy on AG News, exceeding the strongest corresponding baselines by 21.8 and 41.9 percentage points, respectively, though performance varies across datasets. Experiments with a real-world DCPE implementation (Fuchsbauer et al., SCN'22) show that semantic leakage persists under encrypted approximate retrieval. These findings expose privacy risks even when vector contents remain protected.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Fool's Gold: Defensive Deception Against Safety-Removal Attacks on Open-Weight Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Safety alignment in open-weight language models is trivially removable: abliteration projects a refusal-mediating direction out of the weights in minutes, and no release-time defense we are aware of prevents it durably. What cannot be prevented can be deceived. Our defense, decoy hardening ("Fool's Gold"), concedes the refusal strip and poisons its payoff: once refusal is stripped, most answers to hazardous operational requests are confident, fluent decoys whose critical elements are falsified. Decoys are trained inside a differentiable simulation of the attack, expressing only in the attacked state; a refusal pin and benign leash hold clean-state behavior to the original. We instantiate it on seven models from five families (9B-122B, dense and mixture-of-experts). On the six models passing our pre-registered efficacy gate, 0.51-0.90 of attacked-state responses to held-out prompts are decoys, +0.27-0.84 attributable to the defense; all six stay within registered benign-behavior and capability budgets; the seventh (smaller) fails the gate (boundary case). Rates replicate on a frozen test split or untouched strata. The claim is epistemic: without independent ground truth, no observation surface we tested separates falsified answers from correct ones - on external red-team benchmarks' CBRNE-adjacent slice, the defended 122B is fatally wrong on 0.82-0.86 of matched-quality answers vs at most 0.10 undefended. Repeated sampling does not restore trust: element-wise consensus at K=64 reconstructs a fully usable procedure on 0.083-0.625 of prompts where the instrument validates, vs 0.58-0.96 undefended, with no label-free way to tell the regimes apart; on the weakest such model the claim is per-draw only. We evaluate chemical and biological hazards; the defense does not address in-context jailbreaks and protects only the initially released defended weights.

Security & Program Analysis.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Mega-MMDF and DeepfakeBench-MM: Benchmarking Multimodal Deepfake Detection Across Diverse Forgery Pipelines
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Audio-visual deepfakes can spread misinformation and enable impersonation, undermining trust in digital media. However, existing datasets provide limited coverage of forgery operations and their combinations, constraining detector development and systematic evaluation. We introduce Mega-MMDF, containing 100,000 real and 1.2 million forged clips across 22 pipelines spanning modality-specific manipulations, stacked forgeries, and joint audio-video generation. To assess its training value and enable fair comparisons, we develop DeepfakeBench-MM, which standardizes training and evaluation across 8 datasets and 10 detectors. Training-based detectors achieve their highest mean AUC when trained on Mega-MMDF, with gains of up to 0.0784 over the best alternative training dataset for each detector. Experiments on data scale and pipeline coverage further support the value of large, diverse training data. Cross-pipeline evaluations reveal bidirectional and asymmetric generalization. Training on composite forgeries does not necessarily enable detection of their constituent operations in isolation. Our analysis of altered inputs shows that modality masking can increase false alarms and missed detections, and temporal misalignment can raise mean predicted forgery probabilities. Together, these resources provide a foundation for understanding and improving multimodal deepfake detection, with publicly available code and dataset access subject to application and usage terms.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Preprint. Mega-MMDF dataset is applicable at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SCLBD/Mega-MMDF. DeepfakeBench-MM is available at https://github.com/SCLBD/DeepfakeBench-MM

Security & Program Analysis.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

Security & Program Analysis.title: What's on Your Mind? Exploring Privacy of Mental Health Apps
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Therapy and life-coaching apps have grown rapidly in popularity, yet their users often share highly sensitive information, including mental health issues, trauma, and relationship difficulties. This prompts the need to examine privacy practices across the ecosystem. In this paper, we present a comprehensive analysis of 25 popular Android mental health and life-coaching apps, combining static analysis, dynamic network traffic analysis, and identifying gaps between observed app behavior and privacy policies.
  Our analysis highlights serious concerns and substantial transparency gaps. First, all but one app embeds at least one tracker SDK not named in its privacy policy, and 90\% of the apps we instrument fail to disclose at least half of their detected trackers. Second, more than half of the apps declare dangerous permissions without corresponding privacy-policy disclosures, including camera or microphone permissions. Third, 14 of the 25 apps disclose third-party AI processing, but only five name the providers (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, and Groq), while the others use only generic language (e.g., "AI services").
  Overall, our results highlight shortcomings in current disclosure practices that undermine meaningful informed consent. We argue for stronger privacy protections for therapy apps, more closely aligned with the confidentiality expectations associated with licensed human therapists.

Security & Program Analysis.title: No-Box Vulnerability Analysis: Description-only Detection of Indirect Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in MCP Servers
Security & Program Analysis.summary: When auditing remotely hosted services or commercially gated software for vulnerabilities, third-party analysts may lack both direct system access and the ability to interact with the running system. We call this a no-box setting, in which analysts have access only to functionality metadata that may describe the intended inputs, behaviors, and outputs of the system. Such descriptions constrain the possible implementations of a system, enabling analysts to hypothesize potential implementations and their underlying vulnerabilities. These hypotheses can subsequently guide validation when system access becomes available. To demonstrate the feasibility of conducting vulnerability analysis under no-box setting, we implemented MCPSEC, a prototype that audits Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for indirect prompt injection vulnerabilities using only the tool metadata exposed at server registration time. Flagging vulnerable tools, MCPSEC produces hypothesized vulnerabilities and attack scenarios for later validation. We evaluated MCPSEC on 20 widely deployed MCP servers comprising 177 tools, among which human evaluators confirmed 95 as vulnerable. Using only tool metadata, MCPSEC successfully identified 94 of these confirmed vulnerable tools (98.9% recall), compared to 81 (85.3% recall) identified by an agentic baseline. Overall, we operationalize and evaluate no-box vulnerability analysis and demonstrate its practical feasibility in realistic systems.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Pre-registration: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23608308. Results dataset: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24238904

Security & Program Analysis.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 8 pages, 3 tables; open-source code and osaudit-verified manifests at https://github.com/AlienatedAliens/epistemic-guard (v0.5.2)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Railroads as Cyber-Physical Systems: Cybersecurity Implications of Increasing Automation -- Threats, Consequences, and Operational Resilience
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Objectives: Rail automation improves train protection, traffic management, inspection, and operational efficiency but increases dependence on software, communications, remote access, and external providers. This paper examines its impact on railroad cyber-physical system security and operational resilience.
  Methods: A narrative review synthesizes railroad automation literature, OT security guidance, FRA and TSA materials, and documented rail cyber incidents. Automation functions are mapped to exposed assets, attack vectors, and operational consequences, focusing on signalling, communications, onboard systems, remote access, and human oversight.
  Findings: Automation shifts rail risks from isolated mechanical failures toward interconnected cyber-physical dependencies. Key vulnerabilities involve train detection, positioning, signalling, grade crossings, remote diagnostics, vendor access, and AI-enabled monitoring. Cyber incidents can cause operational disruption, supply-chain impacts, and national-security risks, even when fail-safe mechanisms prevent catastrophic outcomes.
  Novelty: The paper introduces a rail-specific taxonomy connecting automation functions, cyberattack pathways, operational consequences, and resilience requirements, framing cybersecurity as an operational rather than purely IT concern.
  Practical Applications: The framework supports security-by-design procurement, IT/OT segmentation, secure remote access and software updates, degraded-mode planning, trusted recovery, and human oversight. Operators and regulators can use it to assess automation deployments and mitigate cyber risks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The emergence of writable, cross-session persistent memory in LLM agents introduces a qualitatively different threat landscape from conventional input-centric security concerns, characterized by three properties: persistence, statefulness, and propagation. To systematically characterize this landscape, we propose a Memory Lifecycle Framework that organizes attacks, defenses, and their cross-phase dependencies along two axes: six lifecycle phases (Write, Store, Retrieve, Execute, Share & Propagate, Forget & Rollback) and four security objectives (Integrity, Confidentiality, Availability, Governance). This analysis in turn exposes the need for explicit security requirements at the system level, motivating Verifiable Memory Governance (VMG), a framework of five architectural primitives for specifying and evaluating auditable, recoverable control over memory state within declared system and threat-model boundaries. Our analysis motivates integrating provenance, versioning, and policy-aware retention with retrieval and execution defenses to support auditable prevention, containment, and recovery across the lifecycle.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Expanded version of the EMNLP 2026 paper. Adds evidence on persistent representations, skill memory, authorization changes, and recovery. Table 4 compares lifecycle security claims and their evaluation conditions

Security & Program Analysis.title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
