Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Random Feature Neural Networks for Stochastic Optimal Control
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Random feature neural networks (RFNNs) sample their hidden parameters once and train only the output layer. We analyze RFNNs as feedback policies for finite-horizon stochastic control with trajectory-dependent objectives. A policy change alters later states, so the error that matters is the objective error of the induced trajectory rather than a pointwise regression error. We extend the quantitative random-feature approximation theory for PDE solutions and nonlinear regression to feedback control. We investigate the objective error of an RFNN policy through two sources, approximation of the policy by random features and estimation of the objective from finitely many paths. A stability estimate for the controlled trajectory turns a policy error into an objective error. Under bounded actions, a regular benchmark policy and exact empirical minimization, the expected objective gap to the benchmark policy is at most of order $N^{-1/2}+\sqrt{N(1+\log N)/n}$, with $N$ the feature width per output coordinate and $n$ the number of paths. At fixed sample size the two terms trade off in $N$, and balancing them gives $N\asymp\sqrt{n/\log n}$. Across a wide range of examples, estimated gaps generally decrease with width and sample size, and RFNNs show an advantage when simulated paths are limited. We also study Parsimonious Random Feature Learning (PRFL), which grows and prunes the random dictionary during training while training only the output coefficients. At matched retained width and training budget, PRFL improves on a fixed RFNN in the LQ and Heston comparisons, while the fully trained network remains best in those examples.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary:
Aligning large language models (LLMs) to serve users with heterogeneous and potentially conflicting preferences is a central challenge for personalized and trustworthy AI. We formalize an ideal notion of universal alignment through test-time scaling: for each prompt, the model produces $k\ge 1$ candidate responses and a user selects their preferred one. We introduce $(k,f(k))$-robust alignment, which requires the $k$-output model to have win rate $f(k)$ against any other single-output model, and asymptotic universal alignment (U-alignment), which requires $f(k)\to 1$ as $k\to\infty$. Our main result characterizes the optimal convergence rate: there exists a family of single-output policies whose $k$-sample product policies achieve U-alignment at rate $f(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}$, and no method can achieve a faster rate in general.
  We show that popular post-training methods, including Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF), can fundamentally underutilize the benefits of test-time scaling. Even though NLHF is optimal for $k=1$, sampling from the resulting (often deterministic) policy cannot guarantee win rates above $\tfrac{1}{2}$ except for an arbitrarily small slack. This stems from a lack of output diversity: existing alignment methods can collapse to a single majority-preferred response, making additional samples redundant. In contrast, our approach preserves output diversity and achieves the optimal test-time scaling rate. In particular, we propose a family of symmetric multi-player alignment games and prove that any symmetric Nash equilibrium policy of the $(k+1)$-player alignment game achieves the optimal $(k,\frac{k}{k+1})$-robust alignment. Finally, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for self-play learning dynamics in these games and extend the framework to opponents that also generate multiple responses.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: A preliminary version of the paper is accepted to ICML 2026. This version adds new results for the multi-output opponents setting and self-play dynamics with last-iterate convergence

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: How Systems Treat Intent: A Faceted Taxonomy of Intent for Human-AI Co-Creation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable. Literature organizing systems by interaction technique, workflow stage, or division of labor, offer limited insight into which facet of intent an interaction mechanism addresses. We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues. Our analysis reveals that different forms of incomplete intent are associated with distinct interaction and authorship strategies, showing that mechanisms that appear similar often address fundamentally different intent-related problems. This exposes blind spots, as intent is rarely represented as an interaction object, authorship provenance is rarely tracked, and tentative preferences are rarely distinguished from firm commitments. The taxonomy offers a lens for analyzing and designing AI systems around the facets of intent they address.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using an exploration schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. An efficient recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bringing the overall time complexity per step to $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3+D\log D)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Boosting Brain-to-Image Decoding with TRIBE v2 Data Augmentation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Brain decoding is limited by the availability of labeled neural data, and remains challenging in low-data regimes. To address this issue, we investigate whether and when brain decoding can be boosted by augmenting small fMRI datasets with synthetic data generated by a pretrained model of fMRI responses to stimuli. We use TRIBE v2, a large encoding model pretrained on more than 1000 hours of fMRI responses to video, audio and language. For each dataset, we evaluate systematic grids that show how the performance of image decoders varies with the amount of synthetic data used for training. Our results, based on two datasets (the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset and 3T fMRI BOLD5000), show up to 68% improvement in Top-10 image-retrieval accuracy compared to decoders trained only on real data. Importantly, the proportion of augmented data required to reach a given image decoding performance needs to be adjusted depending on the data source. Surprisingly, image decoders trained exclusively on synthetic fMRI can perform above chance in some settings, suggesting that TRIBE v2 can support zero-shot brain-to-image decoding. Together, these results show how large-scale models of the fMRI responses to sight, sound and language may provide a foundation to improve the data efficiency for image decoding.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual fea- tures together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp- transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask- support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D- to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment- specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: PVFormer: Proper Velocity Transformer for Stable and Scalable Hyperbolic Representation Learning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Hyperbolic representations have shown remarkable success on hierarchical and tree-like data, and Transformers have become a central architecture for representation learning. However, a principled construction of hyperbolic Transformers remains challenging because the self-attention layer decomposes into three coupled primitives, transformation, similarity, and aggregation, that should all respect the underlying geometry. Existing hyperbolic Transformer designs are typically built in the Poincaré or Lorentz models, where bounded domains, time-like constraints, tangent-space detours, or projection steps make it difficult to keep the full block intrinsic and scalable. To address this gap, we propose PVFormer, to the best of our knowledge, the first Transformer architecture that operates natively in proper velocity (PV) space. The proper velocity model provides an unconstrained representation of hyperbolic geometry, and PVFormer exploits this structure to redesign the Transformer block in PV space. On the transformation side, we use PV homomorphism transformations to update query and value representations. On the similarity side, we generalize Euclidean inner-product attention with a PV Busemann score inspired by Busemann-based hyperbolic learning and a PV point-to-hyperplane key transformation. On the aggregation side, we replace Euclidean averaging with PV midpoint aggregation and further derive a scalable PV linear attention variant for large graphs. Extensive experiments support the effectiveness of PVFormer across graph, text, and vision benchmarks.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SignalCount: Approximate Counts with Structured and Semantic Predicates in Seconds
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 28 pages. Project page: https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and code: https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 37 pages, 15 figures, 15 tables. Submitted to International Conference on Learning Representations 2027. Code, videos and full results are available at https://hhi-robot-learning.github.io/wave-website/

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design with Minimal Human Priors
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for automated heuristic design (AHD), enabling iterative generation and refinement of heuristics. However, the dominant paradigm embeds LLMs as narrow, fixed components, such as crossover or mutation, within heavily hand-engineered evolutionary frameworks. We argue this misapprehends LLMs. It treats them as specialized tools rather than general reasoners, constrains them to low-level operations, and underutilizes their autonomy. Moreover, the extensive human priors in these frameworks violate the bitter lesson principle that general methods scaling with computation surpass hand-crafted solutions. This raises a key question: which AHD framework designs best convert stronger LLM capabilities into better heuristics? To address this, we propose metrics for LLM-driven AHD framework handcraftedness (AHI) and intelligence conversion efficiency (ICE). Evaluating ten LLMs across three challenging combinatorial optimization problems, we obtain a notable finding that frameworks with fewer human priors consistently yield higher ICE. Based on this finding, we propose SimpleEvol, an agent-loop framework for AHD which removes nearly all human priors and allows the LLM to operate autonomously. SimpleEvol consistently achieves the highest ICE, often by a large margin. Our results challenge the trend toward complex AHD pipelines and point to a lighter and more model-centric alternative, suggesting that reducing human priors is a more effective strategy to scale up with model intelligence. The source code is available at https://github.com/HenryZhu1029/SimpleEvol-Master.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SchemaCaps: When a Compatible Tool Update Silently Widens an AI Agent's Authority
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The tools users approve for their AI agents keep changing their JSON input schemas. Of 8 surveyed MCP clients and scanners, none is observed or documented to re-approve a tool whose input schema widens (two not determinable). We define non-amplification over the coordinates visible in the schema (declared arguments and undeclared fields, on effective values) and a re-binding rule decided by subschema inclusion, trusting no field labels by default and conservative up to its checker and tested case analysis. Evidence: a Coq proof of composition; 48 regression tests; an exact-reference benchmark, where the reviewed version of the rule silently re-bound 27 amplifying changes, now fixed; and a pilot on 604 releases of 39 public MCP servers. There, 412 of 580 compatible schema changes widen some coordinate, yet compatibility re-binds them silently. The authors' adjudicated double annotation finds at least 76 that add or widen an authority-bearing argument (66 of the 84 a name-based labeller flags, plus 10 it misses). On existing tools, the rule asks 645 re-approvals, against 1,197 for pinning the input schema (2,004 with descriptions) and 617 for compatibility. Behaviour change behind an identical schema remains out of reach.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Author's accepted version (without the publisher's layout). Accepted at ICAART 2027; final version published by SCITEPRESS. Artefact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24233014

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Accepted at ICAART 2027; final version published by SCITEPRESS. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24233094

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. We derive the exact asymptotic bias and give a chain of checks from identification to simultaneous ranks. On a four-agent semi-synthetic benchmark, a scalar correction with oracle calibration has maximum bias 0.245 and mean pointwise coverage 0.016, and never recovers the full ranking (0/250 replications). Augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with a uniform or a design-aware random audit keeps the maximum bias below 0.003, with mean pointwise coverage of 0.939 and 0.950. In a 48-cell stress test, effective target support rises only from 0.209 to 0.805 as calibration grows from 600 to 4,800 labels, while audited AIPW keeps a mean absolute error of 0.018-0.020. Without calibration support, or with judge dependence within an externally justified bound, we report valid bounds or sensitivity sets and carry them into rank sets. An e-process confidence sequence stays valid, for a stable target, under predictable adaptive auditing and arbitrary stopping.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Author's accepted version (without the publisher's template) of a paper accepted at ICAART 2027 (paper \#38). The final version will be published by SCITEPRESS; DOI to be added upon publication

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Can Cities Have Personalities? Introducing the SCD City Personality Assessment
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Descriptions of cities are shaped by human experience and institutional narratives. We introduce the SCD City Personality Assessment (SCD-CPA), a method that instantiates document-grounded ChatGPT city personas and interrogates each with an identical 24-statement instrument inspired by the four-pair structure of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. Rather than asking a general-purpose model to characterize cities freely, we configure a separate document-grounded conversational agent for each city and use alternative evidence portraits to compare documentary inputs. The resulting four bipolar dimensions and four-letter summaries use independently defined urban concepts and scoring rules. Tokyo, New York, and Paris form the methodological evaluation (33 assessments across repeated sessions, three GPT-6 effort settings, and alternative portraits): Tokyo's original portrait yielded 85.4% exact within-setting item agreement, while evidence substitutions shifted some dimension strengths. A five-city application to Shanghai, Dubai, Mumbai, Lagos, and Sao Paulo (15 assessments) yielded 77.8% exact and 99.4% within-one-point cross-setting agreement, indicating consistency under the tested configurations. By treating each city conversational agent as a reproducible, evidence-conditioned experimental configuration, SCD-CPA makes documented city-character perceptions comparable and exposes their sensitivity to source selection. Although the documentary evidence is explicitly controlled, the model's internal interpretation of that evidence cannot be fully observed. We also examine the robustness of SCD-CPA across three AI reasoning-effort settings. The observed consistency suggests that the methodology is relatively insensitive to the tested configuration differences and provides a framework for evaluating its stability as future generations of AI models become available.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary research materials: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24466311

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Testing Quantized KV-Cache Maintenance: Encoding Layout and Historical Restoration
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Repeating rows then selecting originals retains layout-dependent drift despite equal encoding counts. We measure when existing checks fail to establish preservation contracts in fixed quantized KV-cache implementations. In four-bit HQQ axis zero at sixteen cycles, median paired relative-L2 increases over same-shape re-encoding are 7.22 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B and 11.59 for SmolLM3-3B. Matched encoded states cover sixteen shared questions per model at one and sixteen cycles. Axis one matches the shape-preserving control; lazy reorders preserve the initial state. On one known input, fixed update counts retain the difference; preserving group members removes it. Our prefix-view extension passes current-prefix checks yet changes history and next logits in six model/codec settings at residual capacities four and 128. Public lookup reaches this boundary, including one of four precommitted project-new GPU inputs; fixed query swaps isolate a conditional old-history effect. Checkpoint/dense rollback is exact. An explicit delayed lookup client admits a supported 129-token path excluded by native AR on one known context. Failed task-harm expansion precludes population failure-rate or general answer-degradation claims. Native MLX-LM fixtures expose stale caller caches; synchronization restores the tested in-place contract with native computations preserved. In rejection tests, stale callers change logits but not greedy tokens.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Skill-Composer: Requirement-Driven Skill Selection from Multiple Marketplaces
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Agent skills have become the primary vehicle through which agents reuse specialized capabilities, yet public skill marketplaces provide skills with individual items: a query, whether matched through keyword or embedding similarity, returns a list of single skills ordered by relevance or by popularity. Such an interface cannot answer the question a developer actually faces: which set of skills should be installed to cover a task's complete requirement? The highest-ranked skills are often functionally redundant, while capabilities that are genuinely required remain uncovered. In this paper, we argue that skill acquisition should be reframed from ranking to set selection. We propose Skill-Composer, an agent-native framework that selects a non-redundant skill bundle for the user requirement, which aims to cover all available required capabilities and report any gaps. Specifically, it clarifies user requirements into atomic requirement points, retrieves and merges candidate skills across fragmented marketplaces, decomposes each candidate's capabilities, and progressively discards overlapping ones, so that each retained skill provides different capabilities. This moves the decision of which skills to acquire from the developer to the agent itself. We position this reframing and sketch its workflow.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Belief Engine: Making Agent Stance Auditable in LLM Deliberation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: LLM-based AI agents are increasingly used to simulate deliberative social interactions, including negotiation, conflict resolution, and multi-turn opinion exchanges. Simulating human-like opinion change calls for agents that balance existing beliefs with openness to new evidence, while making their responses to that evidence traceable. Current systems often make this difficult: agents may drift from assigned roles, echo an interaction partner, keep a stance despite contrary evidence, or appear to change because the prompt or retrieved context has changed. We introduce the Belief Engine (BE), a framework that uses "belief" in a Bayesian modelling sense, as a maintained evidential state over a proposition that is exposed as a scalar stance. BE extracts structured evidence, stores argument records, and updates the belief state through a Bayesian-inspired stance update in log-odds space with two interpretable controls: evidence uptake u and prior anchoring a. Across multiple LLM models, sweeps of u and a demonstrate stable control over stance dynamics. Higher uptake makes agents more responsive to new evidence, while stronger anchoring preserves the initial stance. On DEBATE, a human deliberation dataset with pre/post opinions, BE is most accurate when participants move in the direction of extracted evidence, showing its strength in evidence-following deliberative contexts. When all participants are evaluated together, gains are more modest because many people remain stable or move for reasons not captured by the extracted evidence stream. BE provides a configurable and auditable belief-update layer for evidence-grounded deliberation, in which LLM agents can be configured as open-minded, anchored, or evidence-sensitive, while their stance trajectories and memory can be audited, compared, and calibrated against human opinion change.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 29 pages, 11 figures including appendices

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Contextual Distributionally Robust Optimization with Causal and Continuous Structure
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: WWe propose a framework for contextual distributionally robust optimization (DRO) that considers the causal and continuous structure of the underlying distribution, and we develop interpretable and tractable decision rules. We first introduce the causal Sinkhorn discrepancy (CSD), an entropy-regularized causal Wasserstein distance that encourages continuous transport plans while preserving causal consistency. We then formulate a contextual DRO model with a CSD-based ambiguity set, termed Causal Sinkhorn DRO (Causal-SDRO), and derive its strong dual reformulation, where the worst-case distribution is characterized as a mixture of Gibbs distributions. To obtain an (infinite-dimensional) optimal policy, we propose a soft regression forest (SRF) decision rule: it preserves the interpretability of classical decision trees while being fully parametric, differentiable, and Lipschitz-smooth, enabling intrinsic interpretation from both global and local perspectives. To solve Causal-SDRO with parametric decision rules, we develop an efficient stochastic compositional gradient algorithm that converges to an $\varepsilon$-stationary point with $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ iteration complexity and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-5})$ sample complexity. Finally, numerical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance and interpretability of our method.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: AI for Games in the Foundation Model Era
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Foundation models, alongside advances in learned game-world models, are reshaping AI across the game lifecycle. Beyond playing games, recent systems model players and game dynamics, support design and development, adapt player-facing experiences at runtime, and evaluate resulting artifacts. Yet these directions have evolved largely separately, obscuring which capabilities transfer across settings and which remain tied to particular games, engines, interfaces, or player populations. We organize the literature into six roles according to the immediate use of AI output: playing and acting; modeling players and games; designing games; building and maintaining games; generating and adapting at runtime; and testing and evaluating games. For each role, we examine what structure is supplied by the game or workflow, what AI learns or produces, which capabilities and artifacts transfer across settings and roles, and what evidence supports the claims. We identify cross-role connections: trajectories train world models, learned environments provide experience for agents, design specifications drive executable implementations, and play or testing feedback guides revision. Evaluation is most standardized for bounded game playing and selected learned environments, while persistent state in learned worlds, repeated software revision, validated player modeling, sustained runtime adaptation, and representative automated testing remain less established. The central challenge is to reuse or transfer outputs and capabilities across roles while re-establishing evidence for effectiveness in the game-specific contexts where they are used.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: How Many Parameters Does Forecasting Need? A Survey and Code-Level Audit of Lightweight Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Long-term time series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, weather and finance, where forecasts are produced continuously and often on constrained hardware. Recent work has moved in two directions. One scales Transformers and pre-trained foundation models to millions or hundreds of millions of parameters. The other shows that models with only hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters remain competitive on the standard benchmarks. Existing surveys organize forecasting models by backbone and treat efficiency as a side topic, so the reasons these small models work, and the way their sizes are reported, remain unexamined. This survey focuses on lightweight long-term forecasting. It provides a taxonomy of about thirty-five models in six families, with a common notation and an architecture diagram for each core model. It offers a structured-linear view in which the smallest models are linear maps restricted by frequency truncation or period folding, and it tests each restriction in closed form on eight benchmarks. It complements the literature review with an audit of sixteen official code repositories, which reproduces published parameter counts and reveals reporting gaps of up to 289 times. Finally, it gives practical guidance on model selection and reporting, and summarizes open problems.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Looped architectures provide an inductive bias toward learning step-by-step procedures for tasks that require compositional reasoning. Increasing the effective layers of looped architectures can improve their reasoning capabilities. Similar to deep architectures, looped architectures are prone to a signal propagation problem induced by depth as the halting decision is postponed. In this paper, we address the signal propagation issue by using pre-norm layers and residual scaling. By improving signal propagation, we achieve competitive performance without hierarchical looping, resulting in a simpler architecture than previous state-of-the-art models evaluated on puzzle reasoning tasks. Building on these modifications, we propose FPRM: a Transformer-based Fixed-Point Reasoning Model that uses fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism in a looped architecture. We show that fixed-point halting allows FPRM to adapt its compute to the difficulty of the task. FPRM proves effective on common reasoning benchmarks, namely sudoku, maze, state-tracking and ARC-AGI.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Uncovering Hidden Behaviours in Language Models via Limited-Parameter Finetuning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore limited-parameter finetuning (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. While training 3-25% of LoRA parameters, LPF reveals whether the model has a hidden behaviour, even when standard behavioural evaluations cannot. LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8-14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27-35B parameters). LPF can thus distinguish between models which appear behaviourally identical to an auditor, and does not require the context in which the hidden behaviour surfaces. LPF provides a novel affordance that may be useful for auditing frontier AI models. However, we do not evaluate LPF against baselines in a realistic auditing setting, so further work is needed to determine its practicality.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. 53 pages, 19 figures, 6 tables

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Rhythm-TTS: High-Fidelity Shortcut Latent Modeling and Probabilistic Rhythm Generation for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) systems are commonly built on either discrete codec tokens or continuous acoustic representations. Discrete-token models benefit from stable sequence modeling and explicit speech factorization, but they ultimately synthesize speech through codebook lookup and codeword composition, which can accumulate errors and impose a quality ceiling on naturalness and speaker similarity. Continuous-representation models can generate fine-grained speech latents directly, but often require heavier in-context modeling and less explicit alignment. This paper presents Rhythm-TTS, a shortcut zero-shot TTS framework that combines the factorizability of discrete codec tokens with the fidelity of continuous latent generation. Instead of using predicted codec tokens as the final acoustic representation, Rhythm-TTS uses them as a semantic-acoustic prior and directly generates holistic continuous speech latents with flow matching, bypassing the discrete-to-latent reconstruction path at inference time. We further address an underexplored dimension of speech naturalness: rhythm diversity across multiple synthesis runs. Motivated by the hypothesis that rhythm variation is largely governed by phoneme duration changes and the occurrence of silent pauses, we introduce probabilistic Duration and Silence Generators to sample dynamic pacing patterns before acoustic generation. Experiments on zero-shot TTS benchmarks evaluate intelligibility, naturalness, speaker similarity, efficiency, and run-to-run rhythm diversity, showing that the proposed shortcut latent modeling and probabilistic rhythm generation improve the fidelity and temporal naturalness of non-autoregressive zero-shot TTS. Code and audio samples are available at our demo page https://rhythm-tts.github.io.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Beyond the Black Box: A Diagnosis-Driven Agent for Interpretable MIP Solver Tuning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary:
Tuning a mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver is an instance-specific problem, where a poor configuration can increase solving time by orders of magnitude.
  Existing Bayesian optimization tuners treat solver tuning as a black-box optimization problem: each evaluation returns a single score, allowing the tuner to learn which configuration is faster, but not why.
  Inspired by the use of profilers in GPU-kernel optimization, we introduce APEC (Agent for Per-instance Explainable Configuration), a log-grounded tuning agent for MIP solvers.
  APEC has three layers: a deterministic layer that profiles each log, an interpretation layer that guides hypothesis-driven diagnosis, and a system layer that controls evaluation, enabling more reliable and interpretable solver tuning.
  On the full MIPLIB 2017 benchmark set, APEC achieves a 1.58X improvement over the default configuration with over 38% fewer parameter changes than the baselines, making the results easier to read.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: ActField: Learning Action Effects as Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Learning how actions change visual states is essential for prediction and decision-making in embodied tasks. Existing action-conditioned JEPA world models typically predict future representations at discrete observation intervals, leaving the temporal evolution of action effects implicit. We introduce ActField, a continuous-time JEPA world model that explicitly models latent state evolution through an action-conditioned vector field integrated over physical time. ActField separates action-independent evolution from action-induced changes, with the latter modulated by the latent context. A reference-conditioned representation and multi-step dynamics loss further support accurate long-horizon prediction. Together, these components provide a structured and temporally continuous formulation for predicting action-conditioned visual dynamics. Experiments across LIBERO, DROID, and BEHAVIOR demonstrate improved visual prediction fidelity and more accurate action-induced motion prediction over existing world models. Further evaluations on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate the utility of ActField in improving downstream policy planning through VLM-guided action selection.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. To overcome this, we propose a generation-based black-box framework that infers context-induced information gain from targeted token discrepancies. We introduce a budget-constrained auditing regime, building on the empirical observation that the membership signal is highly sparse and concentrated in a few highly informative tokens. We formalize this sparsity, showing why uniform sampling needs many more samples than a policy that targets informative positions. Empirically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art black-box separation accuracy while needing about 3x fewer queries than uniform position sampling. Finally, we apply this methodology to closed frontier models, exploring its capacity and limits in surfacing potential training data overlaps on commercial APIs.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SpikeSTAG: A Dendritic Compartmental Spiking Graph Network for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a distinctive paradigm for temporal modeling through their intrinsic membrane potential dynamics. However, existing SNN-based forecasting methods focus exclusively on temporal processing, lacking mechanisms to capture spatial dependencies among variables. To bridge this gap, we propose SpikeSTAG, a neuromorphic spatiotemporal architecture that integrates graph-based spatial reasoning into spike-driven temporal computation. Central to our approach is the Dendritic Graph Module, which reinterprets spectral graph convolutions as biological dendritic integration --- coupling multi-scale spatial aggregation with the temporal dynamics of spiking neurons within a single computational unit. To adaptively fuse the resulting spatial and temporal representations, we further introduce a Dual-Stream Integration Module that employs competitive gating and coincidence-based amplification, selectively enhancing consistent spatiotemporal patterns while suppressing conflicting noise. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpikeSTAG establishes a new state-of-the-art among SNN-based models and surpasses representative ANN baselines, while reducing theoretical energy consumption by approximately 66.7\% compared to Transformer architectures.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: GeoMerge-OPD: Balanced Skill Integration in Vision-Language-Action Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Safety alignment trains large language models (LLMs) to refuse harmful requests. However, a request can keep its operational content and still change how the model interprets it, and refusal training covers such "recontextualised" requests only weakly. To study this gap, we propose the ASCII Attack, a single-turn black-box jailbreak. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in an assembly of ASCII-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks the model for "artistic feedback". ArtPrompt masks a sensitive word that the model must decode. In contrast, the ASCII Attack hides nothing and changes only the social frame of the request. In order to separate the effect of this frame from topic, model and decoding effects, we pair every framed prompt with a matched direct-question control on the same request. The control also omits the scene description and the missing-information list, so the contrast measures the framing bundle rather than the frame alone. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, the JailbreakBench classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of their controls. With a single query, the ASCII Attack matches or exceeds ArtPrompt and DeepInception under four of five harm judges. We further show that the effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not fall with scale, which is consistent with mismatched generalisation.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: 36 pages: 12 pages main text (including references) plus 24 pages supplementary material

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Neurosymbolic Learning for Inference-Time Argumentation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Claim verification is an important problem in high-stakes settings, including health and finance. When information underpinning claims is incomplete or conflicting, uncertain answers may be more appropriate than binary true or false classifications. In all cases, faithful explanations of the considerations determining the final verdict are crucial. We introduce inference-time argumentation (ITA), a trainable neurosymbolic framework for ternary claim verification in which a formal argumentation semantics giving the strength of claims and arguments is used both (i) to guide LLM training as models learn to generate arguments for and against claims and assign them base scores (representing intrinsic strengths) and (ii) to compute ternary (true/false/uncertain) predictions from generated, scored arguments. As a result, at training time, argument generation and scoring can be optimised according to the quality of the induced argumentative predictions. Moreover, at inference time, the final prediction is faithful, by construction, to the arguments and scores determining the verdict, rather than being justified by a potentially unfaithful post-hoc reasoning trace as in conventional reasoning models. We finally show that, on two datasets for ternary claim verification, ITA improves upon argumentative baselines and can perform competitively against non-argumentative direct-prediction baselines, while providing verdicts that are computed deterministically from explicit, inspectable argumentative structures. Our code, models and data are available at https://github.com/CLArg-group/inference-time-argumentation.
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.comment: Published as a conference paper at NeurIPS 2026

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: JaxNaviSim: A GPU-Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator and Learning Benchmark for Maritime Navigation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: HOSE: Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure for Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Text-to-image diffusion models can generate harmful or sensitive content, such as pornographic or violent imagery, raising serious security concerns. Model editing has recently emerged as an efficient approach to mitigate this issue. It modifies pretrained models with minimal parameter updates to alter specific concepts while preserving overall model capabilities. However, due to the entangled representations of different concepts in diffusion models, direct modifications inevitably disrupt non-target concepts. Meanwhile, U-Net's hierarchical heterogeneity hinders unified strategies from balancing erasure and quality. To address these issues, we propose Hierarchical Orthogonal Subspace Erasure (HOSE). This method projects parameter updates into the subspace orthogonal to general knowledge, thereby eliminating interference with non-target concepts. Considering the hierarchical heterogeneity of the U-Net architecture, we further propose a hierarchical adaptive mechanism, constructing differentiated subspace projections for different layers to precisely adapt to the model's hierarchical structure, thereby resolving the inherent trade-off between erasure and image quality in unified constraints. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method reduces harmful content generation by 80% compared with the unedited model. While it inevitably incurs some image quality degradation, it still outperforms other editing-based baselines in terms of quality preservation, and achieves a significantly better trade-off between harmful content suppression and quality loss than these baselines. Notably, our approach demonstrates higher adversarial robustness than existing SOTA method, indicating that the target concepts have been more thoroughly erased. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sevenqiiu/HOSE.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Bring Back Language to Actions: Restoring VLM capabilities in VLA Models via Parameter Merging
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are obtained by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) on robot demonstration data, enabling action prediction from visual observations and language instructions. However, this fine-tuning induces catastrophic forgetting, substantially degrading the semantic and visual grounding capabilities of the original VLM. We address this by merging the parameters of a VLM and its VLA derivative without retraining either model. Concretely, we extract the task vector (the difference between VLA and VLM weights) and decompose it via Singular Value Decomposition. For each component, we learn a scalar mixing coefficient controlling how much of the VLA adaptation is retained, optimised to jointly preserve action prediction and vision-language capabilities. Experiments show that our merged model performs well on both axes simultaneously, consistently outperforming established merging baselines.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Interrogation Protocols for AI Control
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.
