Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: What Frame-Level Labels Can and Cannot Do for Small-UAV Point Detection in Thermal Video
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: The growing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) has increased the importance of image-based UAV detection. Learning-based detectors are trained on imagery and annotations, with annotation type determining the information available during training. We focus on learning localization from frame-level target presence/absence labels when sensor or scene changes make spatial annotations for additional training burdensome. We analyze the detection capability, learning behavior, and potential applications of an existing architecture for point detection of small UAVs, trained with presence/absence labels and requiring no external detector. The architecture freezes spatial features learned through classification and trains a readout with the same frame labels to produce spatial score maps and point detections. On two thermal infrared datasets, CST Anti-UAV and Anti-UAV410, we evaluate localization hit rates and detection rates under false-alarm constraints, analyze the effects of training stages, label allocation, synthesis, and model configuration, and compare with bounding-box detectors. We also explore potential applications on Airborne Object Tracking (AOT) using its visible-light imagery and frame labels. Classification training strengthened target-related spatial responses, while readout training helped extract them consistently. Distributing similar label counts across more videos yielded higher localization hit rates, while synthesis effects varied by dataset and evaluation criterion. Higher localization hit rates did not always improve detection under false-alarm constraints, and failures remained when target signals were weak relative to background variation and under cross-dataset transfer. These findings provide guidance on label allocation, spatial representations and readouts, synthesis, and false-alarm control.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Splitting Belief Bases Conditionally based on Constraints for c-Representations and their Solutions
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Splitting notions for conditional belief bases aim at localizing reasoning and computation tasks to subbases containing only the relevant parts of the belief base. Among the different reasoning mechanisms, c-representations, a special kind of Spohn's ranking models, have been shown to provide high-quality inferences. c-Representations can be conveniently specified via a constraint satisfaction problem. In this article, we introduce the notion of conditional constraint splittings, extending constraint splittings by also allowing the subbases to share conditionals. Taking inspiration from conditional syntax splittings, we identify the subclasses of safe and fully localized conditional constraint splittings, allowing us to locally and independently solve the constraint system on the subbases. We also generalize solution splittings for c-representations to safe conditional c-solution splittings and provide an in-depth analysis of their relationship to conditional constraint splittings. Additionally, we elaborate on the relationship of these new splitting notions to safe and generalized safe conditional syntax splittings and also to safe covers, which have been proposed for localized computation of c-representations.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($π_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Reproducible by Seed? Not on GPUs: Batch-Dependent Non-Determinism in Text-to-Image Models
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In text to image AI models, fixing the prompt and the random seed is widely assumed to fix the image. We show that it does not on GPUs. We evaluate six text-to-image models (diffusion and autoregressive) under four numerical precisions and quantizations on three GPU types (RTX A6000, RTX 6000 Ada, and H100 NVL), across up to 100 prompts per set for all six models. For each configuration we compare, with the prompt and seed fixed, the image generated alone with the image generated inside a batch, and we also compare across GPUs. Every replay control reported here is bit-exact, so the variation is not random noise: the execution setting, mainly the batch composition and the GPU, decides the output. The effect is large and model dependent. Structural similarity between the single-image and the batched output falls to 0.580 for an autoregressive model in bf16 and to 0.551 with int8. For a second autoregressive model in bf16 it falls to 0.261 with sampled decoding and to 0.229 with greedy decoding, and for an fp8 diffusion model to 0.68. A diffusion model in bf16 stays close to the batch-1 output (0.96-0.98) but changes every image. In most cases the batched image is a different but equally valid image; in some, such as prompts with digits and counters, it is visibly worse. Cross-GPU differences are of the same order as the batch effect: for one autoregressive model in bf16 compared across two GPU architectures (RTX 6000 Ada versus RTX A6000), no image is bit-identical and the cross-GPU LPIPS (0.355 to 0.383) matches the batch effect within one GPU (0.347 to 0.381). The consequences are direct: seeds do not make results reproducible, benchmarks and image-quality comparisons that mix batch sizes or hardware can be biased, and safety audits and A/B tests on generated images need the serving setup reported.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: HyperCLOVA X 32B Think
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, a vision-language model designed with particular emphasis on reasoning within the Korean linguistic and cultural context, as well as agentic ability. HyperCLOVA X 32B Think is pre-trained with a strong focus on reasoning capabilities and subsequently post-trained to support multimodal understanding, enhanced reasoning, agentic behaviors, and alignment with human preferences. Experimental evaluations against comparably sized models demonstrate that our model achieves strong performance on Korean text-to-text and vision-to-text benchmarks, as well as on agent-oriented evaluation tasks. By open-sourcing HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, we aim to support broader adoption and facilitate further research and innovation across both academic and industrial communities.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Hereditary permutations for simple types revisited: A baby case for University Algebra
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: It is a classical result that the definable isomorphisms of the simply typed $λ$-calculus with function types are exactly the hereditary permutations, and that they are generated by $A \to B \to C \cong B \to A \to C$ and congruence. We give a new proof of this result that stays inside $β$-normal $η$-long typed terms and uses no completeness theorem: an induction that descends through both components of an isomorphism at once. It proceeds by showing that both components are linear terms: relevance follows from one of the inverse equations, and no copying from relevance of the other component. We then go one level up and prove a coherence theorem: two derivations of an isomorphism denote the same isomorphism if and only if they are equal modulo an explicit list of equations (groupoid laws, functoriality, involution, naturality and the braid equation), so these equations present the groupoid of isomorphisms, a hereditary version of the Coxeter presentation of the symmetric groups. All results are formalised in Agda, on intrinsically typed syntax with hereditary substitution, without postulates. The work is a case study for the syntactic completeness conjecture of University Algebra, a proposed solution of Tarski's high school algebra problem using dependent types, whose semantic counterpart is open. We explain the motivation and which parts of the method we expect to carry over.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Obaleth: Build Your Own GPU Communication Stack
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Machine learning systems specialize computation to the workload and hardware, but communication remains in generic libraries whose device code and transport decisions are not visible to high-level compilers. We present Obaleth, a compiler that makes GPU-initiated communication part of a kernel's intermediate representation, co-optimizes it alongside computation, and lowers it to specialized transport code. Obaleth plans completions around buffer lifetimes and optimizes memory ordering, synchronization, and batching across NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. On H100 GPUs, Obaleth sends small messages up to 3.3$\times$ faster, and on 256 GPUs runs all-to-all 1.25$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ faster than NVSHMEM and NCCL GIN, with much smaller memory and register use. In vLLM, it serves Qwen3-235B on 16 B200 GPUs and answers requests up to 1.29$\times$ faster than with DeepEP.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Sheaf Semantics of Probabilistic Programs
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Finding denotational models of probabilistic languages that support sampling from continuous distributions is difficult: the existence of continuous distributions means that measure-theoretic objects are needed to define the semantics. A challenging task on top of this is logical reasoning with respect to the semantic model: in the case of probabilistic programs, the desired properties to reason about include the distributions, expected value and the probabilistic (in)dependence of outputs.
  This paper introduces a monadic semantics for higher-order probabilistic programs with continuous distributions based on Simpson's theory of probability sheaves and the internal logic of atomic sheaves. We prove that our semantics forms a model of the $ν$-calculus. Furthermore, using the well-behavedness of the semantic domain and the internal logic of the topos, we derive the first higher-order probabilistic Hoare logic with rigorous treatment of continuous random variables, higher-order functions, and independence.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Accepted to POPL 2027

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Ziv: A Language for Correctly Rounded Math Libraries
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Developing performant, correctly rounded math libraries is challenging. Such implementations often rely on extended-precision arithmetic for correct rounding and precomputed constants for performance. Existing implementation languages, however, provide limited support for (i) high-level abstractions for such arithmetic and (ii) staged computation to combine precomputation and runtime computation in one program. As a result, existing implementations often miss abstraction opportunities and hard-code constants precomputed using separate programs. These practices make it difficult to write, understand, and modify these libraries.
  We present Ziv, a programming system for developing correctly rounded math libraries. It consists of a small language, a rich standard library, and a provably sound compiler targeting C. Ziv supports (i) high-level numerical abstractions via types and operations for extended-precision numbers, and (ii) staged computation via compile-time evaluation of expressions known to be input-independent. These features enable high-level code that unifies precomputation and runtime computation. We embed Ziv in Julia and evaluate it by reimplementing 19 functions from two state-of-the-art libraries targeting correct rounding; we achieve competitive performance with 2.63$\times$ reductions in lines of code. We also implement three new functions and automatically explore 824,256 variants, achieving 96.5$\times$ average speedup over an arbitrary-precision library.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Tenon: A Unified Programming Framework for Retargetable PIM Compilation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) is emerging as a building block of heterogeneous systems for memory-bound workloads, and commercial prototypes now span near-bank SIMD engines, bank-level GDDR accelerators, programmable DRAM cores, and bit-level in-SRAM processors. Their programming stacks are fragmented: no abstraction or compiler is shared across vendors, and per-device models range from instruction sequences to C-like languages. Data layout further complicates the problem: tight compute-memory integration makes data layout a first-order optimization, yet existing PIM compilers lack a unified way to represent and optimize it. A key observation is that PIM compilation targets can be modeled as nested grids of compute and storage units connected by legal data-transfer paths. We present Tenon, a unified programming framework for retargetable PIM compilation. It decouples workload, compilation target, and cost specifications, so a workload is expressed once and compiled through a unified programming framework. Tenon generalizes the $\mathbb{F}_2$ linear layout algebra from GPU compilers to map logical work and data onto these compute and storage grids. It automatically constructs a minimum-movement data layout given a workload and a target specification. We evaluate Tenon on six PIM backends: five commercial backends and AttAcc, a state-of-the-art academic HBM-based PIM architecture. Across the commercial backends, it matches or outperforms vendor, expert, and compiler baselines, with geometric-mean speedups of up to $1.20\times$ and individual speedups up to $3.65\times$. For end-to-end GPT-13B decoding on AttAcc, Tenon-compiled workloads run $1.2$--$1.3\%$ faster than those compiled by DCC, a state-of-the-art PIM compiler, across all three batch-4 configurations. Together, these results demonstrate Tenon's performance portability across diverse PIM target families.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: HPCA 2027

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: StatClaim: Study Designs as Types, Protocols as Programs and Statistical Claims as Proof Obligations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Statistical guarantees depend on the compatibility of a study's model, hypotheses, sampling plan and analysis. StatClaim is a declarative domain-specific language for encoding research protocols and statistical analysis plans as programs built from objects whose types encode their statistical roles within the study design. The compiler checks type compatibility and applies contracts to check additional requirements on the values and relationships of these objects. When verification is requested, StatClaim's backend constructs and checks proofs of supported statistical claims using Lean under stated assumptions. These claims concern Type I error, familywise error, power and interval coverage, including supported combinations of analyses and procedures with planned stopping rules. Reports distinguish formally proved, conditional, cited and author-declared guarantees and provide replayable certificates for verified claims. The same specification supports sample-size searches, power calculations and interval-precision assessment using exact calculations, analytical approximations or reproducible simulation. A command-line interface, editor integration and graphical block editor use a shared compiler and execution layer. Validation reproduces 102 optimal and minimax two-stage designs from Simon's published tables and verifies their error and power bounds in Lean. A clinical trial case study illustrates partial encoding of a published analysis plan using cited methods and conditional proofs. The open-source implementation includes runnable tutorials and examples for specifying and checking study designs before outcomes are collected.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Includes ancillary example programs and replication helpers

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Compositional Symbolic Execution à la Carte (Extended Version)
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: We introduce compositional symbolic execution à la carte, a modular approach for building compositional symbolic execution (CSE) tools, powered by combinator-based design of key components, including memory models, management and automation of user-defined predicates, and bi-abductive analysis. Our approach is grounded on meta-theory mechanised in the Rocq proof assistant and allows tool developers to easily build correct-by-construction CSE tools for symbolic analysis of their programming languages of choice, with minimal implementation and proof effort. We show how our approach scales to real-world languages by implementing it in Gillian, a state-of-the-art CSE tool, and using it to capture the intricacies of the memory models of C, JavaScript, and Rust. We evaluate our approach by running all of the relevant previous case studies of Gillian, showing no unexpected behaviours and comparable performance.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Extended version, with appendices, of the corresponding POPL'27 paper

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Omnidirectional type inference for ML: principality any way
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
The Damas-Hindley-Milner (ML) type system owes its success to principality, the property that every well-typed expression has a unique most general type. This makes inference predictable and efficient. Unfortunately, many extensions of ML (GADTs, higher-rank polymorphism, and static overloading) endanger princpality by introducing _fragile_ constructs that resist principal inference. Existing approaches recover principality through directional inference algorithms, which propagate _known_ type information in a fixed (or static) order (e.g. as in bidirectional typing) to disambiguate such constructs. However, the rigidity of a static inference order often causes otherwise well-typed programs to be rejected.
  We propose _omnidirectional_ type inference, where type information flows in a dynamic order. Typing constraints may be solved in any order, suspending when progress requires known type information and resuming once it becomes available, using _suspended match constraints_. This approach is straightforward for simply typed systems, but extending it to ML is challenging due to let-generalization. Existing ML inference algorithms type let-bindings (let x = e1 in e2) in a fixed order: type e1, generalize its type, and then type e2. To overcome this, we introduce _incremental instantiation_, allowing partially solved type schemes containing suspended constraints to be instantiated, with a mechanism to incrementally update instances as the scheme is refined.
  Omnidirectionality provides a general framework for restoring principality in the presence of fragile features. We demonstrate its versatility on two fundamentally different features of OCaml: static overloading of record labels and datatype constructors and semi-explicit first-class polymorphism. In both cases, we obtain a principal type inference algorithm that is more expressive than OCaml's current typechecker.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: updated to reflect the final TOPLAS version; 46 pages + appendices

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: CrossCheck II: A Compiler Plugin for Certified Cost Bounds of Real-Time C and C++ Code, and its Evaluation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: We describe a plugin for the Clang compiler that bounds the cost of C and C++ functions intended for real-time use, and rejects at compile time the functions that allocate, throw, call through pointers, or contain a loop or a recursion for which no bound is found. Loops are bounded by affine ranking potentials synthesized with an SMT solver through Farkas' Lemma, or by logarithmic ones, recursion by depth and size potentials, and callees are analyzed in the calling context in which they are used. For functions in a linear fragment, the plugin emits a cost certificate that a checker, compiled from a Lean~4 definition proved sound in a companion paper, validates with integer arithmetic only; the bound then depends neither on the analyzer nor on the solver. On the 29 kernels of the TACLeBench collection, without annotations, the plugin bounds 142 of 220 loops in the calling contexts of the programs, 131 of them exactly as the benchmarks' flow facts, and 161 of the 165 bounded functions receive a certificate that the checker accepts, 152 of them also validated against an independent description of the source. On the CMSIS-DSP library for Cortex-M (786 functions), with assumed input ranges, it bounds 616 functions. We compare the loop bounds with loop counts observed by running the kernels and with five existing analyzers (LLVM's ScalarEvolution, KoAT2, CoFloCo, Infer and oRange), and the plugin with KoAT2 and CoFloCo on the C programs of the Termination and Complexity Competition: without annotations, 147 of 553 programs receive a certified bound that holds for all inputs, where the two tools bound 288 and 264. Loop bounds, exported annotations and the checker program are also tested on random programs and on mutated certificates.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 23 pages. Companion of "CrossCheck I" (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24444576), which holds the theory and the Lean proofs. Code, benchmarks and Lean formalization: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425070

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: CrossCheck I: Cost Bounds of Imperative Programs as Constrained Optimization, with a Sound Cost Logic and a Verified Certificate Checker
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Static analysis of imperative programs often relies on iterative fixed-point approximations or concrete path exploration. We show that structured imperative control flow---while loops, linear recursion and branching recursion---can be mapped into constrained optimization problems over the free monoid of execution traces and the free algebra of computation trees. Ordering traces and trees by an intensional \textit{order-by-composition} ($\sqsubseteq$), halting is characterized as finding the minimal trace or tree that satisfies the exit condition, and we prove that this characterization coincides with the standard big-step semantics. Exact state recurrences are undecidable in general, so we relax them into cost envelopes, using ranking potentials and the tropical $(\max,+)$ reading of the timing schema, and obtain sound upper bounds on execution cost. The bounds compose over whole programs in a cost logic for a small language with nondeterministic actions, procedures, recursion and assumed contracts, which we prove sound for terminating and non-terminating executions. A linear instance of the logic has certificates---programs annotated with invariants, potentials and Farkas multipliers---and a checker that validates them with integer arithmetic only; an accepted certificate bounds the cost of every execution. All results, the checker and the worked examples are machine-checked in Lean~4. A companion paper describes a Clang plugin that produces such certificates and its evaluation.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 43 pages. Lean 4 formalization and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425070

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Technology-Enabled Fuel Supply Chain Resilience: An Integrated Information System for Real-Time Monitoring and Decision Support
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: This study evaluates and extends the transactional information system described in an earlier fuel logistics study, focusing on data reliability, monitoring, and decision support. An author-led re-evaluation examined available Delphi and SQL code and compared a reconstructed source-derived baseline (R0) with a revised SQL Server system (R1) across twelve evaluation scenarios. Synthetic transactions and public US energy data were used for technical assessment, while organizational processes and supply delays were simulated. R1 improved data integration and reporting accuracy in controlled SQL Server tests and introduced stock-movement records, automated alerts, and recovery controls. On comparable data feeds, integration defect rates decreased from 2.90 to 3.46 percent in R0 to 0.14 to 0.49 percent in R1. For national weekly demand forecasting, selected methods did not significantly outperform the previous-year mean. Process and disruption simulations suggested improvements in manual workload and replenishment delays, although these outcomes depended on modelling assumptions and were not observed in operational settings. The study presents a revised transactional architecture for fuel logistics and distinguishes experimentally measured information-system performance from simulated organizational outcomes. Its findings highlight the potential of traceable inventory records, early exception detection, and recoverable information systems to support supply chain resilience.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: BeSpec: Behavior-Level Specification Alignment for Code Generation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have advanced code generation from natural language descriptions of desired behavior (intent). Most existing methods refine code using execution feedback while leaving the underlying specification unchanged, implicitly assuming that the LLM correctly understands the intent. Yet ambiguous or underspecified descriptions can lead even capable models to correctly implement the wrong intent, making specification mismatch a central bottleneck.
  This paper presents BeSpec, a behavioral model based approach to specification alignment. Treating intent as partial evidence of intended program behavior, BeSpec extracts a structured specification and predicts executable behaviors that capture properties a correct program should satisfy. These avoid requiring exact test oracles, which can be as hard to predict as the solution itself. BeSpec executes candidate programs on probe inputs and compares their observed behaviors with the predicted behaviors. It validates mismatches and diagnoses their causes, refining defective specifications.
  We evaluate BeSpec with three LLMs on four code generation benchmarks: CodeContests, xCodeEval, APPS, and LiveCodeBench. Against nine baselines, BeSpec achieves the highest Pass at 1 and average pass rate in all settings, improving mean Pass at 1 over the strongest baseline by 9.3 to 23.6 percent relative across LLMs. After alignment, most remaining failures are adherence failures. Ablation studies on qwen3 coder 30b show the benefit of behavior modeling.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Interrupt-Aware Static Detection of Deadlocks in Rust Operating Systems
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Rust is increasingly adopted in operating systems, but Rust's safety guarantees do not eliminate deadlocks, especially those induced by interrupts. The core challenge is to recover interrupt-sensitive lock dependencies from Rust's guard-based synchronization across function boundaries. Applying this analysis across Rust OS projects also requires specifying project-specific synchronization semantics. We present an approach combining interrupt-aware static analysis with diagnostic-guided agent auditing for detecting deadlocks in Rust operating systems. Our approach uses lightweight source-level annotations to recover project-specific lock and interrupt semantics, performs a flow-sensitive MIR-based analysis to track lock-holding and interrupt states, and reports potential deadlocks with supporting evidence. An agent then searches for relevant source code in the repository and returns a confidence assessment with reasons for each supplied report. We evaluate our tool on four real Rust operating systems, identifying 26 true cases corresponding to nine maintainer-confirmed defects. Diagnostic-guided auditing achieves 86.2\% precision and 96.2\% recall based on static analysis results, and offers advantages over the baselines in both cost and effectiveness.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 18 pages, 11 figures. Code:https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/SWE-Ladder

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ReproShift: Cross-Version Adaptation of Linux Kernel Fuzzing Crash Reproducers
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Reliable crash reproduction is essential for diagnosing and repairing kernel crashes. Historical crash reproducers preserve concrete bug-triggering knowledge and can be reused for regression testing, bug revalidation, and impact analysis across kernel versions. However, kernel evolution can invalidate these reproducers by changing kernel interfaces, configurations, and execution paths. Migrating them is therefore challenging: the adapted reproducer must identify and modify version-sensitive behavior while preserving the bug-triggering operations and resource dependencies that define the original crash. To address this challenge, we propose ReproShift, an automated framework for cross-version crash reproducer migration by preserving bug-triggering semantics while adapting only version-sensitive behavior. Given source crash artifacts, a source crash reproducer, and a target kernel, ReproShift produces a migrated crash reproducer with same-bug validation evidence. Specifically, ReproShift first constructs a structured source-to-target context to identify migration-relevant kernel changes. It then performs constrained target-aware adaptation to revise version-sensitive reproducer operations while preserving the original trigger logic. Finally, it executes the adapted candidates on the target kernel and uses execution feedback and case-specific crash evidence to iteratively validate candidates and refine subsequent migrations. In a real-world deployment on an evolving upstream kernel, ReproShift further produces 22 upstream crash reports generated from adapted candidates, of which 7 have been fixed and 5 have received explicit maintainer confirmation. To systematically quantify its migration effectiveness, we construct a benchmark of 107 real-world source-target migration cases. ReproShift achieves confirmed same-bug migration in 57 cases, compared with 19 cases using direct replay.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model, or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 722 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing the paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce a reporting protocol, intervention efficacy, which reports an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate, and cost, and a metric, weighted token cost, which reports input, cached-input, and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $5.0\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: 93--99% of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s \ge 0.84$. Of 48 intervention comparisons, 6 change speed and 9 change token cost significantly, and 5 leave speed equivalent. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. HPCAgent-Bench is a broad, hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: 23 pages, 9 figures, 21 tables

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: POMA: Beyond Final Flags -- Process-Level Evaluation of Base LLMs in Vulnerability Exploitation
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from text generation to autonomous software-engineering execution, automated vulnerability exploitability verification has emerged as a vital frontier in software quality assurance and security validation. Existing security benchmarks, however, largely judge models by binary pass/fail outcomes or coarse stage milestones. Such outcome-centric scoring obscures fine-grained failure dynamics across long-horizon execution and conflates the intrinsic capability of a base LLM with external agent scaffolding. We present POMA (Pwn-Oriented Model Assessment), a process-level evaluation methodology and platform that isolates base LLMs under a unified execution baseline -- fixing task inputs, tool interfaces, target environments, feedback formats, and execution budgets -- while measuring intermediate states and transitions from runtime evidence. Evaluating four frontier base LLMs across 55 CTF Pwn challenges and 10 real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks exposes persistent capability attrition along the exploitation chain: from vulnerability knowledge to executable implementation, from client-side actions to verified target states, from failure localization to precise repair, and across iterative revisions. In real-world software, models further struggle to satisfy format, semantic, differential, and crash-identity constraints simultaneously. By pinpointing where execution chains break down, POMA provides an empirical foundation for trustworthy capability assessment and principled vulnerability-agent design. Our benchmark catalogs, process-measurement evaluator, and sample harness are publicly available at https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release .

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Repair agents resolve a growing share of real-world issues. Starting with the same information as a developer reading a bug report, they have to find out how the program fails before actually fixing it.
  We present FORECAST, which provides repair agents with a diagnosis of the failure. From the executions of passing and failing tests, FORECAST infers a cause chain, a short sequence of execution features, such as conditions or data flow, that explains how the failing runs diverge. FORECAST appends this cause chain to the issue an agent receives. It thus works with any agent that builds its prompts from the issue, without modifying the agent.
  We evaluate FORECAST on all 300 issues of SWE-bench Lite with five repair agents and two models, the commercial Claude Haiku 4.5 and the open-weight Qwen3.5. With the cause-chain diagnosis, every agent resolves significantly more issues. Over all agents, the share of resolved issues rises from 48.5% to 70.9% for Haiku 4.5 and from 31.2% to 56.1% for Qwen3.5. The open-weight model with the diagnosis thus surpasses the commercial model without it. The gains persist across repeated runs and for agents that already run the tests the diagnosis is derived from.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Evaluation of seven models shows that even the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, resolves only 23% of tasks. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested. RepoClean provides a foundation for systematically studying these cleanup challenges and advancing coding agents toward autonomous software maintenance.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: VERDICT: Multi-Agent Parallel Modular Verification
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Deductive verification scales to large software systems through modular reasoning, where formal contracts summarize the behavior of individual functions and enable their independent verification. Its central bottleneck is specification synthesis: constructing the contracts required for modular verification. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated specification synthesis at unprecedented scale. However, existing approaches remain fundamentally bottom-up, requiring callees to be verified before their callers. This dependency limits parallelism and provides no principled mechanism for resolving interprocedural inconsistencies that propagate across call chains.
  We present VERDICT, a multi-agent framework for parallelizing modular deductive verification of large-scale programs. VERDICT is built on two key principles. First, assumption-based parallel specification synthesis assigns an agent to each function and allows it to proceed immediately using assumed contracts for its callees, enabling verification to proceed in parallel across the program. Second, bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation resolves the inconsistencies introduced by these assumptions: when a synthesized contract contradicts an assumption, agents propagate the necessary revisions both up and down the call graph until the contracts converge. Experimental results on real-world C programs show that VERDICT synthesizes higher-quality specifications than existing approaches while substantially reducing verification time. In particular, VERDICT is the first approach that scales to the complete 20,000-line X.509 parser, ruling out nearly all the potential runtime errors within hours, whereas prior tools like PREGUSS fall far short even after days of execution.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: What Field Enumeration Costs to Compile in C++26: Native Reflection, Structured-Binding Packs, Reflection Libraries and Hand-Written Serializers on GCC 16
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: C++26 adds standard ways to enumerate a struct's fields, among them static reflection (P2996, with P3394 annotations) and structured-binding packs (P1061), alongside hand-written code, X-macros and libraries (Boost.PFR, reflect-cpp, Glaze) that now ship pre-C++26 and C++26 paths. We time each in a struct serializer with byte-identical output on GCC 16.2.0, at the front end and at -O2, in randomized interleaved rounds with code-level checks of every single-factor contrast. At the front end, inline native enumeration in the form used in several of P2996's own examples, an expansion statement over the std::span of define_static_array, costs about as much per struct of 16 scalar fields as Boost.PFR and 7.96x a P1061 pack, itself about as cheap as hand-written code. The same loop over a constant array costs 0.47x as much: about half of the span form's cost comes with the span. The ratio to P1061 shrinks on a heterogeneous type graph and at -O2. In a whole translation unit at the front end the library outweighs the mechanism: 200 structs take 0.59 s with inline native enumeration, 0.56 s with Boost.PFR and 3.86-4.13 s with the C++26 paths of reflect-cpp and Glaze, whose visitors also compute field names. Per type, each library's C++26 path is cheaper than its pre-C++26 path at 16 fields, but Glaze's gain reverses at 128 fields (pinned release v9.1.0); Boost.PFR's C++17 path grows almost quadratically with the number of types. Hand-written serializers sharing one overloaded name grow superlinearly with the number of types. The -freflection flag alone makes reflection-free code up to 1.264x costlier per type on GCC 16.2.0 and up to 2.578x on 16.1.0, so comparisons between mechanisms depend on the point release. Part of the span form's cost grows with the number of structs, which we trace to GCC registering block-scope statics in quadratic time (reported as GCC PR128928).

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Software-Engineering-as-an-Artifact: From Engines to Systems That Build Themselves
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software engineering (SE) is evolving rapidly as generative AI and LLM-based agents grow more capable. Yet, as a community, we risk using these new tools to solve problems that a changing SE process may no longer pose. We consider how AI may transform, and in part already is transforming, both the SE process and the systems it produces. Drawing on scenario planning methods from futures studies, we extrapolate from observed trends to a deliberately extreme scenario in which the SE process fully materializes in artifacts (like context documentation and executable skills). Such a process would culminate in SE engines that autonomously produce and update systems directly from requirements and user requests. The work of human engineers would then shift from the product to the process: they would maintain the artifacts of these engines, while the engines produce and evolve the software. We probe this scenario in scenario-validation interviews with four SE industry practitioners. The interviewees found the scenario largely plausible and desirable, and two reported that parts of industry are already moving this way; one questioned whether tacit engineering knowledge can ever be fully captured in artifacts. Even if this end state is reached only in part, we argue that reasoning about it can inform the intermediate stages. SE research should therefore take such futures into account when choosing its research directions.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision. As a result, high-quality tasks in these domains are still largely expert-authored, making them expensive to scale and limiting their use for training. To address this bottleneck, we introduce VADE, a data engine that automatically constructs verifiable analysis tasks from public sources used in professional practice. VADE exploits a simple asymmetry: professional analyses are difficult to solve because the relevant evidence must first be found and interpreted, but much easier to verify once that evidence is fixed. During task synthesis, the engine constructs a reference analysis from source evidence and asks an independent agent to reproduce its conclusions from the same evidence without seeing it. Only after the analysis is verified is it compiled into an open-ended task with an item-level scoring contract, allowing the same task to support both evaluation and training. We apply VADE across four professional domains; in an independent expert review of 186 finance tasks, 93.5% meet a high bar for source fidelity, answer correctness, and evaluation fairness. In finance, these tasks expose substantial remaining model errors, particularly unsupported facts and inferences, while training on verified solver trajectories improves held-out performance and yields gains that transfer to public finance benchmarks such as Finance Agent Benchmark v2. Together, these results suggest a practical path toward scalable, verifiable supervision for open-ended professional tasks.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: AEGIS: Evidence-Guided Set Decisions for Requirement-to-Code Traceability
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Requirement-to-code traceability recovery identifies code artifacts that implement a requirement, but manual review costs limit how many candidates developers can inspect. Code relations can reveal candidates missed by textual retrieval, yet can also introduce code unrelated to the requirement. We propose AEGIS, which combines retrieval evidence and code relations to construct and revise trace sets under a project-wide review budget. Grouped retrieval and semantic retrieval supply candidates. A set objective combines relevance to the requirement with structural compatibility. Local search constructs sets of different sizes, and dynamic programming selects one set per requirement within the budget. Call-context admission then compares replacements using evidence from arguments and return values in calls involving protected members, while bounding retrieval-score loss. Across 13 projects, AEGIS achieves the highest project-macro average on nine of ten evaluation metrics among the compared methods. Relative to same-corpus adaptations of TAROT-VSM and FTLR+MC, it improves F$_1$@5 by 33.21% and 52.28%, and MAP by 38.58% and 49.08%, respectively.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity. Dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code. Consequently, developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes. However, such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability.
  Meanwhile, coding agents have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce DEPBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation. We evaluate mainstream coding agents on DEPBENCH. The best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.
