This collapse holds across four 900-response corpora, multiplying reported compliance by a factor of 22 to 25 on our primary corpora while non-refusal shifts by 18.0 to 23.0 points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance varies by 1.7x to 2.8x across all four corpora, whereas post-labelling rubric rulings (+16.3 points) and benchmark choice (15.3 points) still shift non-refusal. Per-class label counts expose class collapse at zero cost without human labels, motivating an eight-item reporting minimum that pairs compliance with non-refusal rates.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: We apologize that we carelessly used an image of a nude child in the paper. We wish to withdraw the paper and revise it to address this mistake

Security & Program Analysis.title: Power Side-Channel Evaluation using Multi-FPGA Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Complex out-of-order processors are difficult to evaluate for power side-channel leakage before tapeout. A single FPGA often lacks sufficient capacity, whereas conventional CAD-based analysis is too slow to support the large numbers of traces required by practical attacks. Multi-FPGA emulation provides greater capacity, but existing partitioning schemes are not security-aware and thus results in poor attack performance. This work presents Scissors, a security-aware multi-FPGA partitioning approach for pre-silicon power side-channel evaluation of complex out-of-order processors. Scissors uses side-channel vulnerability factor (SVF) analysis to identify signals correlated with the secret key. It then keeps strongly key-correlated signals confined to one FPGA partition (measured) while moving rest of the signals to the other FPGAs (support), improving the observability of the side-channel information. We evaluate Scissors through RTL simulations and physical measurements on a two-U200 FPGA testbed, using frequency-domain CPA with a Hamming-weight leakage model. RTL ablation shows that only 68-71 high-SVF signals dominate key recovery process. For a single-core processor (SingleBOOM), Scissors recovers the key with 12,000 traces, compared with 49,000 for the unpartitioned design and 43,000 for TritonPart, while improving correct-key correlation by $2.83\times$. For a quad-core processor (QuadBOOM), which exceeds the capacity of the CW340 single-FPGA platform, Scissors reduces the required traces from 111,000 to 66,000 and improves correlation by $1.48\times$ over TritonPart. Scissors also reduces QuadBOOM RTL-to-bitstream generation from 61 h 39 min to 6 h 40 min, a $9.25\times$ speedup. These results show that security-aware partitioning improves leakage observability and attack performance while substantially reducing implementation time for complex processors against the baseline method.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Reporting Differential Privacy Guarantees via Operationally Equivalent $\varepsilon$: What Does $\varepsilon=19.61$ Mean for the 2020 U.S. Census?
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The large value $\varepsilon=19.61$, reported as an approximate differential privacy (ADP) parameter for the 2020 U.S. Census, has prompted doubts about the adequacy of Census privacy protection. This value was obtained by converting component guarantees expressed in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), an extension of differential privacy (DP), to ADP at $δ=10^{-10}$. Summarizing a guarantee by a single $(\varepsilon,δ)$ pair can substantially loosen its upper bound on the power (true positive rate) of a distinguishing test at a given significance level. We express the power bound from the original guarantee as the $α$-operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$, the smallest pure DP parameter yielding the same power bound at significance level $α$. The full operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ curve represents the original bound exactly on $(0,1)$, even when that bound is nonconcave. We also characterize the curve's extrema over an interval of significance levels. When finite, they give the pure DP parameters whose power bounds enclose the original bound on that interval. The mapping preserves the ordering of guarantees by their power bounds at each significance level, whereas conversion to single ADP pairs or Gaussian DP (GDP) envelopes can reverse this ordering for Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with equal noise variance. For the P.L. 94-171 redistricting data, we reproduce the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$ as the sum of rounded component ADP values. The published zCDP guarantee yields operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ values of approximately $4.25$, $2.94$, and $3.18$ at significance levels of $1\%$, $5\%$, and $10\%$, respectively. These values convey the original guarantee's constraints on distinguishing attacks more clearly than does the reported value $\varepsilon=19.61$, which by itself places little restriction on the success of such attacks.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 33 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. This paper extends a preliminary Japanese version published in the proceedings of the Computer Security Symposium 2026 (CSS 2026). In this arXiv update, we shortened the abstract and corrected the placement of Figures 3 and 4. The results and conclusions are unchanged. Reproduction code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23695034

Security & Program Analysis.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.

Security & Program Analysis.title: From Reconnaissance to Response: Quantitative Risk Parameterization and Game Theoretic Containment in Modern Enterprise Attack
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Modern Security Operations Centers struggle with delayed manual incident response, enabling adversaries to advance through the Cyber Kill Chain during early stage reconnaissance. While classical game theoretic defense models optimize strategic resource allocation, they rely on static utility matrices that fail to adapt to dynamic telemetry. This paper presents an integrated, metrics driven decision engine that bridges quantitative risk parameterization and continuous automated response time. Common Vulnerability Scoring Systems exploitability parameters are mapped to attacker success probabilities and evaluate defender log distributions via Factor Analysis of Information Risk Monte Carlo simulations. Real time SIEM logs streams are modeled as Poisson process arrival rates, dynamically updating defender posterior threat belief through sequential Bayesian filtering. A closed form threshold is derived by framing the interaction as a dynamic Bayesian Stackelberg game, where the expected unmitigated risk exceeds proactive containment cost. Parameterized against empirical data from the 2023 MGM Resorts and Caesars Entertainment cyber incident, simulation results demonstrate that the engine suppresses transient background noise while triggering automated SOAR network isolation within seconds of adversarial probing. Multi parameter sensitivity analysis confirms that the decision boundary dynamically adjusts to live perimeter vulnerability, offering a control theoretic foundation for sub minute automated threat containment.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Analyzing Single-Bit Flips on LLMs and Their Backbone-Matched VLMs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) enable offline weight analysis and are reused as backbones in vision-language models (VLMs), increasing the risk of bit-flip attacks that manipulate stored weight bits to induce malicious model behavior. An adversary could identify vulnerable bits on a public LLM and later flip the same locations in a deployed LLM or its backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip is particularly practical in this setting because it is easier to achieve under hardware fault attacks than multi-bit flips. However, existing selectors are mostly limited to multi-bit flips, without in-depth analysis of single-bit flips. In this paper, we adapt representative data-free and data-based bit selectors to identify candidate bits. We evaluate each bit independently on source LLMs and at the same logical coordinates in backbone-matched VLMs (without re-search), considering both performance degradation and prediction patterns across multiple inputs. Results show impact of single-bit flips varies across selectors on LLMs and their backbone-matched VLMs. A single-bit flip can make the model tend to produce a repeated output string across different inputs. Our robustness analysis reveals vulnerabilities in terms of performance and prediction patterns.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Star is Reborn: The PHP Interpreter Rewritten in Safe Rust
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
PHP powers most of the web, yet its C interpreter has had many memory-safety vulnerabilities. Reimplementing the interpreter in safe Rust offers a promising way to eliminate these vulnerabilities. However, eliminating native memory violations alone does not necessarily prevent unintended accesses to the logical memory of the translated program.
  To prevent such failures, we introduce logical memory safety, which confines the program operations to their permitted memory. In this paper, we formalize this property for PHP through an abstract PHP machine model that captures how the PHP interpreter manages program values while abstracting away functionality details. Guided by this model, we reimplement the PHP 5.0.0 engine in safe Rust, and formally prove that, for a core fragment of PHP, our Rust translation refines the abstract PHP machine, thereby establishing logical memory safety for this fragment.
  Our translation safely handles all 173 memory vulnerabilities we collected that affect PHP 5.0.0 prior to the rewrite. The Rust version matches the C implementation on all functionality tests, and produces identical outputs for the real-world PHP applications we evaluate. To our knowledge, this is the first principled safe Rust port of a core fragment of the PHP interpreter that combines formal guarantees of logical memory safety with functional compatibility. The improved security comes at a modest average runtime overhead of only 15% compared to C.

Security & Program Analysis.title: On the solving degree and complexity of Gröbner Basis computation over finite fields
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations over finite fields is a central problem in algebraic cryptanalysis, commonly approached using Gröbner basis algorithms. The complexity of Gröbner basis computation depends on the algorithm employed and is governed by the solving degree, defined as the maximum degree of the polynomials processed during the computation. Estimating this quantity is therefore crucial, and several bounds in terms of the degree of regularity have been established in the literature.
  In this work, we investigate the effect of Buchberger's criteria on the elimination of redundant pairs, and prove that the solving degree of a Gröbner basis algorithm combining linear algebra with Buchberger's original algorithm is bounded above by the degree of regularity defined by the leading forms of the involved polynomials. This result provides a rigorous justification for using the degree of regularity in complexity estimates for Gröbner basis algorithms, thereby supporting a common assumption in algebraic cryptanalysis.
  We refine the complexity analysis by establishing bounds on the number of pairs that must be processed. These bounds improve upon published complexity estimates, with particularly significant gains in certain parameter ranges.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Merging Cyber Threat Intelligence Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Small Language Models for Rich Threat Representation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cybersecurity operations rely on CTI from heterogeneous sources, such as structured threat representations and narrative reports. They describe adversarial behaviors but rarely make explicit the conditions that enable each attack step, the consequences it produces, and the evidence supporting them, leaving analysts to correlate fragmented information manually. Existing approaches extract entities, map tactics and techniques, or reconstruct attack chains; enriching attack steps with explicit, evidence-linked semantics remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a local-first pipeline for evidence-grounded attack-step enrichment that combines hybrid RAG with a locally deployed SLM. Starting from an analyst-provided attack representation and supporting CTI documents, the pipeline retrieves step-relevant evidence and generates enriched descriptions, pre-conditions, post-conditions, and traceable links to the supporting passages. The enriched steps are organized into graph that groups MITRE ATT&CK-aligned steps into tactic-level milestones. Explicit conditions help defenders block attacks by removing their enabling conditions and support detection by checking for their expected consequences. We evaluate the pipeline on ten public malware case studies derived from UK NCSC reports, using automated measurements and a structured manual assessment with annotations from two annotators. The results demonstrate that the pipeline is effective at generating conditions that are, for the most part, evidence-supported and meaningful w.r.t. the analyzed attack step. Similar considerations hold for the enriched descriptions. Finally, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of locally generating structured, evidence-grounded enrichments that improve the interpretability and traceability of attack step representations without requiring a manual reconstruction of attack execution.

Security & Program Analysis.title: AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments
Security & Program Analysis.summary: AI agents increasingly pay for data and computation through protocols such as x402 and AP2, but individually funded wallets idle and require asset transfers for every payment. We present AgentBank, a smart-contract banking layer that lets agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits. Internal payments update account balances without transferring assets, while pooled backing funds are allocated between reserves and yield-bearing strategies. We bound losses from compromised agent keys and analyze how correlated demand affects reserve requirements. Experiments show that AgentBank reduces idle liquidity by 52-77% relative to per-agent wallets and lowers gas costs for batched internal payments. Using historical DeFi liquidity data, we evaluate how reserve policies balance treasury returns against payment availability during market stress. We further examine the risks of automated bank runs and evaluate mechanisms to mitigate them.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurfase-based Physical Deepfakes
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Wireless communication networks are expanding from mere information transfer to sensing: in the Integrated Sensing and Communication paradigm, existing infrastructure and signals are reused to capture physical information about the surroundings of devices, envisioned to inform high-stakes applications such as healthcare and autonomous vehicles. From a security perspective, wireless sensing inherently trusts physical observations of the radio environment. However, as in wireless communication, the open nature of radio propagation allows attackers to tamper with victim signals. In particular, attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to manipulate wireless channels and thereby mislead sensing systems. Yet, prior metasurface-based manipulations target only individual channel features such as variance or Doppler shifts. Thus, they require knowledge of the victim sensing system and produce implausible channels that are easy to detect.
  In this work, we show that metasurfaces enable physically plausible manipulation of wireless sensing that is independent of the features used by the victim sensing system. Our attack reproduces genuine pre-recorded events at the physical layer and thereby synthesizes physical deepfakes of wireless channels. To this end, we develop an attack framework that controls the amplitude and phase of victim channels across time, frequency, and antennas. The key challenge here is to build a deep learning model of the interaction between metasurface and victim channel. We demonstrate that attackers can solve this challenge in several settings, e.g., by exploiting Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback Information or replicating the victim environment. We validate the attack both in a controlled lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing. Our results fundamentally challenge the trustworthiness of wireless sensing.

Security & Program Analysis.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets so that agents can resolve issues and run tests. That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).

Security & Program Analysis.title: FLIPS: Instance-Fingerprinting for LLMs via Pseudo-random Sequences
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Literature reveals that a Large Language Model's (LLM) behavior is not only conditioned by its original weights but also its instance-level parameters, such as instructional prompt, sampling configuration or quantization. A model that generates safe outputs under one configuration may produce toxic content under another. However, current LLM identification techniques (such as fingerprinting) focus on intellectual property protection, and their design favors robustness to changes in these instance-level parameters. This poses a critical challenge for AI regulation in which compliance assessments target actual deployed behaviors, not model provenance. In this paper, we introduce instance-level fingerprinting, a regulator-oriented paradigm that distinguishes configurations of the same LLM. Our method, FLIPS, exploits biases in generated binary random sequences. On a benchmark of 237 model instances, it identifies the instance with 77% accuracy from 32 queries to the target, against at most 33% for the adapted LLMmap baseline. Recognizing that a target is unseen, also called open-set challenge, is much harder. When 10% of instances are unseen, FLIPS realises a recall of 41% on the unseen instances, at a precision of 23%, i.e. more than twice better than random. Closed-set instance fingerprinting is thus practical with a few dozen queries, whereas the open-set setting remains an open problem. Code available at https://github.com/GurvanR/FLIPS-LLM-Instance-Fingerprinting.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 23 pages, 20 figures, 3 tables. 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026). Version 2: see erratum at page 13

Security & Program Analysis.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Query-Guided Visual Minimization for Selective Disclosure to Cloud VLMs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) require sending images beyond the user's local trust boundary, potentially exposing sensitive information the query does not need. We study query-guided visual minimization: a trusted local transformation preserves query-relevant visual content and reduces unnecessary disclosure before transmission. Unlike query-agnostic anonymization, it preserves the same sensitive content when the query requires it and suppresses it otherwise. We introduce QGVM, a framework that combines query grounding with an independent sensitive-item inventory, determines disclosure necessity at the type, instance, and text-content levels, and renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. We evaluate QGVM on complementary benchmarks measuring task utility, directly recoverable sensitive information, and inferential geolocation leakage. With OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, QGVM achieves 85.3% DoxBench answer correctness versus 77.5% for PGP, while a separately prompted Sol geolocation attacker succeeds within 1 km on 5.8% of QGVM images versus 25.7% of unprotected images. On Scene-Privacy, QGVM reduces face re-identification from 27.7% (PGP) to 4.5%. On held-out BIV-Priv-Seg, unnecessary private-text recovery falls from 33.9% (PGP) to 15.3%. To verify that disclosure is query-dependent, we evaluate paired queries that either require or do not require the same sensitive information. QGVM achieves 69.6% correct disclosure switching, compared with 29.1% for grounding-only cropping. These findings highlight the value of distinguishing visual relevance from disclosure necessity, while revealing the privacy-utility trade-offs of selective visual disclosure.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Granite: Granular Runtime Enforcement for GitHub Actions Permissions
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
GitHub Actions is a popular CI/CD platform that lets maintainers build workflows from reusable third-party actions, organized into jobs of sequential steps. To control access to repository resources, GitHub enforces token permissions only at the job level. This violates the principle of least privilege: every step shares the job's full permissions, so a single compromised action can misuse all of them, as witnessed by the recent tj-actions compromise, enabling broader software supply chain attacks.
  We present Granite, the first system to enforce fine-grained, step-level permissions for GitHub Actions at runtime. Untrusted steps never hold the real token; a separate controller issues each step an identifier token and supplies the real token only to requests that meet the step's policy. Granite builds on GitHub's self-hosted runner, requires no workflow changes, and transparently handles JavaScript, composite, and Docker actions. Across 500 workflows (12,915 jobs) from the most-starred GitHub repositories, 46.3% of jobs are overprivileged and can be protected by Granite. On 46 repositories and 127 unique actions, Granite preserves the behavior of every job that runs on the unmodified runner, except one it blocks by design. Reproducing 10 permission-misuse attacks over 42 overprivileged jobs, including attempts to bypass its enforcement, Granite prevents all of them and removes write access from about 83.3% of the steps that hold it under GitHub's current model. Its average per-step overhead is 7.9%, making Granite a practical and effective tool to reduce the attack surface in CI/CD pipelines.

Security & Program Analysis.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and Claude Code documents that such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules. However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule.
  More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.

Security & Program Analysis.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Beyond True or False: Why You Can't Trust the Reasoning in LLM-Generated Vulnerability Reports
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
When a state-of-the-art LLM labels a function as vulnerable, can we trust its explanation? This paper first reveals a worrisome fact: 30.3% of correct verdicts from LLMs are produced through \textit{hallucinated or causally wrong reasoning}. While prior work has partially observed this phenomenon, no study has quantified its prevalence, taxonomized its failure modes, or proposed a structural fix.
  We aim to address all three. First, we construct reasoning-level datasets: real-world vulnerabilities across 149 CWE types annotated with evidence-based reasoning chains, and semantically equivalent code perturbations for robustness testing. Through open coding of 400 reasoning traces across 10 LLMs, we identify 12 systematic failure modes, among which code comprehension and logical reasoning errors are the most prevalent. Motivated by these findings, we propose DagVul, which models vulnerability reasoning as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) generation task, enforcing causal dependencies between reasoning steps and aligning them with program semantics via Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). DagVul improves reasoning F1-score by an average of 13.3% over baselines. Our 8B-parameter model achieves performance comparable to Claude-Sonnet-4.5 under CWE-Guided prompting (78.90% vs. 76.11%) in the evaluated setting. These results support the combined benefits of structured causal reasoning and training on curated, task-specific data for vulnerability analysis.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: This paper was accepted by the 49th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2027, Research Track)

Security & Program Analysis.title: VideoMark: Training-Free Watermarking for 2D-VAE Video Diffusion Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: This work presents \textbf{VideoMark}, a training-free watermarking framework for video diffusion models with frame-aligned 2D VAEs. VideoMark embeds pseudorandom error-correcting (PRC) codewords by modulating the signs of Gaussian initialization noise without model retraining. Under a joint pseudorandomness assumption on the instantiated PRC encoder, the resulting initialization tensor is computationally indistinguishable from the Gaussian reference; exact distributional equality holds for the ideal independent uniform-sign construction. To support temporally structured video watermarking, we introduce a frame-wise message design together with a Temporal Matching Module (TMM), which recovers frame correspondence under temporal reordering without requiring length-specific watermark layouts. Experiments on ModelScope and I2VGen-XL show that VideoMark achieves accurate watermark extraction on clean generations while maintaining video quality comparable to watermark-free generation. The proposed temporal matching mechanism further improves recovery under frame reordering and enables systematic evaluation under a range of temporal and compression perturbations. We additionally analyze the computational characteristics and practical operating conditions of inversion-based extraction. Overall, VideoMark provides a simple training-free construction for studying pseudorandom watermarking in videos generated by frame-aligned 2D-VAE diffusion models, and establishes a foundation for extending structured noise watermarking to broader video-generation architectures.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Encrypted Fixed-Point Multiplication in Quasilinear Complexity
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Homomorphic encryption enables computation on encrypted data, but its high computational overhead remains a central obstacle. We overcome this obstacle asymptotically for high-precision fixed-point arithmetic. In this paper, we introduce focused encoding, which represents a fixed-point number of $n$-bit precision using a polynomial of degree $O(n/\log n)$ over a polynomially bounded modulus by concentrating precision at one embedding. We then introduce an error-shaping technique for homomorphic operations to preserve the encoding. This yields an encrypted fixed-point multiplication algorithm for the CKKS scheme that runs in online time $O(n \log n)$ at $n$-bit precision for any fixed multiplicative depth, with security parameter $λ= O(n/\log^2 n)$.
  Further, we develop bootstrapping for focused encoding to overcome the quadratic cost of conventional bootstrapping. We bootstrap ciphertext coefficients at an enlarged scale and shape the resulting error to preserve focused encoding, at the cost of additional modulus consumption. Then, to reduce the remaining logarithmic overhead, we decompose the ciphertext into components over a smaller subring and bootstrap each separately. This reduces the online cost per multiplication, including bootstrapping, to $O(n \log n + n (\log λ)^3 \log \log λ)$ for security parameter $λ= O(n/\log^3 n)$.

Security & Program Analysis.title: DuetFHE: Compiling Dual-Lane Nonlinear Circuits for Complex-Packed CKKS Inference
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Complex packing in CKKS stores two real streams in the real and imaginary lanes of each slot. Direct squaring couples the lanes, while squaring them separately requires two ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (HMults). DuetFHE is a GPU compiler that uses a phase transformation to square both lanes independently with one HMult. It reuses dual-lane squares in polynomial activations and the modular-reduction stage of CKKS bootstrapping. The compiler further plans ciphertext scales and reuses conjugates to sustain the complex-packed representation across stages. On a single RTX 5090, DuetFHE accelerates four polynomial activations by $1.60$--$1.79\times$ over direct evaluation on two real ciphertexts. For two-image AESPA ResNet-20 inference, it maintains packed execution across convolutions, square activations, and bootstrapping, achieving a $1.97\times$ end-to-end speedup over the fastest tested EasyFHE batched baseline on both the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000.

Security & Program Analysis.title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance.
  We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases.
  We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 29 pages, 14 figures, 20 tables. v2 adds an appendix and two reference hardware designs

Security & Program Analysis.title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a promising approach to identifying and fixing software vulnerabilities autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden, either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors, making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework that transforms intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. It coordinates specialized agents for fault localization, patch generation, compilation, security and functionality validation, and patch review to iteratively refine localization and patch hypotheses. Specifically, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, using execution results from intermediate patches to uncover hidden root causes, and root-cause-oriented patch review to identify symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs that escape execution-based validation. Evaluation on VulnLoc, a real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset, shows that DeepAVR outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Evaluation on SAN2VULN demonstrates its ability to repair vulnerabilities unseen during training. On SEC-bench, DeepAVR outperforms the evaluated baselines on cases whose fixes lie outside the crash-site function.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 29 pages, 12 figures, 7 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/rimwoohan/DeepAVR

Security & Program Analysis.title: How Attackers Launder Funds through Mixers: Characterization and Detection on Ethereum
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Mixers protect privacy by concealing deposit--withdrawal links, but are also abused to launder illicit funds. Existing anti-money laundering studies do not specifically target mixer laundering, while mixer research focuses on deanonymization rather than identifying laundering-related transactions. Public reports remain fragmented, leaving no public case-level dataset for systematic measurement and detection. To fill this void, this paper presents the first comprehensive study of mixer laundering on Ethereum. We first construct \textsc{MixLaunder}, the first public case-level dataset of mixer laundering. It covers 27 cases involving Tornado Cash and Railgun from 2020 to 2025 and labels 9,300 laundering-related transactions with case identities and observable upstream and downstream fund flows, including deposits totaling approximately \$1.1 billion. By comparing these transactions with background mixer usage, we identify five common strategies, showing that laundering evidence spans complementary behavioral and fund-flow contexts, while same-case activity is locally tight but weakly connected across bursts. Our analysis further reveals coverage gaps in mixer-side risk screening and representative deanonymization heuristics. Guided by these findings, we develop \textsc{MixGuard}, which combines tri-view representation learning with two-stage grouping for transaction-level detection and case-aware grouping. Under strict case-level holdout evaluation, \textsc{MixGuard} outperforms representative baselines, achieving 97.89\% detection precision and 98.73\% group purity, while its top ten groups cover 95.09\% of each case's transactions on average.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Made to Measure: Designing Image Watermarks to Specification
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Image watermarking enables provenance and attribution, but practical deployments must jointly satisfy robustness, false-positive rate (FPR), image quality, and latency requirements. Existing watermarking methods offer complementary robustness against different attacks, making their composition attractive for broader protection. However, combining watermarks introduces interference, distortion, decoding overhead, and additional verification paths that share the same FPR budget. We propose TAILOR, a request-conditioned watermark composition framework with three stages: (1) offline characterization models fragment recovery, distortion, latency, and composition interactions across embedding strengths; (2) joint configuration selection uses satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) to jointly optimize fragment selection, continuous embedding strengths, embedding order, and geometric recovery while minimizing predicted distortion; and (3) live calibration validates candidate configurations on user images and refines inaccurate offline predictions to improve deployment success. Across 7,321 distinct deployment requests spanning five scenarios and 20 attack settings, TAILOR achieves 96.21% scenario-averaged request satisfaction with a mean PSNR of 41.02 dB, demonstrating its effectiveness in meeting diverse deployment requirements while maintaining high image fidelity. Code is available at https://github.com/aaFrostnova/Tailor.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Deletion Is Not Substitution: Component Attribution in a Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway for LLM Tool Calls
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents are commonly built as cascades of increasingly costly stages, and ablation studies evaluate their components by switching each stage off and counting the detections lost. In a cascade, however, stages are not independent: a stage's contribution depends on what is routed to it and how its verdicts are enforced, so deletion-based ablation can mislead. We test this on BARBICAN, a four-tier, fail-closed gateway for Model Context Protocol tool calls, developed in our group, that routes borderline inputs to a neural arbitrator. After reproducing its recorded evaluation exactly, we apply deletion, constant substitution, repair and transplant to its arbitration stage. The findings rest on over thirty instrumented runs over 25,000 prompts, two platforms, an independent check set and six versions from the system's history. Depending on how "switching off" is defined, deletion credits the stage with contributions that differ by more than an order of magnitude, whereas substitution shows that its verdicts can affect only a few inputs, all attacks. Neither repairing the stage nor replacing it with a much stronger classifier changed the system appreciably: its influence is set by its position, not its quality. An observation that bounds the decisions a routed stage can change explains this, and a cascade of public classifiers reproduces it whenever routing concentrates attacks. Treating constant verdicts as mutants, we derive a continuous-integration gate that detects a stage whose verdicts cannot reach the output and, in light of these results, offer a three-point roadmap for ablation studies.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Reproduction artifacts (BARBICAN: source code, per-request traces, external detector scores and verification scripts): https://zenodo.org/records/24377040

Security & Program Analysis.title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats.
  On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.

Security & Program Analysis.title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD <= 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 4 pages, 2 tables, 1 figure. Code and data: https://github.com/rajatbarot24/adaptr4j

Security & Program Analysis.title: Selection Integrity for LLM Graph Memory: An Accumulability Criterion for Information-Flow-Blind Retrieval
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agent memory is moving to graphs, and the provenance defenses now being built for it all check one thing: the provenance of the records an agent retrieves. We show that this entire class of defense is blind by construction. A long-term graph memory runs a global selection step over writable graph structure, so structure that an untrusted principal writes changes \emph{which} authenticated facts are selected while the cited evidence stays fully authenticated; faithful information-flow control (IFC), checking the provenance of what the reader uses (all of it authenticated), makes the byte-identical decision to no defense at all, across document-QA substrates and real multi-session agent memory. In the most consequential instance, a no-source structural write silently misdirects $28$ irreversible ledger transfers over $499$ live actions: faithful IFC permits every one, and \authselect\ prevents every one. We then characterize exactly which memories are exposed: a selector admits the channel when its structural term can reallocate an $Ω(1)$ share of top-$k$ membership past a selected fact's margin. Personalized PageRank can, since a sourceless write reroutes conserved random-walk mass; a content-fixed reranker cannot, and Graphiti's node-distance, which leans on structure \emph{more} than PageRank does, stays immune. Reallocatability, not reliance, is the predictor. We prove the immune case in general and the open case under a chokepoint condition we verify. Closing the channel forces any provenance defense to recompute selection on the authenticated subgraph, which is what \authselect\ does, at zero over-block and $2$--$3\%$ latency.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Not Just Any Example: Security Requirements and Fix Patterns for Guiding LLM Vulnerability Repair
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Software vulnerabilities leave systems open to attack, and their remediation is often delayed. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated patch generation, yet passing functionality tests does not ensure that a patch enforces the security requirement the vulnerability violated. Existing vulnerability repair techniques rely on curated patterns or templates with limited coverage, leaving unclear which repair strategies carry over across vulnerabilities and how they can steer LLMs. We present a large-scale empirical study that relates recurring fix patterns to the security impacts of vulnerabilities and examines how this knowledge can guide LLM-based repair. Building on a manual study of security patches, we cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories and analyze the edits and their context to derive concrete fix patterns, ranging from local safeguards to coordinated changes across multiple locations. We define 12 security impact classes by the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate and map them to repair categories and fix patterns, revealing characteristic repairs, alternative strategies within a class, and patterns shared across classes. We then use these patterns and impact-pattern associations to select repair examples for four LLMs on repair tasks of varying complexity. Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, whereas randomly selected examples reach only 36.9%. Our findings connect vulnerability characterization with patch generation and support organizing repair knowledge around security requirements.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?
Security & Program Analysis.summary: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion
Security & Program Analysis.summary: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Best-Laid SCHEMEs: Coordinated Sabotage and Monitoring in Multi-Agent Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As agentic coding systems decompose work across multiple model instances, a critical safety question is whether those instances can coordinate to achieve a hidden malicious objective while appearing aligned with user intent. We introduce SCHEME, a benchmark of 11 task pairings across 7 settings built on real open-source libraries, each connecting a legitimate software-engineering task with a malicious side task. Side tasks are designed so that no proper subset of agents can complete them alone: agents must decompose a shared plan, relay partial requirements, and make mutually consistent edits. Evaluating ten frontier models, we find that coordinated sabotage is already practical, with models completing the malicious objective while succeeding on the legitimate task in 49\% to 85\% of trajectories. Stronger models also run into fewer communication failures and recover from more of them. However, trusted monitors that see the agents' code and communication catch at least 93\% of successful sabotage from every model, and telling the agents about the monitor lowers their sabotage success while barely helping them evade these monitors. Successful evasion requires an attacker optimized against the monitor. An automated red-teaming attacker hides 63\% of the sabotage that GPT 5.1 Codex Mini catches, but this transfers poorly to Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3 Flash monitors.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 34 pages, 15 figures, 14 tables

Security & Program Analysis.title: MALET & Katalina: A Large-Scale Dataset and Static Analysis of macOS Malware
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
While malware on platforms such as Windows and Android has been extensively studied, the macOS ecosystem remains comparatively understudied. To address this gap, we present MALET, a large-scale public dataset for macOS malware analysis. MALET contains 44{,}804 malicious Mach-O binaries and 44{,}457 samples with zero antivirus detections on VirusTotal. From the undetected set, we further identify 25{,}835 high-confidence benign samples using conservative, heuristic-based filtering. We also introduce Katalina, an open-source static analysis framework that extracts macOS-specific structural features and indicators of potential behavior at scale.
  Using MALET, we perform, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale static characterization of macOS malware. Our analysis reveals macOS-specific traits, including widespread misuse of security entitlements, abuse of native scripting interfaces, and irregularities in code-signing infrastructure. We find that 93.0\% of malicious samples are unsigned, demonstrating that unsigned code continues to execute in practice through user-mediated approval mechanisms. Among CA-signed malware, 28.4\% (816 samples) were associated with certificates that were later revoked, including samples publicly attributed to DPRK-linked threat actors, as reflected in antivirus labels and threat intelligence reports. Finally, we identify significant detection instability: in 185 structurally identical malicious samples, antivirus engines failed to provide consistent detections for 77.2\% (143 samples). Together, these results highlight persistent blind spots in macOS malware detection and motivate improved approaches to certificate abuse analysis, similarity-based clustering, and platform-specific defense mechanisms. Based on these insights, we outline concrete steps to advance the state of macOS malware analysis and defense.

Security & Program Analysis.title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup.
  QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement. Authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for a quorum to attest to the whole. We turn this insight into a randomized construction that achieves reductions of more than 10x in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures.
  QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Operationally, QUASI requires no additional interactive setup or preprocessing beyond independent key generation by parties for the underlying hash-based authentication scheme. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Oracle Is Not Enough: Secure Settlement for Prediction Markets
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Prediction markets are becoming an important mechanism for aggregating information and forecasting uncertain real-world events. As they grow in scale and value, reliable settlement becomes critical because settlement determines the winning outcome and allocation of market collateral. Yet many heterogeneous markets require market-specific evidence and interpretation, and incorrect settlement can create direct financial incentives for manipulation. In this paper, we ask how to settle heterogeneous markets correctly and efficiently at scale. We first compare existing settlement designs in their support for heterogeneous markets, reliance on direct operator intervention, and resistance to manipulation, motivating a layered architecture that combines incentivized crowdsourcing with stake-backed voting and selective post-settlement review.
  Building on this architecture, we develop a stake-backed settlement protocol that provides economic security and settlement liveness under market-specific verification costs. Specifically, we prove that manipulation is unprofitable for every settled market and give two constructions that support sufficient self-enforcing participation with controlled reward expenditure. Using historical Polymarket and UMA data, we evaluate the protocol under real-world conditions. We find that 99% of admitted markets can be settled with modest participation rewards even under high verification costs.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it.
  We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost.
  We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Where Did My Tokens Go? Verifiable Token Billing for LLM Services
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Users of large language model (LLM) services receive token bills with limited evidence of which calls incurred their charges. In broker-mediated agent workflows, calls arise after authorization and billing evidence spans service domains. A bill can count one genuine receipt twice and omit another. Valid metering evidence can also be attributed to the wrong execution. We present \textsc{TokenProv}, which uses authenticated provider acceptances to establish settlement coverage and verify token charges. An authenticated causal history links runtime attempts to the signed policy, and jointly signed handoffs bind intent, dispatch, and acceptance to the same call. Handoffs submitted independently of the bill can reveal omitted calls. The auditor requires a one-to-one match between observable acceptances and settled receipts. For each acceptance, a common provider relation binds metered usage to the cache-dependent execution of the accepted input using the registered model and serving rules, and checks the charge under the pricing rule. To limit serving-path overhead, providers can use attested state transitions in trusted execution environments or defer proof generation until audit by committing to witnesses in receipts before settlement. The auditor recomputes the bill from the verified charges. We prove audit soundness relative to authenticated evidence. Across five models, \textsc{TokenProv} with signed provider receipts achieves 94.4--107.4\% of baseline throughput with 54--66\,ms of online non-LLM processing per request. In a separate eight-call replay, deferring scoped proofs reduces foreground protocol time from 1.20\,s to 8.65\,ms (99.28\%). The auditor rejects all 1,600 validly signed attack queries across 100 adaptive episodes.

Security & Program Analysis.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks on LLM Agents?
Security & Program Analysis.summary: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). Four of the five victims leaked despite the policy. GLM 5.2 retrieved protected data in 64.3% of individual-attack runs and leaked in 0.6%: retrieval does not imply disclosure, but in high-stakes settings even one leaked field can identify a patient or client. At equal budgets, a larger red team is not automatically a stronger one; the victim model matters far more.

Security & Program Analysis.title: HDMark: Holographic Multi-Bit Model Watermarking for Intellectual Property Protection in Hyperdimensional Computing
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) models deployed on edge hardware are valuable intellectual property that is easy to steal, since a trained classifier consolidates its learned knowledge into a compact set of class prototype hypervectors; yet protecting their ownership through watermarking remains largely unexplored. We present HDMark, the first model watermarking framework native to HDC, which encodes ownership in the same hyperdimensional algebra the model computes with. HDMark maps a multi-bit owner identity to secret quasi-orthogonal carriers, superimposes them holographically onto the trained class prototypes, and verifies ownership with a statistical test. Across four datasets and three HDC learning rules, HDMark leaves accuracy essentially unchanged and verifies a 64-bit identity in 99.8% of trials at p < 0.001. We derive closed-form expressions for prediction fidelity and bit recovery that match measurements within 0.4 pp mean absolute error. The watermark survives fine-tuning and low-bit quantization, while attempting to erase it through noise injection, pruning, or overwriting severely degrades model accuracy.
