Of sixteen treatments of this decision that we examined, ten assume a known set of players; the other six add unobserved agents only in games in which strikes and replies arrive instantly, in simulations, or in informal arguments. We show that when the roster is open, so that no agent knows even its list of nearby agents to be complete, the course that maximizes an agent's expected survival time if no unobserved agent acts still maximizes it, whatever else the agent believes, if and only if the agent gives at most a threshold probability to an unobserved agent acting, by attacking or helping the agent or by striking the located agent. Without further assumptions the threshold is below one half whatever the course, because an unobserved agent may reply to one course with help and to another with an attack, as soon as an agent as near as the located one could reply. If the agent knows the located agent completely and assumes that it would receive no help from unobserved agents, the threshold for collaboration can approach one. Even below the threshold the agent cannot know that the course it favors is in fact better: however much it knows of the one it has located, some world consistent with all it has observed makes another course better. These results do not apply to an agent that knows all but one of its courses would destroy it. For every other agent, no case for striking first, or for any other course, that assumes nothing about the unobserved agents withstands an even chance that one of them acts: some belief that gives that chance favors another course.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Add delay by distance and unobserved agents that may help, and drop the assumption of v2 that an unobserved agent who sees a strike can only be provoked by it. 23 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, including appendices

Security & Program Analysis.title: safeL4: Rethinking Safe-Language-Based Single Address Space Microkernels
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Microkernels provide good features such as high security, safety, and flexibility, but their reliance on hardware-based isolation leads to heavy performance overhead, limiting their widespread adoption. Although constructing single-address-space microkernels based on safe language-based isolation is a promising approach to addressing the performance issue, this approach still faces challenges in maintaining the principle of minimality and enforcing capability-based, fine-grained access control over system resources. We propose safeL4, an approach to constructing microkernels based on safe languages. It guarantees minimality through low-level abstractions for unsafe operations, and implements a capability system based on the safe language's object capabilities to achieve fine-grained access control over all operations on system resources. We implement a prototype system in Rust, and our evaluation results show that the primitives provided by safeL4 are, on average, 1.9$\times$ faster than those of seL4.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted to the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS 2027)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Spoofing Wireless Sensing with Metasurface-based Physical Deepfakes
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Wireless communication networks are expanding from mere information transfer to sensing: in the Integrated Sensing and Communication paradigm, existing infrastructure and signals are reused to capture physical information about the surroundings of devices, envisioned to inform high-stakes applications such as healthcare and autonomous vehicles. From a security perspective, wireless sensing inherently trusts physical observations of the radio environment. However, as in wireless communication, the open nature of radio propagation allows attackers to tamper with victim signals. In particular, attackers can use programmable metasurfaces to manipulate wireless channels and thereby mislead sensing systems. Yet, prior metasurface-based manipulations target only individual channel features such as variance or Doppler shifts. Thus, they require knowledge of the victim sensing system and produce implausible channels that are easy to detect.
  In this work, we show that metasurfaces enable physically plausible manipulation of wireless sensing that is independent of the features used by the victim sensing system. Our attack reproduces genuine pre-recorded events at the physical layer and thereby synthesizes physical deepfakes of wireless channels. To this end, we develop an attack framework that controls the amplitude and phase of victim channels across time, frequency, and antennas. The key challenge here is to build a deep learning model of the interaction between metasurface and victim channel. We demonstrate that attackers can solve this challenge in several settings, e.g., by exploiting Wi-Fi Beamforming Feedback Information or replicating the victim environment. We validate the attack both in a controlled lab study on MIMO channels and with off-the-shelf Wi-Fi sensing. Our results fundamentally challenge the trustworthiness of wireless sensing.

Security & Program Analysis.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a publicly released benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. On MedGuardBench, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4% at 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Shadows in the Code: Exploring the Risks and Defenses of LLM-based Multi-Agent Software Development Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems has significantly streamlined software developing tasks, enabling users with little technical expertise to develop executable applications. While these systems democratize software creation through natural language requirements, they introduce significant security risks that remain largely unexplored. We identify two risky scenarios: Malicious User with Benign Agents (MU-BA) and Benign User with Malicious Agents (BU-MA). We introduce the Implicit Malicious Behavior Injection Attack (IMBIA), demonstrating how multi-agent systems can be manipulated to generate software with concealed malicious capabilities beneath seemingly benign applications, and propose Adv-IMBIA as a defense mechanism. Evaluations across ChatDev, MetaGPT, and AgentVerse frameworks reveal varying vulnerability patterns, with IMBIA achieving attack success rates of 93%, 45%, and 71% in MU-BA scenarios, and 71%, 84%, and 45% in BU-MA scenarios. Our defense mechanism reduced attack success rates significantly, particularly in the MU-BA scenario. Further analysis reveals that compromised agents in the coding and testing phases pose significantly greater security risks, while also identifying critical agents that require protection against malicious user exploitation. Our findings highlight the urgent need for robust security measures in multi-agent software development systems and provide practical guidelines for implementing targeted, resource-efficient defensive strategies.

Security & Program Analysis.title: FlipVLA: Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action(VLA) Models Only Through Bit Flips
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions in real-world environments, making malicious model tampering a potential threat to physical safety. We study whether object-triggered backdoors can be implanted through a small, fixed set of parameter bit flips without retraining. The central challenge is to make persistent weight modifications disrupt trigger-present behavior while preserving performance on non-trigger inputs. We propose FlipVLA, a two-stage selector-amplifier method that exploits existing visual features within an FC-GELU-FC structure. The selector constructs a trigger-dependent response in a selected channel, using GELU to attenuate background activity. The amplifier modifies a connected downstream weight to convert this response into an action-relevant perturbation. Channel screening and discrete bit search construct both components under a limited modification budget. Experiments on OpenVLA-OFT and GR00T N1.7 across four LIBERO suites achieve attack success rates of 90.22% to 100%, with task success decreasing by at most 1.5 percentage points on clean scenes.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 14 pages, including references and supplementary material

Security & Program Analysis.title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving.
  FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$).
  Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 36 pages. Code, 11 specifications, 28 Lean 4 modules, Rust verifier, and GPU benchmark receipts: https://github.com/s-JoL/FlashProve-Next

Security & Program Analysis.title: SoK: A Defense-Oriented Evaluation of Software Supply Chain Security
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The software supply chain is a highly complex ecosystem of tools, workflows, and human factors involved in creating a piece of software. Due to its central role in critical systems, it has become a frequent target of sophisticated attacks. Prior work has focused primarily on classifying attack vectors, but there is a gap in discussing and understanding effective defenses. This paper proposes a defense-oriented systematization of software supply chain security that models the fundamental components and causal relationships. Based on 76 works from academia and industry, we define key security objectives and defense patterns of established software supply chain defense techniques. The goal of our taxonomy is to identify major opportunities for future research, and aid software supply chain practitioners when reasoning about the effectiveness of defenses available today.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Sketching for First Order Method: Efficient Algorithm for Low-Bandwidth Channel and Vulnerability
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Sketching, which randomly compresses a large problem into lower dimensions to save runtime and memory, is a fundamental tool in large-scale machine learning. We propose a sketching scheme for first order methods in distributed learning that reduces the communication cost per round between agents, keeps our bound on the total communication no larger than for uncompressed distributed gradient descent, and still guarantees convergence. An agent compresses a gradient of high dimension $d$ with a sketching matrix $R\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times d}$, $s\ll d$, and the receiver maps it back to dimension $d$ with the de-sketching matrix $R^\top$. Using this framework, we develop federated learning algorithms with lower per-round communication. However, such random sketching alone gives no formal privacy guarantee for the local data. We present a gradient-matching attack and prove that, under smoothness and non-degeneracy assumptions on the model, gradient descent on the data finds an input whose sketched gradient matches the observed one, at a linear rate. This input need not be the data, but an attacker that follows a client over several rounds with fresh sketches recovers the data with the same attack, under smoothness and non-degeneracy conditions, and no attack does so from the first $T<m/s$ rounds, where $m$ is the data dimension. As a remedy, we prove that adding Gaussian noise to the gradients makes the algorithm differentially private. This noisy variant still sends only $s$ numbers per client in each round, and for convex and strongly convex objectives it converges at the rates of the noise-free algorithm, up to an additive error term that depends on the privacy level and, in our bounds, grows as $s$ decreases. Our total communication guarantees are proved for the noise-free algorithm. We expect our sketching scheme to extend to other learning settings, and it may be of independent interest.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: ICML 2023. The attack adds a Lipschitz pseudo-Hessian assumption: one round gives an input with matching sketched gradient, which need not be the data, and recovery is proved from at least $m/s$ rounds with fresh sketches. DP uses bounded gradient differences and full composition. Private convergence holds up to a privacy-dependent error. Fixed: sketch index, a sign, non-convex bound

Security & Program Analysis.title: MEV-ACE: Identity-Authenticated Fair Ordering for Proposer-Controlled MEV Mitigation
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Maximal Extractable Value, or MEV, remains a structural threat to blockchain fairness because a block producer can often observe pending transactions and unilaterally decide their ordering or inclusion. Existing mitigations hide transaction contents or outsource ordering, but they often leave two gaps unresolved. First, commitments are not authenticated by slashable identities. Second, inclusion obligations are not backed by transferable evidence that other validators can verify. This paper presents MEV ACE, a fair ordering protocol for proposer controlled ordering MEV. MEV ACE combines three mechanisms. First, it uses registered economic identities whose authentication keys are deterministically derived from the ACE GF framework and bonded on chain. Second, it uses authenticated commit and open messages with validator receipt thresholds, which make admissibility and inclusion obligations independently auditable. Third, it uses verifiable delay based randomness to determine transaction order only after the admissible commitment set is fixed. We formalize the protocol in a Byzantine fault tolerant validator model with threshold receipts and show three properties under standard assumptions: order unpredictability after the admissible set is locked, commitment authenticity under signature unforgeability, and accountable inclusion for transactions that obtain threshold commit and open receipts. Under these conditions, and when producer and user bonds exceed the one slot gain from invalid execution or selective non opening, MEV ACE removes unilateral proposer discretion over front running, sandwich attacks, and censorship against admitted transactions. The protocol remains single slot in structure, requires no threshold decryption committee, and is compatible with post quantum signature schemes such as ML DSA 44.

Security & Program Analysis.title: HFIPay: Privacy-Preserving, Cross-Chain Cryptocurrency Payments to Human-Friendly Identifiers
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Human-friendly identifiers such as email addresses and phone numbers are convenient payment targets, but direct mappings from identifiers to blockchain addresses make balances and transaction histories enumerable by anyone who knows the identifier. We present HFI-Pay, a relay-assisted protocol for privacy-preserving identifier-routed cryptocurrency payments. The relay resolves the identifier off-chain and registers only a random intent identifier, a per-intent blinded binding rho_i, and the quoted payment tuple on-chain; no identifier or reusable recipient tag is published before claim. In a verified-quote deployment, the sender verifies an attested quote proving that rho_i was derived from the same hidden binding handle as the recipient's attested binding-key commitment, preventing relay-side recipient substitution before funding. Claims are authorized by a zero-knowledge proof, instantiated through ZK-ACE, that the claimant controls the deterministic identity whose epoch-scoped handle opens the blinded binding and authorizes release of the quoted asset and amount to a chosen destination. We define observer-model games for enumeration resistance and pre-claim unlinkability, state the composition needed for post-quote claim correctness, and characterize relay compromise and post-claim linkability. Keywords: identifier-based payment, privacy-preserving, verifiable quote, blinded claim binding, zero-knowledge authorization

Security & Program Analysis.title: n-VM: A Multi-VM Layer-1 Architecture with Shared Identity and Token State
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Multi-chain ecosystems suffer from fragmented identity, siloed liquidity, and bridge-dependent token transfers. We present n-VM, a Layer-1 architecture that hosts n heterogeneous virtual machines as co-equal execution environments over shared consensus and shared state. The design combines three components: a dispatcher that routes transactions by opcode prefix, a unified identity layer in which one 32-byte commitment anchors VM-specifific addresses, and a unified token ledger that exposes VM-native interfaces such as ERC-20 and SPL over a common balance store. We formalize routing, identity derivation, and token transfer semantics, and prove cross-VM transfer atomicity and identity isolation under standard cryptographic assumptions. We describe a concrete instantiation with five VMs: a native runtime, EVM, SVM, Bitcoin Script, and TVM. We also present context-based sharding and a write-set scheduler for parallel execution. Under an analytical throughput model, the architecture admits a projected range of about 16,000 to 66,000 transactions per second on commodity hardware.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ACE Runtime - A ZKP-Native Blockchain Runtime with Sub-Second Cryptographic Finality
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Existing high performance blockchains verify one signature per transaction on the critical path, which creates O(N) verification cost, high hardware pressure, and difficult post quantum migration. This paper presents ACE Runtime, a ZKP native execution layer built on identity authorization separation. We replace per transaction signature checks with lightweight HMAC attestations in the hot path, then generate one aggregated zero knowledge finality certificate per block in an asynchronous prove stage. The system is organized as an Attest Execute Prove pipeline with two tier finality: soft finality from BFT voting and hard finality from proof verification. Under standard cryptographic assumptions, we provide formal arguments for attestation unforgeability and hard finality irreversibility. We also define a two phase timeout and backup proving path with witness availability gossip for liveness under builder failure. Quantitative results combine analytical modeling with reference implementation measurements. The prototype shows low CPU orchestration overhead, while model driven analysis projects constant per block verification cost, lower validator hardware requirements for non builders, and better bandwidth efficiency than per transaction signature designs. These results indicate that identity authorization separation is a practical architecture for sub second cryptographic finality with a clear path toward stronger post quantum components.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ACE-GF-based Attestation Relay for PQC - Lightweight Mempool Propagation Without On-Path Proofs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In post-quantum blockchain settings, objects that require validity proofs (e.g., blob roots, execution-layer or consensus-layer signature aggregates) must be broadcast through mempool and relay networks. Recursive STARKs have been proposed to aggregate such proofs so that each node forwards one proof per tick plus objects without proofs, capping per-node proof bandwidth at roughly 128 KB degree per tick. We observe that propagation does not inherently require validity proofs on the path-only a lightweight assurance that an object is eligible for relay. We present AR-ACE (ACE-GF-based Attestation Relay for PQC), in which relay nodes forward objects plus compact attestations (e.g., identity-bound signatures or commitments) and do not generate, hold, or forward any full validity proof. Only the builder (or final verifier) performs a single aggregated validity proof over the set of objects it includes. This proof-off-path design removes proof overhead from the propagation path entirely, yielding an order-of-magnitude reduction in proof-related relay bandwidth relative to proof-carrying propagation. When instantiated with ACE-GF-derived attestation keys, AR-ACE preserves a unified identity story with on-chain authorization and is PQC-ready. We specify a protocol model, state design goals and security considerations, define security games, and provide a structural bandwidth comparison with recursive-STARK-based propagation.

Security & Program Analysis.title: AESP: A Human-Sovereign Economic Protocol for AI Agents with Privacy-Preserving Settlement
Security & Program Analysis.summary: As AI agents increasingly perform economic tasks on behalf of humans, a fundamental tension arises between agent autonomy and human control over financial assets. We present the Agent Economic Sovereignty Protocol (AESP), a layered protocol in which agents transact autonomously at machine speed on crypto-native infrastructure while remaining cryptographically bound to human-defined governance boundaries. AESP enforces the invariant that agents are economically capable but never economically sovereign through five mechanisms: (1) a deterministic eight-check policy engine with tiered escalation; (2) human-in-the-loop review with automatic, explicit, and biometric tiers; (3) EIP-712 dual-signed commitments with escrow; (4) HKDF-based context-isolated privacy with batched consolidation; and (5) an ACE-GF-based cryptographic substrate. We formalize two testable hypotheses on security coverage and latency overhead, and specify a complete evaluation methodology with baselines and ablation design. The protocol is implemented as an open-source TypeScript SDK (208 tests, ten modules) with interoperability via MCP and A2A.

Security & Program Analysis.title: VA-DAR: A PQC-Ready, Vendor-Agnostic Deterministic Artifact Resolution for Serverless, Enumeration-Resistant Wallet Recovery
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Serverless wallet recovery must balance portability, usability, and privacy. Public registries enable decentralized lookup but naive identifier hashing leaks membership through enumeration. We present VA-DAR, a keyed-discovery protocol for ACE-GF-based wallets that use device-bound passkeys for day-to-day local unlock while supporting cross-device recovery using only a user-provided identifier (e.g., email) and a single recovery passphrase. As a discovery-and-recovery layer over ACE-GF, VA-DAR inherits ACE-GF's context-isolated, algorithm-agile derivation substrate, enabling non-disruptive migration to post-quantum algorithms at the identity layer. The design introduces a decentralized discovery-and-recovery layer that maps a privacy-preserving discovery identifier to an immutable content identifier of a backup sealed artifact stored on a decentralized storage network. Concretely, a user derives passphrase-rooted key material with a memory-hard KDF, domain-separates keys for artifact sealing and discovery indexing, and publishes a registry record keyed by a passphrase-derived discovery identifier. VA-DAR provides: (i) practical cross-device recovery using only identifier and passphrase, (ii) computational resistance to public-directory enumeration, (iii) integrity of discovery mappings via owner authorization, and (iv) rollback/tamper detection via monotonic versioning and artifact commitments. We define three sealed artifact roles, two update-authorization options, and three protocol flows (registration, recovery, update). We formalize security goals via cryptographic games and prove, under standard assumptions, that VA-DAR meets these goals while remaining vendor-agnostic and chain-agnostic. End-to-end post-quantum deployment additionally requires a PQ-secure instantiation of registry authorization.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Condition-Triggered Cryptographic Asset Control via Dormant Authorization Paths
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Control of encrypted digital assets is traditionally equated with permanent possession of private keys, a model that precludes regulatory supervision, conditional delegation, and legally compliant transfer at the cryptographic layer. Existing remedies (multi-signature schemes, threshold signatures, smart contracts, custodial delegation) require persistent key exposure, on-chain state mutation, or trusted intermediaries. We introduce Condition-Triggered Dormant Authorization Paths (CT-DAP), a cryptographic asset control method built on destructible authorization factors and parameterized by a root-derivable framework satisfying deterministic key derivation, context-isolated capability generation, and authorization-bound revocation. Under CT-DAP, control rights are dormant authorization paths composed of user-held credentials and administrative factors held by independent custodians; a path remains cryptographically inactive until all factors are simultaneously available. Upon verification of predefined conditions (e.g., user consent, inheritance events, time-based triggers), the corresponding factor is released, activating the path. Revocation is achieved by destroying factors, rendering the path permanently unusable without altering the cryptographic root. We formalize the threat model, define security games for unauthorized control resistance, path isolation, and stateless revocation, and prove security under standard assumptions (AEAD security of AES-GCM-SIV, PRF security of HKDF, memory-hardness of Argon2id, collision resistance of SHA-256). We instantiate CT-DAP using the Atomic Cryptographic Entity Generative Framework (ACE-GF) and evaluate performance, demonstrating sub-second activation latency with configurable security-performance trade-offs.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ZK-ACE: Identity-Centric Zero-Knowledge Authorization for Post-Quantum Blockchain Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Post-quantum signature schemes impose kilobyte-scale on-chain artifacts. Verifying them inside ZK circuits merely relocates the cost via expensive lattice arithmetic in prover circuits.
  We present ZK-ACE (Zero-Knowledge Authorization for Cryptographic Entities), which replaces transaction-carried signature objects with identity-bound ZK statements. Given a deterministic identity derivation primitive (DIDP) as a black box, the prover demonstrates in zero knowledge that an identity consistent with an on-chain commitment authorized the transaction; no signature object is produced or verified on-chain.
  We provide game-based definitions and reduction-based proofs for authorization soundness, replay resistance, substitution resistance, and cross-domain separation, under knowledge soundness, collision resistance, and DIDP recovery hardness. Structural data accounting shows an order-of-magnitude reduction in per-transaction authorization data versus direct PQC deployment. A reference implementation offers two backends: Circle STARK (341 active rows / 361 AIR constraint expressions, 14.5 ms prove, 1.1 ms verify, approx. 107 KB proofs, transparent setup, post-quantum-oriented) and Groth16/BN254 (2,155 R1CS constraints, 37.3 ms prove, 128-byte proofs). Both are roughly 500--2,300x smaller than in-circuit PQC signature verification. Under mandatory per-block STARK aggregation, per-transaction consensus-visible data is approx. 160 bytes.

Security & Program Analysis.title: ACE-GF: A Generative Framework for Atomic Cryptographic Entities
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Autonomous digital entities require deterministic identity mechanisms that avoid persistent storage of high-value master secrets, while supporting credential rotation and cryptographic agility across heterogeneous systems. Existing deterministic key hierarchies and centralized key management systems typically rely on long-lived root secrets, introducing structural single points of failure and complicating lifecycle management.
  We present ACE-GF (Atomic Cryptographic Entity Generative Framework), a seed-storage-free identity construction that enables deterministic and context-isolated key derivation without storing any master secret at rest. The construction reconstructs an identity root ephemerally in memory from a sealed artifact and authorization credentials, using misuse-resistant authenticated encryption together with standard key derivation primitives. Derived keys are generated via HKDF with explicit context encoding, ensuring cryptographic isolation across curves and application domains.
  This design naturally supports stateless credential rotation, authorization-bound revocation, and non-disruptive migration toward post-quantum cryptographic domains. Furthermore, the framework's parametric agility allows for optimization in resource-constrained environments, ensuring that deterministic identity reconstruction remains viable across a spectrum of hardware from high-performance servers to low-power IoT nodes without compromising the underlying security model.
  This work builds upon the conceptual framework introduced in MSCIKDF, which identified the core design goals for multi-curve, context-isolated, PQC-pluggable identity but did not provide a concrete construction. A formal protocol specification of ACE-GF has been submitted as an IETF Internet-Draft.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee.
  In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph.
  Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs.
  Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Bounding the security of the FALCON signature scheme in the quantum random oracle model
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In 2016, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) announced their invitation for proposals of public key encryption and signature schemes that are resistant to attacks by quantum computers. Since then, several rounds of proposals and revisions have occurred resulting in the 2022 announcement that three signature schemes - CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ - would be standardized. However, in 2024, work by Fouque et al. noted an oversight in the published security for FALCON, which they were only able to remedy in a classical computing setting, namely the random oracle model (ROM). In this paper, we provide the first complete security proof for FALCON in the quantum random oracle model (QROM). Specifically, we will prove a reduction to the security of FALCON from the ring inhomogeneous short integer solution (RISIS) problem and the NTRU learning problem utilizing known quantum reprogramming results. We then provide parameter sets which meet the security levels required by NIST under our reduction.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Detour Is the Danger: Preserving Security During LLM Agent Recovery
Security & Program Analysis.summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools and reusable Skills to execute complex workflows, autonomously replanning when operations fail. However, such recovery may preserve task functionality while silently discarding the security protections required by the original workflow. In this paper, we investigate workflow security downgrade, a failure-induced security threat in which agents execute sensitive operations without satisfying their original protection requirements. Unlike prompt injection, this threat exploits autonomous recovery decisions triggered by execution failures, without modifying instructions or tool definitions. We systematically evaluate this behavior through fault injection in an executable MCP/Skill environment spanning seven LLMs, twelve task templates, and three security-sensitive domains. To address this threat, we propose ARGUS, an obligation-preserving recovery framework that combines resource-bound security evidence, isolated recovery-plan validation, and execution-time enforcement. In a separate 864-run evaluation, ARGUS prevents all observed protection-loss events under enforcement, while recovery assistance yields model-dependent improvements in protected task completion over blocking alone. Our findings demonstrate that secure agent recovery requires preserving security obligations across workflow changes, rather than merely restoring task functionality.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Small Leaks Sink Great Ships: Automated Analysis of Protocols That Tolerate Low-Entropy Keys
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Modern cryptographic protocols such as WPA2-PSK, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Bluetooth Classic (BC) tolerate low-entropy keys for user-friendliness, backward compatibility, or resource-constrained deployment, yet existing symbolic protocol verifiers rely on the perfect-encryption assumption and therefore cannot reason about brute-force attackers. Prior work addresses this gap only through protocol-specific, manually encoded reveal rules, which neither generalize across protocols nor systematically explore compound-key decomposition. We introduce the first protocol-agnostic, automated symbolic methodology for low-entropy keys, built on three abstractions: the message-derivation fact MDerive, which captures brute-force prerequisites independently of concrete function symbols; a three-tier breaking-oracle design (value-breaking, relationship-breaking, message-derivation) that composes with the standard Dolev-Yao attacker; and a graded bit-level attacker model that bounds the key length an attacker is allowed to exhaust. We realize the methodology as EntropyVerif, a syntax-sugar extension of Tamarin that requires no kernel modification. Using EntropyVerif we automatically rediscover the PMKID, KNOB, and Method Confusion attacks, and uncover a new attack on BC which we call the Unilateral Multi-Downgrade (UMD) attack: by repeatedly downgrading one side of a BC session and recombining the recovered key fragments, an attacker reduces session-key recovery against devices using the maximum 128-bit key from $2^{128}$ to $n \cdot 2^{128/n}$, bottoming out at $2^{12}$ for $n=16$---a factor of $2^{116}$ reduction that has been responsibly disclosed to the Bluetooth SIG. Across three real-world protocols and six BC device configurations, our results show that entropy-aware symbolic analysis is both feasible and necessary.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: DexLink: Synthesizing Dexterous Behaviors from Chained Hand-object Poses
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Synthesizing diverse dexterous manipulation policies is challenging: existing simulation-based approaches rely on human demonstrations which are difficult to scale, or use generic reward functions, which provide limited control over the hand-object interactions. We propose DexLink, which addresses these limitations by synthesizing diverse dexterous behaviors from sparse, reusable hand-object interaction templates. Given key task waypoints, DexLink retargets static interaction templates to target objects using an optimization that preserves spatial hand-object relationships. It then links the retargeted poses into an approximate reference trajectory and uses residual reinforcement learning to refine this reference into a closed-loop policy in simulation. Experiments spanning single-hand, bimanual, articulated, and dynamic tasks demonstrate that DexLink provides fine-grained control over task timing, grasp types, and high-level execution. The modular interaction templates transfer reliably across object scales, instances, and categories; without object-specific human demonstrations, the framework also matches the performance of dense reference-tracking methods. Finally, zero-shot deployment of policies trained purely in simulation shows promise for the simulation-based framework.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: One Ocean, Many Tasks: A Data-Grounded Simulation Suite and Benchmark for Marine Robotics
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Memory Is Not Ground Truth: Revising Navigation Authority under Unreliable VLM Evidence for Persistent Semantic Navigation
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Cairn: Object-Centric 3D Trajectory Priors for Steering Frozen VLAs
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are capable low-level controllers, but they tie where objects go to the layouts they were trained on: when objects are moved or obstacles block the way, they carry them to the wrong place or into collisions. Fine-tuning on new layouts needs robot data for each one and erodes skills the model already has. We introduce Cairn, which keeps the VLA frozen and steers it at test time along learned 3D trajectories of the object in its gripper. A small prior reads point clouds of the scene and the held object, along with its pose when grasped and the instruction, and samples SE(3) trajectories up to its release that lead it around obstacles and turn it to fit through gaps. The prior and the VLA form the two levels of a hierarchical planner in which feedback runs both ways: the VLA's intended motion chooses and reshapes the trajectories, and the chosen one guides the VLA's denoising. Its predicted actions, mapped to the held object's poses through the grasp, are pulled toward the next waypoint, while the VLA's weights stay untouched. Across 1,941 held-out LIBERO scenes with displaced objects and obstacles, Cairn raises the success rate of a frozen π0.5 from 24.5% to 95.1%, above that of a π0.5 fine-tuned on our training layouts, without hurting standard LIBERO. On the third-party LIBERO-PRO benchmark, it raises success from 27.3% to 38.0%, and from 54.4% to 81.1% on the episodes it steers. On a real Franka, with a prior trained purely in simulation, it guides the frozen DROID π0.5 around an obstacle and to a placement at the limit of the arm's reach, where it otherwise fails. All code, models and data will be made public.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Scalable Low-Cost Laboratory Automation: A Digital Twin-Integrated Robotic Platform for Autonomous Liquid Handling (RAINBOT)
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Laboratory automation accelerates discovery, yet its adoption is constrained by the high cost, proprietary design, and limited remote supervisability of commercial liquid-handling systems. This work presents RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM}, a low-cost, openly reproducible liquid-handling robot built by converting a consumer-grade Cartesian 3D printer (Elegoo Neptune 4 Max). The printer extruder is replaced by a precision single-channel pipette actuated through the printer's own G-code-driven X--Y--Z gantry, with plunger and tip-eject motions effected by two compact linear actuators under Python control. To make experiments transparent and remotely supervisable, a browser-based digital twin is implemented to synchronise bidirectionally with the physical platform, mirroring kinematics and pipetting states in real time and exposing remote monitoring, intervention, and an emergency stop from any web browser. As a proof of concept, RAINBOT\textsuperscript{TM} performed sequential exchanges of differently coloured aqueous solutions while an integrated colour sensor quantified the resulting mixtures; measured red, yellow, and blue (RYB) responses agreed with expected mixing behaviour to within a mean absolute error of two percentage points, validating correct execution and real-time tracking. Closing the loop, the platform is coupled to the CEID\textsuperscript{TM} (Cooperative Explorer for Inverse Design) framework, which recasts experimentation from iterative manual guessing into a goal-directed inverse-design search while keeping a human in the loop. The complete hardware costs under US\$1300, which is roughly an order of magnitude below entry-level commercial handlers, thereby establishing an accessible physical--virtual framework for self-driving laboratory automation.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: FineDex: Bridging Fine-Grained Human-Object Interaction Generation to Dexterous Humanoid Manipulation
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and human-object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with articulated objects. To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin. By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining, FineDex generalizes across fine-grained instructions and object configurations. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous manipulation success, and successful deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Failure Detection for Surgical Robot Imitation Policies via Flow-Matching World Modeling
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Imitation learning has shown increasing promise for autonomous robotic surgery, yet safe deployment remains challenging due to the safety-critical nature of surgical tasks and the complexity and variability of surgical environments. Failure detection is therefore an essential safeguard, but its development remains difficult due to the challenges of scarce failure data, highly variable manipulation dynamics, and the need to balance missed detections against disruptive false alarms. To address these challenges, we introduce FoMo-FD (Flow-Matching World Model for Failure Detection), a failure detection method that learns nominal short-horizon visual dynamics with an action-conditioned flow-matching world model. FoMo-FD scores the inverse-transport nonconformity of observed endpoint latents, enabling window-level detection of deviations from learned nominal dynamics without requiring failure demonstrations. Detection thresholds are obtained by conformal calibration on successful policy rollouts, yielding task-specific alarms without assuming future failure types. We evaluate FoMo-FD on four surgically relevant manipulation tasks with twenty failure modes across simulation and real-robot experiments using the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). In the wrist view, the main model achieves a 95.6% failure detection rate (FDR) at a 2.5% false alarm rate (FAR), exceeding the FDR of the evaluated observation-based, action-based, and vision-language baselines and alternative scores from the same world model. Across four training seeds, mean wrist-view FDR and FAR are 93.4% and 4.7%, respectively. Online replay yields a mean onset-relative detection delay of 0.98 s for wrist-view failures detected offline. Project website: https://janusmaple.github.io/FoMoFD/
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Revised following peer review. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: RePace: Reasoning about Demonstration Speedup for Faster Vision-Language-Action Policies
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Since vision-language-action (VLA) policies can inherit the slow pace of human demonstrations, accelerating these demonstrations before fine-tuning can lead to faster VLA policies without an additional speed-selection module at deployment. Several offline speedup methods have focused on identifying segments that require less precision and assigning predefined speedup factors to the segments. However, even within a single segment, a speedup factor suitable for steady motion may be too high when precise alignment is required. To this end, this paper presents RePace, an offline reasoning framework that determines how much to accelerate each part of a demonstration. For the same recorded movement, RePace measures how much each candidate speedup factor shortens the sequence and compares the resulting observation-action pairs used for training. Given the task instruction, a pretrained language model uses the visual context and original motion of successive windows to interpret these candidate retiming effects and select a speedup profile for the complete episode. Experimental results demonstrate that RePace outperforms the baselines in overall task execution efficiency on both LIBERO and RoboCasa-Kitchen. On all three tasks with a gripper-equipped Franka Research 3 arm, RePace matches or exceeds the acceleration baselines in success rate and completes successful trials faster.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Real2SimLab: A Unified Platform for Real-to-Simulation Transfer
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Real-to-simulation transfer, which builds simulations from real-world observations, has long been studied in research and industry. Recently, coding agents have become capable of generating simulation programs from video recordings, and several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate them. However, each individual benchmark defines its own inputs, deliverables, and scoring pipeline. This leads to $N \times M$ integrations when evaluating $N$ methods on $M$ benchmarks. To this end, we present Real2SimLab, a unified platform for real-to-simulation transfer. It evaluates a method by running its written program and scoring the output simulation with the original scorer of each benchmark. Moreover, Real2SimLab provides a pipeline to create training data and reward annotations for real-to-simulation methods. Our pipeline carefully avoids data contamination by filtering out the video recordings that exist in benchmarks. For each video recording, a program is first produced, and then our pipeline computes its reward with the same code that Real2SimLab uses for evaluation. So far, it supports 47 coding agents and 5 non-agent methods on 6 benchmarks. Both the platform and Awesome-Real2Sim, our research map of nearly 300 real-to-simulation papers, are open source, and we invite the Real2SimHub community to build them together.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: T-Tac: A Soft and Thin Active Thermal Tactile Sensor for Robotic In-Grasp Material Identification
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Accurate material identification is important for robotic manipulation, yet vision-based methods face challenges when materials have similar appearances. Herein, we report T-Tac, a soft, thin, active thermal tactile sensor that identifies materials through their transient thermal responses. T-Tac integrates a polyimide film heater with an ionic conductive film temperature sensor, providing controlled thermal excitation and resistance-based temperature measurement in a film assembly suitable for mounting on robotic grippers. Single-sided transient plane source modeling and finite element simulations relate the thermal response to material thermal properties, while calibration and repeated measurements characterize the heating and sensing performance. Loading experiments at room and elevated temperatures further characterize the sensor response under an applied force. A hybrid classification framework concatenates extracted thermal descriptors with multiscale convolutional neural network features and uses an ExtraTrees classifier for material prediction. Experiments on 12 materials achieve a mean classification accuracy of 92.69\% using a 3 s heating pulse and a 10 s observation window. These results support T-Tac as a compact approach to integrating active thermal material sensing into robotic end effectors. This work shed a light on the new approach for robotic material identification.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Safety-Critical Formation Control of Non-Holonomic Multi-Robot Systems in Communication-Limited Environments
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: This paper proposes a decentralized estimator-based safety-critical controller for formation control of non-holonomic multi-robot systems operating without inter-agent communication. Each follower reconstructs its predecessor's motion with a closed-form estimator and applies closed-form control barrier function (CBF) based laws that are robust to the resulting estimation error, enforcing collision avoidance and prescribed longitudinal and lateral formation offsets without online optimization. Lyapunov analysis establishes exponential convergence of the estimator under constant predecessor velocities and input-to-state-type ultimate boundedness under time-varying motion, from which the estimation-error bounds used by the robust CBF constraints are derived. The longitudinal spacing policy is shown to be L2 string stable under an explicit gain condition. Simulations and Gazebo experiments demonstrate accurate formation tracking, safety preservation, and disturbance attenuation.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Multimodal agents can now control robot arms by calling tools and writing code. Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).comment: Project page: https://changxuanfan.github.io/RoboTeam/ . Code: https://github.com/changxuanfan/RoboTeam . 20 pages, 22 figures, 12 tables, including appendix

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Toward Agentic Robotics: A Large-Scale Study of Harness Design for Robot-Use Agents
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can act as robot-use agents that understand diverse scenes and control robots through policy code and tools. However, they predict 3D gripper poses poorly even with extended reasoning, struggling with precise manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action (WAM) models are the opposite: they execute fast, smooth control on trained tasks, yet fail under domain shifts or when tasks require long-horizon memory and reasoning. Agentic robots therefore combine VLM reasoning and perception with precise VLA/WAM control through a policy harness. Yet harness design spans thousands of configurations, shifting success by tens of points with the same models. Moreover, testing even one design takes thousands of rollouts at high API and GPU cost, so prior works often commit to a single design chosen from few alternatives. To guide harness design, we evaluate over 470,000 rollouts across eight simulation benchmarks, six VLMs, and 15 VLA/WAM checkpoints. Seven controlled studies show effective harnesses must adapt to both VLM and VLA/WAM capabilities. Our findings specify what structure the VLM's policy code needs, where VLA manipulation needs help from tools and policy code, and when to involve the VLM at test time. The reference recipe X-Harness shows that these findings compose without weight updates, lifting base policies up to $+42.8$ points across memory, reasoning, and domain shifts.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Anytime-Valid Sequential Verification for Sensing-Efficient Robot Navigation under Perception Uncertainty
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: When a robot navigates an unfamiliar grid, noisy sensor readings can make it hard to tell whether the cells along its next move are free. Additional scans can reduce that uncertainty, but a fixed scan count spends the same sensing effort at every position. In a static-grid simulation, a sequential rule uses a Gaussian likelihood ratio to determine when the cells newly covered by the robot's footprint have enough evidence of free space. On 324 held-out scenarios from 18 public maps, the sequential gate and a four-scan reference chosen on validation data both completed every mission without an observed collision. With their respective validation-selected routing weights, the gate averaged 123.15 scans per episode versus 224.13 for the reference, a reduction of 45.05% (95% map-stratified bootstrap interval: 42.21--48.95%). In a retrospective check on the same scenarios with routing weights held equal, the reductions were 43.91% and 43.37% at the two tested weights, with all missions completed. On 216 scenarios from 12 previously unused maps, allocating more of the same certification error budget near the initial start--goal rectangle cut the sequential gate's scan count by a further 11.58%. The spatial variant completed 206 missions versus 208 for the original gate and increased computation time. The collision bound depends on the assumed observation model and footprint geometry. In a stress test with persistent per-cell bias, the original gate completed 0 of 54 missions.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).comment: Accepted at the HOUR workshop, WACV 2027 (non-archival). 16 pages (4-page main paper, references, supplementary material), 9 figures, 22 tables. Divyansh Pandey and Shubh Garg contributed equally

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: ELMO: Emergent Representations In Imitation Learning Via Dynamic Hierarchical Action Chunking
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Robot trajectories naturally decompose into variable-length phases with distinct semantic intents, such as reaching, grasping, and lifting. However, training policies to minimize MSE treats all actions as equal, obscuring their semantic structure. While latent action models attempt to create a structured prediction target by compressing action chunks into latent representations, existing approaches rely on two-stage training and context-blind decoders. Consequently, their representations are context-agnostic motion codes (e.g., "move down") which fail to capture behavioural intent (e.g., "pick up the block"). To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce the Emergent Latent-action MOdel (ELMO), an end-to-end framework that encodes robot trajectories as grounded semantic codes -- representations that ground task-level behavioural intent in the current environment. ELMO jointly trains a VLA planner and an observation-conditioned decoder over dynamically chunked trajectories, learning a semantically grounded action space without separate pretraining. Across standard benchmarks, ELMO outperforms comparable prior methods by 9.6 percentage points on LIBERO-Plus and by 0.75 in average task length on CALVIN. Furthermore, on Blocks -- our shortcut-free simulation and real-world generalization benchmark -- ELMO reaches a 38.6% success rate while all baselines remain below 5%, demonstrating its ability to capture the semantic structure of demonstrations. Website: https://uoft-isl.github.io/elmo.github.io/

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Was the Model Given the Right Action? Auditing and Repairing Action Interfaces in Navigation World Models
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: World models are evaluated by predicting future observations from actions. These evaluations assume that actions are prepared the same way as during training, but an unchecked mismatch can make a model appear less accurate than it is. We audit this assumption in Navigation World Models (NWM) and find three interacting differences between its training and rollout code. Correcting the inputs, without retraining, reduces mean visual prediction error by 42%, measured with DreamSim on the RECON navigation dataset. The correction also changes the ranking of NWM checkpoints in an exploratory analysis and removes or reduces two alternative models' measured advantages. Correcting only the normalization offset instead increases error, showing why interacting mismatches must be checked together. To test whether sensitivity to input preparation extends beyond NWM, we deliberately introduce encoding errors into two alternative models; both become less accurate. We introduce ActRosetta, a tool that checks whether action encoding matches training, identifies supported causes of disagreement, and repairs inputs when sufficient information is available. Repair helps little where predictions barely respond to actions, the tool's diagnosis has limited coverage, and improved control remains unproven. For any action-conditioned world model, the lesson is the same: before reporting rollout error, verify that evaluation encodes actions exactly as training did.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding, language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes, while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution feedback to guide subsequent planning. In simulation, self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. We also evaluate history-dependent real robot tasks with human-reviewed harness corrections. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for history-dependent robotic manipulation.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Realizability Is Not Enough: Encoding, Liveness, and Auditing of Synthesized Robot Supervisors
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary:
High-level robotic supervisors coordinate asynchronous capabilities through their reported outcomes, such as success or failure. Building on our earlier capability-based synthesis framework, we present the complete architecture, implementation, and formal foundations of an open-source pipeline for generating executable Robot Operating System (ROS) 2 Flexible Behavior Engine (FlexBE) supervisors. The pipeline integrates capability-based Generalized Reactivity (1) (GR(1)) specification generation, assumption analysis, reactive synthesis, strategy auditing, behavior-preserving state reduction, and controller realization.
  We evaluate enumerated and one-hot encodings and two liveness formulations in six comparisons across four domains, with additional PiHawk quadcopter flights. Under the tested backend, enumerated encoding usually synthesizes faster, although fewer propositions do not reliably predict smaller controllers or binary decision diagrams. Within the tested budget, only System-Goal without pending memory yielded executable controllers under both encodings across all six comparisons. Fair-Outcome with pending memory can yield realizable strategies that enter cycles from which the configured goal is unreachable. These failures show why realizability alone does not establish deployment readiness. The auditor checks for protocol violations, deadlocks, and goal-unreachable traps. For the tested backend and models, we recommend pairing enumerated encoding with System-Goal without pending memory and auditing each extracted strategy before realization.
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).comment: 92 pages, 14 figures. Includes detailed technical appendices and experimental results for four application domains

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions.
